Don’t tell me they finally broke up. Rumour has it Sarah saw them arguing in the library yesterday. Apparently, he was looking at other girl's Instagram. Classic Liam. Drama, drama, drama. I swear, their on-off relationship is more complicated than the plot of a Shakespeare play. Seriously? That’s awful for Maya. She’s been really into him. I feel bad for her. He’s such a wally anyway.

Honestly, Daniel, I feel like a right mess. This cold's taken me completely by surprise. One minute I was fine, the next I was battling a head cold that could knock out a rhino. You do look a bit peaky, love. I’ve already made you some honey and lemon tea. It’s not much, but it’s soothing. You sure you haven't got something worse than a cold? Remember that dodgy prawn sandwich you had last week? Don’t even remind me! I nearly ended up glued to the loo for a full day. I thought it was just the sandwich at first, but now I’m wondering if this cold's got something to do with it. It's just… relentless. Ugh, food poisoning and then a cold. Double whammy. It's possible. Sometimes a weakened immune system is enough to just let everything in. Have you had your flu jab this year? Nah, I keep meaning to. Always saying I’ll do it, but then something else pops up. Work’s been mental, and honestly, the thought of queuing in the pharmacy just… drains me already. Especially when I'm feelin' like this. You really need to prioritise it, Maisie. Honestly, it's a simple thing that can prevent weeks of misery. Especially with all the research you’re doing, you can’t afford to be knocked out like this. Aye, I know, I know. It's just, hospitals give me the willies, you know? All those… germs. And the fluorescent lighting. It's enough to make anyone feel ill just walking through the doors. You’re such a drama queen sometimes. It’s just a quick jab. But seriously, look after yourself. I don't want you laid up for weeks. I was hoping we could finally watch that documentary about AI body language recognition tonight. Remember? Oh, aye! The one about spotting deception? That sounds fascinating. Although, knowing my luck, the AI will diagnose me with some obscure tropical disease. Don’t be daft. It's about subtle cues, microexpressions, not exotic illnesses. It's amazing how much you can tell about someone just from their posture and eye movements. I was reading a paper the other day that… Hold on, hold on. My head’s startin’ to throb again. All that technical talk is too much for a poorly lass. Remember Lloyd Grossman?

“Q… U… E… U… E.” Honestly, this board is mocking me. Queue? Seriously? Who needs to spell 'queue' in a Scrabble game? It's Manchester, not… well, it’s everywhere! "Bit dramatic, love. It’s a seven-letter word, worth a decent amount of points. Besides, you were complaining about needing a 'Q'." He places “ZEAL” across the board. "There you go. Seventeen points. Still behind, though." "Don't be so quick to gloat, Alistair. Zeal is a rather ambitious word for a Tuesday afternoon. And you’ve left me a lovely 'S' to work with.” She adds "SYSTEM" to the board. “Much more reliable, wouldn't you agree, dear?” “My dear Margaret, you always were a stickler for the sensible. Zeal is important, of course, but a solid system… now there's something to be admired. Reminds me of running a boarding school, you know. A rigorous timetable, clear expectations... everything in its proper place." He adds "PAINT" alongside a pre-existing word, securing a good score. "Oh, for goodness sake. You two are conspiring, aren’t you? System? Paint? It’s like you’re deliberately trying to make me feel inept. I'm just trying to remember what I was going to make for dinner. I was thinking that lamb shank recipe your mother used to do, Margaret, with the rosemary and garlic…" "Lamb shanks are a good shout. Though, getting them will be a nightmare. That butcher’s on Wilmslow Road had a queue stretching down the street earlier. Absolute gridlock. I was trying to pop in for some sausages, but gave up. Ended up with chicken, which isn’t quite the same.” "Gridlock? Honestly, the M56 is better than Wilmslow Road on a Saturday! I remember when we used to drive to Edinburgh for Christmas, Alistair. It was an adventure then, not a trial of patience. Though your father always insisted on stopping for scones every single time." "Indeed. Your father did have a fondness for a good scone. Though he'd argue it was more about supporting local businesses. He was a firm believer in that, you know. Said it instilled a sense of community." “Speaking of community, did you see Brenda posted a picture of her cat wearing a tiny hat on Facebook? Honestly, some people have too much time on their hands. Though it did get a lot of likes. I should probably try posting something.

Oh, my aching back! Another pile of flyers sorted, thank goodness. Bit of a scorcher today, innit? Makes the dahlias wilt, it does. You managing alright, Arthur? You look a bit flushed. Perfectly manageable, Margaret. Just a little warmer than I'm accustomed to. Though, compared to the humidity I encountered in Frankfurt… that was something else entirely. Reminds me of a rather unfortunate incident with a printing demonstration. Frankfurt, you say? Fancy! You were over in Germany then? I always did fancy a bit of a trip over the Channel. Never quite got around to it, though. Too much to tend to here, you know. The gallery and all. Oh, yes, regularly for years. Primarily for the Drupa exhibitions. You wouldn't believe the scale of those things. Miles and miles of machinery, flashing lights, the whole shebang. We were pushing our new automated plate-making system – called "ChromaFlow," rather catchy, don't you think? – back in the early nineties. Marketing it to the big European players. ChromaFlow… sounds right clever. You invented that, did you? Goodness, you always were a clever one, Arthur. I remember hearing snippets over the years, bits and pieces about printing systems. Never fully understood the details, mind you. Always been more of a visual person myself – colours, textures… a nice bit of pottery, that’s my thing. Well, I didn’t entirely invent it, of course. It was a collaborative effort, a team. But I was instrumental in the early development and particularly in the marketing strategy. That was my forte, really. Figuring out how to present something complex in a way that everyone could understand – and want. It's surprisingly similar to selling a painting, I suppose, isn't it? Making people see the beauty, the value. Aye, there's something in that. Painting, pottery, printing… all about appealing to the eye and the heart. Though I suppose your work was a bit more… technical. Did you get a good reception over there in Germany? Immense. Absolutely immense. Initially, quite a bit of skepticism, naturally. The Germans have... certain expectations. Precision, reliability, efficiency. They don’t take kindly to things that don't deliver. But when they saw ChromaFlow in action, producing high-quality plates at speeds they'd never thought possible... well, they were converts. So, you made a splash, then? You could say that. Led to a rather amusing situation, actually.

Are we nearly there yet, Dad? My back’s killin’ me. Nearly? Nah, love, we've still got a good few hours. Try and be patient. Cornwall’s waitin’, ya know. Besides, I need a brew. See that sign up ahead? Services in a mile. Fancy a pit stop? Aye, a brew sounds good. And a toilet break. Honestly, this journey’s makin' me realise how much I miss comfortable chairs. Did Mrs. Davies give us back our essays yet? The ones on Chaucer? Chaucer, eh? Bit of a dusty fella, that. Never saw a decent chippy in his life, I reckon. And no, haven't heard anything about the essays. You nervous about them? A bit. She's been bangin' on about "historical context" and "deep analysis." It's just, like, old poems, Dad. Why do I need to deep analyse them? Should’ve just stayed with Shakespeare. At least he had some proper drama. So, about uni… still thinkin’ about that Philosophy course at Manchester? I do, lass. You’ve got a good head on your shoulders. Philosophy’s not for everyone, mind. Lot of thinkin’ involved. But you've always been one for a good debate. Remember that argument we had about whether pineapple belongs on pizza? Oh God, don't remind me. Mum still brings it up. Anyway, it  doesn't  belong on pizza. It's an abomination. But seriously, Philosophy. Is it… useful? Like, will I get a job afterwards? All my mates are doing more practical stuff – nursing, teaching… Useful is a funny thing, isn't it? Being able to think critically, to question things... that’s useful in any walk of life. Besides, you're clever enough to graft and find somethin' afterwards. Plenty of people with Philosophy degrees do well. Just gotta find your niche. It's about understanding the 'why' of things, not just the 'how'. Ever heard of 'quinoa'? Quinoa? That weird grain thing? Mum keeps trying to get me to eat it. Exactly! People go on about how healthy it is, but I’ve never tasted anything so bland. It's like eating cardboard. Someone explained to me recently how the word comes from a Quechua word… fascinating really. Language is constantly changing, isn’t it? Like "literally". People use it to mean "figuratively" now! Drives me mad. Tell me about it! And the spelling of "Worcestershire". How’s even  that  a word?

Right then, nearly ready for this ratatouille. It’s a bit fancy for a Tuesday, innit? But ANON reckoned it was summery and lovely. Reckon it'll be alright, though. I'm usually better wi' a proper roast, if I'm 'onest. Yorkshire puddings, gravy... proper grub. Fancy for a Tuesday? You're calling layered vegetables fancy? You’re the one who booked a falconry display for a corporate event last month, remember? Aye, but that were for millionaires, weren't it? This is just… well, it’s not chips and beans, is it? Be honest, will you try it? Don't be makin' a face at me later. Ratatouille, eh? Sounds French. Is it proper healthy, then? My stomach’s been a bit off lately. Everything seems to sit heavy. Aye, it’s meant to be good for you, Grandad. Loads of veg. Maybe you shouldn’t have had so much of ANON's fruitcake earlier, though. Fruitcake's good for the soul. Doctor said I need to keep my spirits up. Besides, it was delicious. ANON makes a proper fruitcake, she does. Better than my Margaret ever could. You're always comparing ANON's baking to Margaret's, Grandad. Poor Margaret. She’s been gone twenty years. Twenty years and still not a fruitcake that comes close. Anyway, this ratatouille... does it need much salt? I’m watching my sodium, you see. Bloated as a pufferfish, I am. Just a wee bit. It’s already got flavour from the tomatoes and herbs. Listen, Grandad, are you still seeing that nurse, Sarah? She seems a lovely lass. Sarah's alright. Keeps me regular, she does. Reminds me to take my pills. We play whist on Tuesdays. She’s not bad at it, but I beat her most of the time. Keeps her on her toes, that. Beating a young nurse at whist? You're a legend, Grandad. Don't you start. I've still got it, you know. Learned it from my dad. He was a dab hand at whist. Used to play down at the pub every Friday. Proper Friday night ritual it were. My grandad used to take us to the races every Sunday. Doncaster. Loved a good bet. Always swore he was going to win big and buy a proper sports car. Never did, mind. Ended up with a Ford Cortina. Bet your mum still talks about those races.

Right, so, update. My mate Liam finally managed to parallel park without hitting a bin. Took him, like, five attempts, but he did it. Progress, eh? That’s brilliant! Liam’s driving is legendary, isn’t it? My sister had a similar experience. She reversed into a lamppost last week. A small one, thankfully, but still. It’s a surprisingly stressful skill, isn't it? Seriously! I mean, I’m alright, really. Did a bit of driving during uni, got myself a decent feel for it. But still, parallel parking...it's the bane of everyone's existence. You ever find it easy? Not easy, no. More… manageable, after a lot of practice. I did a defensive driving course a few years back. Waste of money in some ways, but it did drill some basic techniques into me. You should look into one, honestly, if you’re worried about Liam or even yourself. It focuses on spatial awareness and hazard perception, which helps. Defensive driving, eh? Sounds a bit intense. But yeah, Liam might benefit. He's got the theory down, understands the rules of the road, it's just… the practical application. Still, I’m practically glued to this pub these days, training for the regional cocktail competition. Oh, really? That's exciting! Which cocktails are you focusing on? I always admire bartenders. It’s more than just pouring drinks, isn’t it? It’s the presentation, the flavour combinations... it’s an art form. It is! It’s mad how much there is to it. At the moment, I’m working on a twist on a classic Negroni - using rhubarb gin, which apparently adds a lovely tartness. Then I’m tackling a passion fruit and cardamom sour. Bit risky, but I think it could be a winner. The competition’s next month. Nerves are kicking in, big time. That sounds amazing! Rhubarb gin… clever. I'm always so impressed by people who have a creative head for food and drink. My creative energy is mostly poured into finding palatable ways to explain the subjunctive mood to teenagers. Oh, don't even get me started on teenagers! My younger sister’s just started A-levels. The drama. It’s a constant stream of angst and exam stress being relayed to me. What do you teach, exactly? French and Spanish, mostly. Years 10 to 13. It can be… rewarding, when they actually engage.

This coffee’s a bit weak, isn’t it, Margaret? Not like that stuff Doreen makes down at the community hall. Proper strong, that is. You know Doreen puts a whole teaspoon of instant in hers, Arthur! It’s practically sludge. And don’t start complaining, I’m late already. Fiona’s expecting me for a bit of a natter, remember? Had to pop round here first to see you, love. Fiona’s pressed for time tonight, I believe. Fundraising committee meeting, isn't it? Lots of banners and bake sales to organise. Must be a headache. Banners! You know, I was thinkin' about those banners for the bell ringers. Something a bit brighter than the usual green, don't you think? They’re always lookin’ a bit drab, bless their hearts. Arthur, you’re brilliant! A nice bright yellow, maybe, with a big picture of a bell? People would notice that! It’d be much better than those faded green ones. It’s about visibility, isn't it? They need to be seen. Though, are we sure that’s the best use of funds currently? I was looking at the accounts last week, and we’re still short on that donation box for the Gambia project. Gambia, eh? Fancy goin' all the way to Gambia. Never been further than Skegness in me life. Seems a long way. It is, Arthur. Sarah’s friend’s brother, he volunteers over there. Said it’s lovely, but they’re desperately short of everything. That’s why we should really get this donation box sorted. Something proper, y’know, not just an old biscuit tin. Precisely. I was thinking a clear acrylic one, with a secure lock. Professionally made. We could even get it engraved with the charity’s name. It looks more trustworthy. Trustworthy… that’s a good one. You know, reminds me of something I read. About that fella... what was his name… the one that pretended to be ill all the time. Munchausen, wasn’t it? Oh, Arthur! Don’t start talking about that now. It's dreadfully depressing. Poor man, really. Munchausen Syndrome? You mean factitious disorder, presenting with a simulated illness? It  is  a rather unsettling condition. A complex psychological disturbance, really. It begs the question of why someone would construct a false reality like that. Well, I don't rightly know  why . Just seemed right strange, the way he'd go 'round tellin’ folks he had all sorts of ailments.

Honestly, this TikTok algorithm is  broken . It keeps showing me videos of people unboxing succulents. Succulents! I haven't shown any interest in succulents in my life. Maybe it’s picking up on your vaguely plant-related Pinterest board from, like, five years ago, Liv? You did have a phase with macrame plant hangers. That was a  very  brief phase, Ben. And it was about the aesthetic, not the plants. This is different. I’m being targeted by a botanical invasion. What about you? What’s your algorithm decided you need to see? Mine’s clearly decided I need more aggressive marketing for yoga retreats. Like, I did one yoga class six months ago in Cornwall, and now my entire feed is downward-facing dogs and chanting. It’s hilarious, and slightly annoying. You guys are lucky. Mine is solely focused on lads with questionable haircuts and even more questionable fashion choices. It's… lacking in quality. I swear, half of them look like they got dressed in the dark. Okay, let's change the subject before I start feeling existential dread about the future of social media. Did you guys see ‘Smile’? ‘Smile’? The horror movie? No, is it any good? I'm in the mood for something genuinely terrifying. Oh my god, Ben, yes! It was brilliant! Properly unsettling. I actually had to sleep with the lights on for a night. The ending… wow. I won’t spoil it, but be ready. I’m not sure I can handle that level of terror. I think I’ll stick to something lighter. Maybe a rom-com? After the disastrous date I had last week, I need something fluffy and predictable. A disastrous date? Tell me everything! Who was it, and what happened? Spill the tea! It was… Mark. You know, the one Sarah set me up with. He spent the entire evening talking about his cryptocurrency investments. Like,  non-stop . And he kept gesturing with his fork, threatening to stab the pasta. Stabbing the pasta? Seriously? I’m not exaggerating! It was so awkward. I ended up pretending I had a family emergency and scarpered. Oh, poor thing! Sarah really needs to get her matchmaking skills checked. You dodged a bullet there, Sophie. Cryptocurrency and aggressive cutlery? Not a good combo. Definitely. At least you have a good story to tell. Speaking of stories, remember last summer when we went to Italy?

That’s a sad-lookin’ little thing, innit? Proper state it is. Used to be a lovely colour, I reckon, but the sun’s got right to it. Makes you wonder how young ANON manages to get about in that. Ah, don’t you fret about it, Arthur. It gets ‘em from A to B, don’t it? That's all that matters, really. Remember old man Perkins’ Austin Allegro? Now  that  was a sight. Square as a bleedin’ box and clunkier than a barge. Couldn’t get a decent turn outta it. You two and cars! It's always the same. Honestly, I’m just glad to see you both. It’s been a few weeks, hasn't it? Such a lovely drive over from Harrow. Though, the M11… don't even get me started. Absolute chaos. Harrow, you say? Is that still chock-full of those… those bypasses and roundabouts? They build more every time you blink. Makes a civil engineer like me shudder, it does. All that concrete… a complete waste, some of it. Not properly thought out, not like when  we  used to design things. Aye, Arthur's right. Used to be a road was a road - straight as a die mostly. Nowadays, you're weaving and dodging like you’re in a bleedin’ maze. And the speed limits! Utter nonsense. You’re sounding like my father, Bernard. Always complaining about the roads. Honestly, at least it keeps you busy. Speaking of getting home, what are your plans for this evening? I'd hate for either of you to miss the last bus. The last bus? Cor, you’re a worry, Diana. I wouldn’t trust those buses anymore. They’re always late, or they cancel 'em at the last minute. Used to be regular as clockwork, back in the day. Now… it’s a lottery. I’m just thinking about a taxi, I reckon. Bit pricey, mind you. Taxi? Fancy that! I’ll be walking, Arthur. Always have. Fresh air does a feller good. It’s only a couple of miles, isn’t it, from here to Costessey? Bit of a stroll will settle me. Though, it's gettin' dark earlier these days. Bernard, are you sure about that walk? It will be quite dark by the time you leave. And with all those new estates being built... More traffic, less pavements. Diana's got a point, Bert.

Honestly, this M6 is a beast. I thought moving south would mean fewer lorries, but it seems they all funnel through here. And the rain! It’s coming down sideways. Tell me about it. Glad we left when we did, though. Wouldn't want to be stuck in this in the dark. How are you feeling about the move, Mum? Still a bit daunted? Daunted is putting it mildly, love. Thirty years in that little house in Dublin, and now I’m uprooting everything. It’s… a lot. Packing up all my books, especially. Each one has a memory attached, you know? The old calculus textbook Mrs. O’Malley made me buy… the well-worn copy of Wuthering Heights I read over and over as a girl… You’ll make space for new memories, Maggie. That’s the point, innit? New books, new favourite corners to sit in. You’ll be overlooking a garden this time, not a grey Dublin alley. Easy for you to say, Barry. You didn’t spend half your life surrounded by those books. And gardens are lovely, yes, but I'm worried about the maintenance! Trying to keep up with the weeding... it’ll be another thing to feel like I’m failing at. Mum, stop. You’re not going to fail. I’ll come visit and we’ll do the weeding together. And even if the garden is a complete wilderness, so what? It’s  your  wilderness. Remember that trip to the Lake District? The one where we ended up hiking through that overgrown path and got completely lost? We laughed for hours. Oh, goodness, yes! Your father was furious, though. Claimed we were deliberately trying to ruin his holiday. Honestly, he was so particular. He just worried about things. Always did. Still, the view from the top of that fell was worth it, wasn’t it? Made my knee ache for a week though! I’m glad we went, though. That was last year, wasn't it? Feels like a lifetime ago. My knees are reminding me of it every day now. Have you been doing your exercises, Dad? The physio gave you those to do, remember? Aye, sporadically. They’re a bit of a bore, to be honest. Prefer sitting with a cup of tea and a crossword. Much more stimulating. You and me both, Barry. Although, I do miss marking papers. Strange, isn't it?

Honestly, Mum, it’s just so annoying. Like, seriously, who steals a bike? It wasn't even a fancy one! Well, apparently, someone with questionable morals and a bit of a sticky finger, love. But don't worry, I have good news. Remember how upset you were about your bike being nicked? Yeah, obvs. My life was basically over. Can’t get to college properly without it, you know? And it was my birthday present! Right, well, a neighbour, Mrs. Higgins - you know, the one with the prize-winning roses? - she called earlier. She’d seen a group of lads pushing a bike that looked exactly like yours down towards the seafront. She recognised it because she’d seen you riding it last week. Seriously? They were pushing it? Did she get a proper look at them? Were they, like, wearing hoodies or something? Not really, no. She just said they looked a bit shifty, to be honest. Anyway, she called the police, and they managed to track them down near the pier. Turns out, they’d been trying to sell it. No way! They were going to  sell  it? That’s so mean! Did the police catch them? They did. It’s amazing, really. They brought your bike back. It's in the shed, all locked up tight. A bit muddy, but otherwise fine. They've taken the lads in for questioning. Apparently, they’ve been causing trouble around here lately, petty theft and that sort of thing. You're joking! Seriously? Mum, that's incredible! I can’t believe it. I was starting to think I wouldn’t see it again. Can I go look at it now? Please? Hold your horses, love. Finish your tea first. It’s raspberry and chamomile, your favourite. And yes, you can go look. But promise me you’ll lock it properly this time. Learn from this, yeah? Okay, okay. Lesson learned. But seriously, how did Mrs. Higgins even recognise it? She's got such good eyesight. Maybe I should follow her around and get her to spot things for me on TikTok. Imagine the followers! "Rose-Loving Neighbour Spots Criminals – Follow Me for More." It'd be a viral sensation! Don’t you start, Amelia. Exploiting Mrs. Higgins for social media fame? That’s a new low, even for you. Speaking of social media, have you been looking at the college open days again?

Right, I’m officially declaring Cardiff my next destination. No arguing. I need to own that route. Alright, alright, you South African strategist you. Just don't expect me to hand you the key to the Principality Stadium. You've been ruthlessly efficient all afternoon, honestly. My trains are still scattered across the Midlands like fallen dominoes. Efficient? You mean monopolising the grey routes, Elara. Leaving the rest of us to fight over the blues and yellows. It’s hardly fair play. Fair play? Rhys, darling, this is  Ticket to Ride . Fairness went out the window the moment we started laying tracks. Besides, someone has to control the industrial heartland. Speaking of heartlands, is anyone else absolutely ravenous? I swear, all this strategic train placement is burning serious calories. I could murder a proper Welsh rarebit. Now you're talking, Mairwen! A proper one, none of this grated cheese on toast nonsense. Back in my day, a rarebit was a thing of beauty. Double Gloucester, a hint of mustard, and a good soak of ale… glorious! Grandad's going full Welsh culinary history again. We’ll need to find a decent pub around here then, likely that will be our main focus for tomorrow’s lunch! Although, having said that, I did pack a few welsh cakes … Welsh cakes? Rhys, you know those are best fresh from the griddle, not transported across England in a plastic container. Better than nothing. Though, truthfully, I miss Mamgu's. She could make Welsh cakes that practically floated off the plate. Remember that time she accidentally put chilli powder in them, though? Oh, good heavens, yes! Uncle Gareth nearly choked! His face was bright red for an hour afterwards. He claimed he was experiencing a sudden heatwave. Ah, those were the days. Mamgu always had a flair for the… unexpected. While you’re reminiscing about culinary mishaps, I’m going to consolidate my dominance here. Rhys, are you going to challenge my claim on Birmingham, or are you just going to admire my strategic genius? Alright, alright. But don't come crying to me when the London to Edinburgh line proves unexpectedly tricky. You’ve been so busy building a nexus in the Midlands, you’ve completely neglected the north. Actually, I’ve just managed to snag a route to Glasgow. Looks like  someone  might be in trouble. You wouldn't dare, Rhys! That’s cutting me off from Scotland entirely!

Right, that’s it. I’m officially declaring war on Baltic Avenue. Honestly, it's the most strategically placed piece of property on this entire board. It’s just… unfair. Unfair? Or brilliant? You’re just intimidated by its efficient revenue stream, darling. You’re too busy trying to monopolise the light blues. A bit predictable, aren't you? Predictable? I’m being pragmatic! The light blues offer a faster return on investment early on. You’re just hoping to bleed me dry with those utilities! It’s a long game, Liam, a  long  game. And I’m playing the long game perfectly, thank you very much. Besides, you spent all your money buying up Reading and a single orange. You’re practically begging for me to land on the Electric Company. That's because your rent on Light Blues would have just wiped me out! It’s a calculated risk. A  necessary  one. Don’t pretend you haven't been banking on my desperation for ages. So, about this game… Monopoly is honestly a fascinating microcosm of, well, everything, isn’t it? The ruthless capitalist drive, the way fortunes can change in a single dice roll... It’s practically sociology in board game form. Absolutely. And the weird cultural obsession we have with property, particularly in a game like this. It’s extraordinary, isn't it? You’d think we’d have evolved past this frantic pursuit of owning everything. And the drinking culture it encourages! My dad used to insist on a pint with every roll of the dice at Christmas. Said it was crucial for strategic thinking. Oh, he sounds delightful. My mum just swore and threatened to flip the board. Though, I do remember a particularly boisterous game of Monopoly at Auntie Brenda’s wedding – fuelled entirely by Prosecco and aggressively competitive cousins. It ended with Uncle Geoffrey flipping over the Chance cards. Sounds textbook. It's odd, isn't it? We tolerate, even  encourage , this level of intense pressure and sometimes outright aggression, passively, over a plastic game. It's not like people get genuinely upset when they lose a football match to the same degree they get upset when they go bankrupt in Monopoly. Exactly! It's the perceived fairness of it all, I suppose. The dice are random. It  should  be down to chance. But then, you spend ages strategically building houses, negotiating trades… it transcends pure luck.

Honestly, the bins are a nightmare here. Kerrie’s bins are TINY. Back in Germany, we had huge ones, you could practically throw a sofa in. And the collection days... I still haven't fully grasped the system. Do they collect recycling on Tuesdays? Or is that Fridays? My brain genuinely short-circuits. It's Tuesdays for blue bins, recycling. Green bins are Thursdays for general waste. Kerrie's probably got a point about the size, though. Peterborough bins were pretty decent. You get used to it, though. What about the washing machine? Did you manage to get that sorted? You mentioned it making a noise like a dying walrus the other day. Dying walrus is a very colourful description, dear! Though I can picture it. Kerrie, you should call that repair bloke, Gareth. He's family friends, bit rough around the edges but knows his stuff. Fixed my fridge when it started making a similar racket. Saves you a fortune going through those big companies. Gareth, okay, I’ll make a note. Kerrie, thank you! It’s just… everything’s new, isn’t it? The house, the bins, the washing machine... and trying to navigate the NHS. I booked that doctor’s appointment, you know, for the persistent cough. The waiting list is ridiculous. Yeah, the NHS is… a process. It wouldn't hurt to get a private consultation if you're really worried. Just a thought. Though, knowing your luck, the private doctor would tell you it's just post-nasal drip. Very funny. But seriously, it’s unsettling. You realize how reliant you are on a system when it’s clearly struggling. I was reading something the other day about the funding cuts... It’s all a mess, isn’t it? When I was training, the NHS was… well, still had its challenges, but it felt more robust. Now… it’s just stretched so thin. I’m glad I finished my accounting qualifications when I did. Got me through a few recessions, that degree. You always were the brains of the operation, Aunty Moira. Me? Sixth form and a vague ambition to “coordinate things.” That’s how I ended up here, apparently. Project Co-ordinator. Sounds grand, doesn't it? Mostly it's Excel spreadsheets and chasing people for updates. Don't sell yourself short, Liam. Coordinating is a serious skill! I mean, I spend half my day just trying to keep the admin side of things at the office from completely collapsing.

Blimey, Mum, this traffic is mental. Seriously, I thought the A12 was bad, but this… this is something else. Feels like we're moving at a snail's pace. Tell me about it, love. Shouldn’t have left when we did. Should’ve waited another half hour. It's always like this on a Saturday. People heading up north, I suppose. Don’t start sighing, though. It only makes it worse. And please, no driving commentary. I'm doing my best here. This old thing isn't exactly a sports car, you know. Right, right. Sorry. Just saying, you should really think about getting something a bit newer. Electric, maybe? Less hassle, better for the environment... And quicker. Imagine whizzing past all this. Electric? Don't be ridiculous. I like my petrol car. It's reliable, I know it inside and out, and it has character. Unlike those soulless, silent EVs. Besides, where would I put my books? This boot is  just  big enough as it is. Speaking of which, are you still planning on bringing all those TLS submissions with you? They’ll take up half the car practically. Yeah, yeah, they're in the rucksack. Need to drop them off before I meet Liam. It’s the deadline, you know. Reckon I’ve got a chance this year? Last time was brutal. Got knocked back for, like, stylistic inconsistencies. What does that even  mean ? TLS? Honestly, darling, that's a world unto itself. Those judges… they're looking for something… elusive. Don’t get disheartened, though. Your writing  is  good. You just need to… refine it. Perhaps lose a bit of the London slang? They’re terribly traditional. Easy for you to say, you’re practically one of them! Editing literary giants all day, surrounded by first editions... Must be a total dream job. I bet you’ve got loads of fascinating stories. Remember that time you met…? Later, love. Later. Right now, I have to concentrate on avoiding this lorry. Honestly! Driving becomes such an endurance sport. I swear, people have no patience anymore. I saw a bloke give someone the finger just because they slowed down to let a pedestrian cross. The absolute audacity! Road rage is getting worse every year. Proper mental, innit? Should we give them a wide berth? Yes, dear. Absolutely. Just… don’t start offering your unsolicited driving advice. Remember when you used to tell me how to parallel park?

Right, right, so then the donkey  actually  bit him! Like, a proper chomp! Not a little nibble, a full-on, “I’m fed up with tourists” bite. Poor Uncle Barry, he was screaming fit to burst. No way! Uncle Barry? The man who can barely handle a plate of chips without complaining? A donkey took him on? Oh, I want to hear this! Where were you all? Greece, last summer. We were at some little farm thing, supposed to be a ‘traditional Greek experience.’ It was… definitely an experience. The kids loved the donkeys, obviously. Uncle Barry, however, decided he needed a selfie with one. Didn't read the signs about respecting the animals, did he? Aye, men and their selfies, eh? Always trouble. You know my cousin tried to take one with a sheep in the Lake District. Ended up being chased halfway up a fell! You lot are a menace on holiday. Always causing chaos. Remember that time Lewis tried to steal a coconut in Tenerife? Oh, Lewis and his coconuts! That was a classic. He swore he was being robbed if he didn’t buy one. Security nearly had to arrest him. It was brilliant! Honestly, the look on his face when he realised he'd been caught... priceless. He tried to argue it was a cultural misunderstanding! "They’re trying to trick a tourist!" You always did have a knack for getting into scrapes, Lewis. What about your incident with the paella? Don’t even  mention  the paella. I thought I was being clever, adding extra hot sauce. Turns out, it was ghost pepper hot sauce. I spent the rest of the week… indisposed. Let's just say the hotel staff learned my name very quickly. You’re a legend, Lewis. Honestly. I've no holiday stories to rival that. My worst was spilling gravy all over a very serious German gentleman during a formal dinner. He was not amused. Gravy, eh? That’s a bit tame. Uncle Barry's donkey bite is a far better story. It's got drama, it's got livestock, it's got a man in deep distress! It's got Uncle Barry! That’s the best part. He’s still blamin’ the donkey, you know. Says it has a vendetta. A vendetta! Oh, he’s unbelievable. So, anyone else got any holiday disasters to share? I went to Amsterdam last year and managed to get locked in a canal-side coffee shop for a solid hour.

Right then. So, Alistair was saying he’s been – what was it, Fiona? – 'winter wilding' recently? Sounds positively barbaric, doesn't it? Though, I suppose you young folk are all about pushing boundaries these days. Don't be such a stuffy old dear, Richard! It's not barbaric at all. It’s… invigorating. Alistair’s been raving about it for weeks. Though, I’ll admit, the thought of it myself...well, my knees aren't what they used to be. Besides, a warm bath is my idea of a perfect evening. Not freezing my bits off in the Highlands. It's more than just freezing, Mum. It’s about a connection, you see. A real connection with the land. Being exposed to the elements, reliant on your own skills...it's profoundly grounding. And the skies! You’ve never seen stars like it, not in a city. Pure, unfiltered. Grounding, is it? Reminds me of my rambunctious nephew who decided to live in a yurt for a year. Ended up with a rather nasty case of hypothermia and a hefty dry-cleaning bill. Though, I suppose that was more about artistic integrity than…communing with the heather. What exactly  do  you do, Alistair? Just… stand there and shiver? No, Richard. It's planned, obviously. Good gear is essential – proper sleeping bag, four-season tent, insulated clothing... We track the weather meticulously. It's not about suffering; it's about responsible engagement with a powerful environment. We spend time observing, tracking animals - I've seen red deer in full rut, even though it was January. Listening for birdsong, even in the snow. It’s remarkably quiet, once you get used to it. I can imagine. It must be good for the soul, in some ways. I mean, my work – nursing and therapy – it's all about the internal landscape. But sometimes, you need a visceral jolt. Something to clear the head completely. I always found that with a good hike, but...snow and ice? Exactly! It strips away all the nonsense. You focus on the immediate – staying warm, finding shelter, making a fire. There's a simplicity to it. And the mental resilience you build... it spills over into every other aspect of your life. I found my anxiety levels have plummeted since I started doing it. Mental resilience, eh? One might argue the resilience required to tackle a crossword puzzle on a frosty morning is quite sufficient, thank you very much.

Honestly, Liam, you wouldn’t  believe  the day I’ve had. The database just decided to throw a tantrum. Three hours I spent battling SQL queries like me life depended on it. Seriously, I'm feelin' like a right daft lass, grappling wi' technology that's got a mind of its own. Sounds about right. Tech having a personality crisis. At least you're good at wrestling them into submission. What were you working on today specifically? Something new? Nah, routine stuff, mostly. Just cleaning up some inconsistencies in the tagged data for the historical fiction corpus. You know, those bleedin' Victorian novels all full of 'thee' and 'thou'. It’s like, nobody just said 'you' back then! Gives me the heebie-jeebies, it does. Though, I did stumble across a passage in a novel about a Sunderland shipyard worker from 1910. It were proper evocative. Reminded me o' me grandad's stories, actually. That's fascinating. So, what was the passage about? Don't leave me hanging! And didn't your grandfather work in shipbuilding too? Aye, he did. It described the smell of the place - the coal smoke, the tar, the saltwater. And the sheer, relentless noise. Said it were like a beast roaring all day long. Proper gut-wrenching, it were. It made me think about how different life was back then, you know? No computers, no internet, just hard graft and a wee bit of hope. It's easy to forget. We live in such a curated, digital world now. Speaking of different worlds, have you seen anything good at the cinema recently? I was thinking of catching Dune: Part Two – everyone’s raving about it. Dune? Nah, not yet. Too much sand for me, I think. Sci-fi's not really me usual cup o' tea, to be honest. Give me a good Agatha Christie any day. Murder on the Orient Express, that’s the ticket! Proper suspense, it is. Full o' twists and turns. You and your mysteries! You’d be brilliant as a detective. Though I suspect examining database errors would give you all the deduction you need. So, Christie...that reminds me. I've been trying to re-read ‘The Name of the Rose’ by Umberto Eco recently. Struggling a bit though. It’s just… dense. Eco? Aye, I tried reading that years ago. Gave it up. Too much Latin, weren’t it?

Right then, sleepyheads. Let’s finish our story about the grumpy badger, shall we? He was still fuming about the missing blueberries, wasn't he? Yes! And he stomped his little badger feet! Stompy badger! That’s right, a very stompy badger. Now, he was about to complain to the squirrels… but then, what did he see? A rainbow! Close! He saw something much more interesting… a tiny little typewriter! Right in the middle of the forest floor. Have you ever seen a typewriter, love? No. Is it like a computer? Well, sort of. It’s… older. Before computers, people used to write on these. Clack, clack, clack! . They’d have to put in a ribbon and everything. It's quite clever, really. I used one once at a museum. Smelled all dusty and old. Clack, clack! I like! You would! It’s a bit noisy. Now, back to the badger. He was so surprised to find a typewriter, he forgot all about his blueberries! He tried to type a letter… but he didn't know how! Let me try! Clackety-clack! “Dear Squirrels, I like blueberries!” Very good! But he wasn’t very good at it at first. He kept hitting the wrong keys. And then… he saw something else. A little pile of Excel spreadsheets! Ex-zell? What's that? It’s… a grown-up thing. It’s for making lists and numbers… like scoring in a game. You know how you keep track of your Lego scores, darling? I get 10 points for a red brick! Exactly! Excel is a bit like that, but on a computer. It helps people keep track of lots and lots of things. The badger was very confused. He just wanted his blueberries! Maybe he could type about blueberries in Excel? Then he’d remember! That’s a brilliant idea! See, you're much smarter than a grumpy badger. Now, before we finish the story, did you have fun at Brownies last night? Did you all renew your Promise? Yes! I said it loud! I had to stand very straight. Mrs. Peterson told us to. Good for you, both! It’s important to remember our Promise. It’s about being kind and helpful. Speaking of helpful, you both were very helpful letting me finish my work on Excel earlier today! I had to sort out the budget for the school trip. Not nearly as exciting as a stompy badger and a typewriter, I can tell you.

Honestly, David, you look like you’ve wrestled a badger. Is that… corduroy? And are those trainers? For breakfast at my house? Well, now, Brenda. Don't be harsh. It's comfortable, isn't it? And I did have a rather early start. Those roadworks on the M62 are a nightmare, you know. Added almost an hour to the journey. Aye, tell me about it. I was listening to the radio this morning - they're saying it’ll be like that for another six weeks. Six weeks! Madness. More toast? I made a fresh batch. With that lovely plum jam, remember? The one from Farmer Giles’ – he's got a cracking crop this year. Plum jam sounds delightful. Yes, please. Giles’ plums are always top-notch. Reminds me of when we were kids, and families used to pick their own. Went to a farm just outside Windsor once, proper sprawling place with acres of orchards. Felt like something out of a children’s book. Ooh, orchards. We used to go to Thorp Fruit Gardens near here. Not quite acres, mind, but enough to keep the bairns entertained. Though, you know, it's all changing around here. Developers are tearing up fields left, right, and centre. Sometimes I drive around and I swear there's nothing but new builds. Makes you think about all the history that’s been lost. It’s a tragic loss, that is. You know, researching for that reservoir project near Skipton, I stumbled across the remains of a deserted medieval village. Proper ghost town, it was. Just foundations and the odd bit of pottery sticking out of the ground. Imagine living there, all those years ago. What happened to ‘em? Disease, famine, war…probably a bit of all three. Creepy, that. Though, on brighter notes, I’ve been trying my hand at growing herbs. Rosemary, thyme, even a little lavender. It's surprisingly therapeutic, getting your hands dirty. Though the slugs are having a field day with my parsley. Basil? Are you growing basil? Excellent choice. That’s brilliant with tomatoes. You know, I always thought people got a bit precious about growing vegetables. Seems like it's all become a trendy thing, doesn't it? For old folks, like us! Aye, well, being "old" has its perks. We can do what we want! Although, speaking of old, did you hear about Mrs. Higgins down the street?

Right then, that’s a decent cuppa. Blimey, this Christmas madness is exhausting, isn't it, David? I'm absolutely knackered. Had Mrs. Higgins on again today, bless her. Forget her meds, she did. Nearly had a right paddy. Tell me about it, love. The department's been mental. Everyone’s off with the flu or trying to cram everything in before the holiday. Had to practically wrestle young Peter away from his desk – he was determined to finish that quarterly report  on Christmas Eve . Honestly, some people. Ugh, Facebook is just a nightmare right now. Everyone’s posting their perfect Christmas trees and perfectly-behaved children. Makes you feel a bit rubbish, doesn't it? I've almost deleted the app. Oh, don't you start, Maisie! Don't let those lot get you down. They just show what they  want  you to see, innit? Remember Auntie Carol's supposed 'relaxing' spa weekend? Spent the whole time arguing with her sister about who got the bigger cucumber slices! True enough. People put on a show. Speaking of cucumber slices, have you lot tried that new facial scrub from Boots? Sarah recommended it - apparently, it works wonders for dry skin. Really? My skin’s been awful lately. All flaky because of the central heating. Is it expensive? Because I'm trying to be sensible with money after that trip to Barcelona. Got stung with baggage fees, you wouldn't believe. Barcelona, you say? Fancy! Always wanted to go. Lovely place, apparently. Although, honestly, I'm happy with a bit of the coast here. Brightlingsea's always been a favourite. Peaceful. Anything’s better than ending up on a ward with a screaming three-year-old who thinks nurses are a type of magical creature. You cope with that, love? You're a saint. I still can't believe you managed to convince little Timmy that you were a fairy godmother who could heal his boo-boo. Needs must, doesn't it? Gets you out of a pickle sometimes. Though Mrs. Peterson’s nephew, who's visiting her, was giving me the eye. Dreadful man! All stares and comments about needing someone to "look after him." Honestly! Gave him his pills and pointed him towards the newspaper. Sorted him right out. You're incredible! Uncle David, are you still planning on getting that ridiculous star projector for the living room? You were talking about it last week.

Honestly, this rain is mental. I swear, London’s just permanently drizzly now. Feels like November already, and we’re barely out of August. Tell me about it. I came all the way from Oxford, thinking I'd get a bit of sunshine before I have to head back and start my dissertation properly. No such luck. Still, nice to be out of the library, eh? And good to see you, Liv! It feels like ages. It has! Life's been a bit… chaotic, to be honest. Work's been absolutely manic. This new client, 'Bloom & Bud', they're a florist, and they want all their ads to sound like whispered poetry. Whispered poetry! It's exhausting trying to come up with evocative descriptions of lilies when all I can think about is how much I need a decent coffee. Whispered poetry about lilies. Sounds… challenging. You’re a trooper though, Liv. Still saving up for that deposit on a flat, I presume? Trying to. It’s like, every time I think I’m getting somewhere, something else pops up. The boiler’s already packed its bags apparently, need to get that sorted. Then there’s Mum... she’s been saying she might need a bit more help around the house. Which, you know, I want to be there for her, absolutely, but it's another drain on the finances. Oh, really? How's Mum doing? Is she managing okay on her own? I remember when she used to take us both to the beach every summer. Those were good times. Yeah, she's mostly alright, a bit slower than she used to be, you know? She's started forgetting things, and it's just… worrying. She’s put off getting anything looked at, stubborn as an ox, she is. Typical Mum. But I'm trying to gently suggest she sees the doctor. That's tough. You're a good daughter, Liv. Speaking of family, how's your brother, Ben? Last I heard, he was still chasing that dream of being a professional gamer. Don't even get me started. He's convinced he's on the verge of something big, you know? Keeps saying “just one more tournament” is all that stands between him and being a sponsored streamer. I'm pretty sure he survives on instant noodles and sheer optimism. Sounds about right. Well, at least he's passionate about something.

Honestly, Eleanor, this place is lovely. You’ve really made it your own. Much more… you, than that sterile box you had in the city. Well, it needed a bit of work, didn’t it? Years of neglect. The previous owner clearly prioritised manicured lawns over actual living space. Though, the lawn  is  rather impressive. Still haven’t mastered the art of mowing it perfectly straight, mind you. Mowing laws? Honestly, both of you. Eleanor, darling, you look exhausted. Did you wrestle a rogue hedge? And Amelia, you're just watching, aren’t you, letting David do all the gardening? Guilty as charged, Patricia. David’s a whiz with the lawnmower. Although, he does get overly competitive with the neighbours. Last week he was muttering about their edging being “sub-par.” It was a perfectly respectable edging, Amelia. Just… not as aggressively symmetrical as mine. Look, about that mowing… It’s not  just  mowing. It's a strategic exercise. Low-impact cardio. Gets the back working. Exercise? From mowing grass? Honestly, David, you invent the most peculiar justifications. I’ve been trying to convince myself that pacing around my study, arguing with characters, is a form of yoga. Now there’s an image! Arguing with characters. You'll be writing a whole other book about that, won’t you? Possibly! It's all research, darling, all research. It’s surprisingly taxing, you know. Far more than building a perfectly straight lawn edge. Though, speaking of taxing, have either of you seen the latest house price reports? Absolutely ludicrous. Don't even get me started. I was looking at properties in the village – just browsing, mind you, purely hypothetical – and the prices are… astonishing. For what? A damp-ridden cottage with a leaky roof? It’s insane. It makes you wonder if you’ll ever see your children own a home. I tell Emily she needs to start saving from birth practically if she wants a shot at anything decent. Honestly, it's a tragedy. My niece, Olivia, is trying to buy a flat in Bristol. She’s a lawyer, earns a decent salary, and she's still struggling to get a mortgage. It's just… unbalanced. I remember when you could buy something perfectly reasonable for the price of a decent car. It's a broken system, that’s what it is. All driven by investors and… well, people with more money than sense, really.

Blimey, look at the size of that thing! Proper Victorian, innit? Never seen so much glass in me life - makes the Baltic Centre look like a shed. It's pretty impressive, isn't it? They've got some extraordinary specimens in here, apparently. Did you know they're trying to cultivate a Wollemi Pine? A what-now? Sounds like somethin' you'd find on a planet in Star Trek. Well, it’s near extinct in the wild. It’s a really rare species. Anyway, enough about plants. You looked a bit stressed earlier. How's the corpus going? Still drowning in tagged data? Oh, you've no idea. It’s mental. They're bringin' in even more historical records. Old parish registers and that. Thinkin' they'll find some hidden language patterns or somethin'. It's like, a librarian’s worst nightmare, multiplied by ten. I spent most of yesterday trying to sort out confusing spellings of surnames from the 18th century. "Smyth" versus "Smith" versus "Smitt"... you wouldn’t believe the arguments people had about it even back then. Sounds... stimulating. Proper forensic linguistics, almost. Civil engineering isn’t always that dramatically frustrating, I’ll give you that. Though, trying to get a particularly stubborn contractor to use the correct concrete mix  was  a battle of wills last week. Aye, I can imagine! So, what are you working on at the moment, then? Still that bridge project down near Ashford? Yep, still battling with the South Downs National Park planning committee. The latest proposal for noise reduction is completely ridiculous. They’re suggesting a ‘living wall’ – essentially, a wall of plants – to absorb sound. As if climbing ivy is going to silence traffic. Honestly! Sounded like tryin' to fill the River Wear with pebbles! They come up with some right crackers, don’t they? Makes me think about this budget announcement coming up. Absolute shambles, I reckon. All cuts here, all increases there. No thought for anyone. It's always the same, isn’t it? They promise the earth during the election and then slash and burn the following year. My dad’s in a right state about it. Small business rates are going up again, apparently. He's been trying to expand his carpentry workshop, but this just… puts a stop to it. Poor lad. Mine's fretting about the energy bills, like everyone else. It’s ridiculous, isn’t it?

Right then, just needs a bit more… warmth, doesn’t it? See how the sun catches it, even on a day like this. Though, honestly, they're threatening rain again, aren’t they? Always threatening. More like moaning about the possibility of rain than actually delivering it, this weather. Aye, spot on, Karl. Typical. Remember that summer of '98? Didn’t see a drop of rain for months. Bloke down the road, Mr. Henderson, he had a paddling pool up all summer long. Kids were delighted. Now, it's like someone's flipped a switch – all drizzle and gloom. Henderson, yeah. He used to tell me about his time in repertory back in the sixties. Said he once played Bottom in  Midsummer Night’s Dream  alongside a woman who went on to be quite famous... Helen Mirren, I think it was. Can you imagine? Little local theatre, and suddenly you're rubbing elbows with a dame like that. Mirren! Blimey. Didn’t expect that. Never knew he had that in ‘im. He was always a quiet fella, Henderson. Did a bit of gardening, mostly. You know, this whole area’s changing, isn't it? All these fancy developments going up. They’re ripping up the old community gardens, putting up those boxy flats. That’s what worries me. Progress, they call it. But it’s just… displacement. Where are these people supposed to go? These gardens were a lifeline for some. It’s not just about growing veg, you know. It’s about connection. About having a bit of green space in the grey. Speaking of grey, I saw something on the news about the new art gallery. Apparently, they’re showcasing a street artist who uses reclaimed materials. Turns discarded scaffolding into these massive sculptures. Absolutely brilliant. Reclaimed stuff, eh? That's the way forward. I’m always rooting around in charity shops and car boot sales. Found a cracking leather jacket the other day. Proper vintage. Paid a fiver for it! Friends of mine were saying, "Why bother, John? Just buy new!" But there’s something about finding a hidden gem, isn’t there? Giving something a second life. Sentimental, I suppose. Absolutely. It’s about appreciating the history, the stories embedded within the object. Like a well-loved book, isn’t it? More character than something fresh off the production line. I’ve been meaning to get round to looking at your painting, John.

Honestly, it’s… uniform, isn’t it? Field after field of, well, nothing much. I was expecting more vibrancy, more… Polish character. Bialka was lovely, all those wooden chalets, but this... this is just green and brown. Aye, it is a bit, innit? But look, there's a village up ahead. See the church spire? That’s a bit more interesting. Poland's a big place, pet. Can’t expect every mile to be a postcard. Besides, we were lucky in Bialka. That was a tourist hotspot. Lucky is one word for it. Overpriced is another. That pierogi place charged me a fortune for what was essentially boiled potatoes and cheese. I could have made that myself for a tenth of the price. Which, thinking about it, I probably  should  have. Expenses are adding up faster than I anticipated. True, true. I reckon we're both eating into our savings a bit quicker than planned. I’m trying to keep track in that spreadsheet, but it's a nightmare. Did you factor in the cost of diesel? Because that’s been a shocker. Oh, don’t remind me. I’m avoiding looking at the fuel gauge. It’s practically a visual representation of my dwindling financial resources. Speaking of dwindling, have you heard from Sarah and Mark? They were supposed to meet us in Krakow. Nah, not a peep. I sent a message yesterday, just to check they were still on track, but nothing back. Probably just busy. Remember how chaotic their wedding was? They’re probably still recovering from that. I’m not holding my breath. Are you gutted if they don't make it? A little. It would have been nice to see them. It does make you think, doesn’t it? About friendships. People drift. Life gets in the way. It’s why I wanted to do this trip, I suppose. A bit of… reconnection. Before I'm entirely swallowed by dust and mothballs back in Cambridge. Dust and mothballs? You’re being dramatic, love! You could declutter that house no end. Remember you were saying you wanted to downsize? You could sell half that stuff and fund another trip! Easy for you to say, Miss Postgraduate Teacher with a sensible career. I’ve accumulated decades of… things. Sentimental rubbish, mostly. Though I did find a rather lovely teapot the other day. It belonged to my grandmother. Sentimental rubbish is the best kind of rubbish, isn’t it?

Are we nearly there yet, Dad? My phone’s got nowt on it, I'm proper bored. Not long now, love. Just gotta get off this roundabout, then it's straight on. Preston’s comin’ up. Right, Eliska, you alright in the back? You were quiet for a bit. Yes, thank you. Just… thinking. This drive is lovely though. St Anne’s is so quaint. Much quieter than Kosice ever was. Remember when I kept trying to convince you all that pierogi were better than fish and chips? Aye, well, pierogi are alright, but they can’t beat a proper chippy. Remember that time I tried to make them, Dad? They were like little doughy bricks. Oh, I remember! Eliska was tryin’ to help, covered head-to-toe in flour. Your mum nearly killed me from laughin’. We ate take-away that night. Those were good times. It's strange how much things change. Remember when we talked about moving back to Slovakia? Now, I can’t imagine leaving England. Especially not now. Dad, have you looked at that new Argos catalogue? Honestly, I need some new stationary for exams. These pens leak, and my highlighters are all faded. It’s a disaster. It's the A-Levels, you know? It makes you think. Aye, I saw it. We'll have a look in Preston. Shouldn’t be a problem. Speaking of things changing, did you hear about that Hay Festival? Fancy going next year, Eliska? You’re always readin’. The Hay Festival? Oh, I used to go with my grandmother when I was little. It was magical. All those books, all those stories… I’d love to go again. Though, with the train strikes going on… travel is a nightmare. Train strikes, aye. My mate, Sophie, missed her History revision session because the trains were all cancelled. She’s proper stressed. They're saying it could go on for ages, innit? Terrible, isn't it? Disrupting everyone's lives. Makes you appreciate just being able to drive, even with me gettin’ on a bit. How are you feeling, Eliska, dear? You seemed a little pale earlier. I’m fine, really. Just a bit tired. It's… It's the weather, I think. And… well, don’t tell anyone, but I think I might be. You might be  what ?! Mum, are you pregnant?! Seriously?! You’re joking, right? You're having a laugh?

Oh, my word. Thirsk. It’s… quaint. Very… quiet. Didn't expect you two to be out having tea. Thought you’d be wrestling with those boxes still. Nan! You scared us half to death! We weren't expecting you today. We were just taking a breather. Cleared out a fair bit of your attic already, though. Mountains of things. Honestly, you’ve been hoarding memories, haven't you? Memories are all I’ve got left, lass. And a few regrets, o’ course. Don’t you go throwing out me old photo albums now, that’s all I'm saying. There's a right laugh in those, you know. Remember that holiday to Blackpool in ‘68? Your Grandad trying to win a coconut? I’ve heard the Blackpool stories, Nan. Loads of times. But you always leave out the bit where he tripped over a seagull. Lewis! Don’t you be telling tales out of school. Your Grandad was a proud man. Some things are best left… romanticised. Honestly, you two! Lewis, go on, tell Nan about that YouTube video you were showing me earlier – the one with the talking cat. It had me in stitches. Right, yeah. It's this one... It's edited, obviously, but it looks so realistic. The cat's doing a parody of a news report. It’s dead funny. A… a talking cat? On that… that contraption? Young people and their… things. Back in my day, if you wanted a laugh, you went to the cinema. Or listened to a comedian. Not this… digital nonsense. It’s changed a lot, Nan. Everything's digital now. It can be overwhelming, I know. But you can find some real gems online, some proper funny stuff. It can be a good distraction, too. Something to occupy your mind. Distraction, eh? That's… that's exactly what I needed. Being cooped up in that flat… it does things to your head, you know. Not like it used to be. Are you alright, Nan? You seemed a bit… quiet when you arrived. Just a bit tired, love. All the travelling. Dizzy spells, though. The doctor says... well, they say a lot of things, don't they? Mentioned something about... 'managing' it. Modern medicine, eh? Not like it used to be. The doctor’s just trying to help, Nan. And we’re here for you. We’re going to make sure you’re comfortable.

Right, so… it's alright, innit? Bit… sleek. Feels a bit… cold, honestly. Never had anything this posh before. My old one was practically held together with duct tape and wishful thinking. Proper dinosaur, that was. Yeah, it's a jump from your old one, Liam. You’ve gone from something that sounded like a jet engine taking off to… well, this. Nice screen, though. What specs did you go for? Looks alright to me. You gonna be able to run Photoshop on it without it turning into a slideshow? That's all that matters, really. Remember when Liam tried to edit photos on that ancient tablet? It took ten minutes to apply a filter. Don’t remind me! It was a nightmare. Yeah, I told them I needed something that could handle Photoshop without wanting to just, like, spontaneously combust. Got a decent graphics card, I reckon. Eight gig of RAM, I think. Not gonna pretend I understood all the techy stuff, you know. Just pointed at one and said, "Yeah, that one looks… expensive enough." Classic Liam. Probably cost you a fortune. Did you get any of that Microsoft stuff with it? ‘Cause you’ll need to upgrade Windows eventually. It’s a pain, but… Yeah, came with the full Windows thing. I'll hold off on upgrading for a bit, will I? See how it runs as it is. Speaking of pains, my neighbour, Mrs. Higgins, she’s got that neighbour from hell situation going on again. Her son’s been blasting that techno music all day. Right, right in your ears. You could hear it through the walls. Oh, Mrs. Higgins! She's always got something going on. Remember when she tried to accuse me of stealing her prize-winning petunias? Said I was lurking suspiciously around the flowerbeds. I remember! You were just admiring them, weren’t you? Anyway, I had to go over and give her a right telling-off. Told her I’ve got better things to do than nick her flowers. Felt a bit bad afterwards, 'cause she's a bit fragile, y'know. Well, you gotta stand up for yourself. Although, maybe suggest to her that her son turns the volume down a bit. Little diplomatic approach. Less chance of a petunia-related incident. Good shout. I'll try that. So, how’s the teaching going, Tom? Any particularly…  interesting  students?

Honestly, darling, I can’t quite believe this is Tarnow. A bistro? With avocado toast? It’s… quite something. Remember when the only place to get a decent coffee was that dreadful little kiosk by the market square? I know, right? It's mad. They’ve really upped their game. It's about time, too. The pierogi are getting a bit monotonous, even for me. Though, I did find a brilliant little shop the other day, just off the main square… selling these gorgeous hand-knitted scarves. Proper woolly, you know? I think you’d love them. Scarves would be lovely. My poor cardigan is looking threadbare, isn’t it? Though I’m trying to… you know… shift the weight. This Polish food, as delicious as it is, isn’t exactly conducive to a trimmer figure. I did try that Zumba class last week, but… well, let’s just say I won’t be winning any competitions. Nearly pulled something. Zumba's brutal! Maybe something a bit gentler? There’s a yoga studio opening up in the centre, apparently. I was thinking of giving it a go. It'd be good to get some proper movement in. Teaching keeps me busy, but it's mostly sitting and correcting essays. Exhausting in a different way, I suppose. It sounds wonderful. Movement… yes. I should probably do something. It’s just… motivation, isn’t it? It’s all so rather daunting. And… feeling like I'm just drifting. Like a leaf. Drifting? You? You always were the most organised of us all. Remember those meticulously planned holidays we used to do before? Everything booked, every minute accounted for. What happened to that woman? Life, I suppose. And… well, you know. The usual. The… It’s hard to explain. It’s like pieces of me have just… disappeared. I hardly recognise myself sometimes. I get it. When I was struggling with uni, and then with applying for jobs... feeling completely lost and like everyone else had it figured out? That’s a horrible feeling. But it doesn’t last, does it? You find your footing again. You rebuild. It's not quite the same, is it? This… this feels deeper. More ingrained. It started with the medication, of course. Trying to… to level things out. And then it just… spiralled. I hate talking about it. I just… I avoid it. You don't have to.

Right, so Dorset Steam Fair this weekend, yeah? It looks brilliant, honestly. All those engines, the crafts, the food… I'm properly buzzing for it. But Dad, have you managed to get us tickets yet? They sold out fast last year, didn't they? Nearly, love. Nearly. Tried online, but the system kept cutting out. Right pain it was. Ended up having to ring ‘em. Got three though, thankfully. Should be here tomorrow. Bit pricey, mind you. Nearly twenty quid each! Twenty quid? Oof. That adds up quick. Still, worth it if you enjoy it. It  is  a lovely day out. Did you remember to check about accessible parking, Liam? Amy’s knees aren’t what they used to be. Aye, spoke to ‘em directly. Got a permit for disabled parking just by the entrance. They’ve got ramps now to most of the areas, and a few designated viewing spots for folks who need to sit down. Apparently, they even have a dedicated welfare tent with chairs and a nurse on hand, just in case. Can’t say I remember that from years ago. That’s brilliant, Auntie Susan! Seriously, good on them. It makes such a difference. I'd hate having to struggle. So, tickets sorted, access sorted… what about food? Should we pack a picnic? It's always a bit of a rip-off at those things. Definitely pack a picnic, Amy. Less hassle, and you know what you're getting. And bring a blanket. Those benches can be a bit hard on the backside. Speaking of hassle… how’s the flat move coming along? Still thinking about getting a removal company? Yeah, I’m seriously considering it. Moving all that furniture up three flights of stairs is… well, it's not ideal. Especially the sofa. It’s a beast! I got a quote from a couple of companies. One was quoted at about £350. Madness, isn’t it? Property prices in this area are just ridiculous. I can't believe someone sold a tiny bedsit for over £200,000. London's even worse, love. Wouldn't surprise me if they were selling sheds for that price these days. Remember when a semi-detached house in Harlow cost you a few grand, Susan? Now... ridiculous. Don't remind me, Liam. Things have changed drastically. £350 for removals isn't terrible, though. It'll save your back, and reduce the risk of something getting damaged.

Oh, this chair's a treat, it is. Much better than that monstrosity at the old place. Though, I do miss the view of the fells. Thirsk's… flat. Terribly flat. Aye, it is a bit different from Kendal, love. But look at the garden! Arthur's put in those lovely lavender bushes you liked, remember? And the roses are already starting to bud. It’ll be blooming lovely in a few weeks. Roses don’t do much for me, to be honest. Instagram’s got way more interesting stuff. Liam Hemsworth just posted a new picture. Liam Hemsworth, eh? Progress, I suppose. At least it’s not just another politician droning on about… well, anything. I saw something on Twitter earlier about a local pottery studio, ‘Clayful Creations’ I think it was called. Apparently, they’re doing workshops. Might be something to write about. Pottery? Hmm. I’ve always fancied a go, actually. Back in university, there was a rather talented potter in my seminar, Archibald Finch. Dreadful name, really, but he could make a teacup that sang, near enough. Used to talk about the theological implications of wheel-thrown forms, you know. The circularity representing eternity, and all that. Only you, Margaret, would find theology in a teacup! You always did have a knack for making things… complicated. Right, young man, put the phone down for a minute. Your grandma's here. What did you learn in school today? Anything exciting? Not really. French test. Failed it. Madame Dubois is being a right misery this year. Says my pronunciation is ‘atrocious.’ Atrocious? That's a bit harsh, isn't it? You've always had a good ear for accents. Remember when you were trying to imitate that Yorkshire farmer we met at the agricultural show? Brilliant! It was funny! But Madame Dubois doesn't think so. She just says I'm disrupting the class. And the rest of French vocab is just ridiculous. "La pomme de terre"? Who needs to know that? You need to learn your roots, dear. Understanding other cultures helps you understand your own. And potatoes are a vital part of civilisation, I’ll have you know! I once met a Belgian agriculturist who swore by them… Okay, okay, Margaret, settle down! We don’t need a lecture on potatoes right now. Your brother's right though, French vocab  is  a nightmare. What about you, John?

Right, so, dentist appointments are booked for both of you. Little ones, you’re in next Tuesday, early. Try and be brave, yeah? No wriggling! But I don't  want  to go! It smells funny. And the chair’s scary. Dentist is boring. Can we go on a school trip instead? Last year we went to that farm and I got to hold a chick! A school trip to the dentist, hmm? I don't think that’s on the cards, love. The dentist is important for shiny teeth. You don’t want a wobbly one, do you? And then you can have loads of Easter chocolate. Really? Lots of chocolate? Even the white one? Even the white one, darling. Though I might hide some of it, you know, for after Easter. Now, speaking of birthdays… we need to start thinking about Leo's. It's coming up so fast. He'll be eight, can you believe it? Can we have a Monet party? Like, with all the water lilies? A Monet party? That’s… ambitious. But I like it! We could get some blue and pink balloons, and maybe print some pictures off. It's rather lovely, isn’t it, Monet’s work? All those colours. Mom, when’s my birthday? Is it before or after Leo’s? Yours is a few weeks after, sweetheart. Remember? The 17th of May. Just after half term. And then, oh goodness, we’ve got Finn’s birthday right after that! Twins, practically. Both born in May and just days apart. It's always a logistical nightmare trying to plan two birthday parties so close together. Finn's having a football party! He's already picked out all the players he wants to invite. He’s obsessed. He certainly is. And look at you two, already thinking of birthdays! So, Ashaad’s friend, Liam – he was asking about your maths homework the other day. Apparently his dad is really good at fractions. Maybe you could ask him for some help? Ashaad says Liam cheats. Does he now? Well, we don’t want to be doing  that , do we? Remember what we talked about? Honest effort. It's more important to understand it than to just get the right answer. Radishes are funny shapes. They’re like little red rockets. They are, aren't they? A little bit spicy too. Okay, dinner’s almost ready.

Right, this is  blessed . Honestly, I'm surprised I managed to get the train back without falling asleep face-first into someone’s shopping bags. Ashford station is a vortex of exhaustion. You look it, love. You massively need a cuppa. Glad you made it though! Mum was starting to worry when the train was delayed. Said you’d be “long lost to the railways.” Mum always does! Honestly, she treats my commute like I’m going on an expedition to the Amazon. It’s just a little hop to London. Anyway, the flat looks lovely! Did you manage to tame the chaos before I got here? Mostly. Jasper was having a field day with the cushions again. He’s convinced they’re his personal jungle gym. See? Little menace. Did you bring any of those fancy biscuits you got from that new bakery near your office? Did I ever! Figured we needed some serious fuel for reunion catch-up. They've got these salted caramel ones that are to die for. Right here. So, tell me everything! Last time I saw you, you were halfway through your placement at St. Luke's. How's the adult acute speech therapy going? Sounds terrifying. It is, some days. Really rewarding though. Just last week, I worked with a gentleman who'd had a stroke – his speech was almost completely gone. We spent weeks doing simple exercises, and yesterday, he managed to say ‘thank you.’ It was… incredible. Emotionally draining, obviously, but brilliant. It’s far more complex than I initially thought. Dealing with families too, you know? Helping them understand the process, supporting them through it... That sounds intense. Far removed from crafting witty ad copy for beard oil. Although, sometimes convincing people they  need  beard oil feels like a form of therapy in itself. Seriously though, that’s amazing what you’re doing. I’m jealous of jobs with actual impact, y'know? My stuff is… cosmetic, by comparison. Don't be silly! Your work is important. You're shaping narratives, influencing culture... It's just… different. Mum keeps asking me if I’m thinking about specialising. Neuro-linguistics, she suggested. Says it's "the future." Oh god, Mum. Always one step ahead of the curve. My Mum keeps asking about dating. Same script, different decade. "Have you met anyone nice, Elara? Don't end up like your Auntie Sheila, living with seventeen cats and a lifetime supply of floral wallpaper.”

It’s funny, isn't it? Thinking back… I remember when I was about ten, my father decided we were all going to cycle to Weston-Super-Mare. The whole family. It took us practically the entire day. We were exhausted, legs aching, but the sheer scale of it… it felt like a proper adventure. No cars then, just us and the bikes and the hills. Do you remember cycling much as children, Arthur? Weston-Super-Mare! Yes, I do. Though my trips were more often to Margate, being from Ramsgate. We'd pile onto a tandem, my brother and I, trying to outpace our parents. Not always a success! Though Weston… that sounds like quite the undertaking for a ten-year-old. You must have been a sturdy little thing. A tandem, you say? Good heavens! Reminds me of trying to teach my students the subjunctive mood – always a precarious balancing act. My own childhood cycling was mostly around Manchester, dodging the trams and the rain. It was a different kind of adventure, I'll tell you. A much grittier one. Cycling. Yes. I suppose I did a bit. More focused on football, myself. Though, that reminds me... When I first qualified as a dentist, the NHS was... well, it was different. The perks were remarkable. You got access to things you couldn't dream of today. Sailing, for instance. One year, they organised a series of lectures – "Lectures all at sea with your oral surgeon!" – aboard a yacht. Absolutely ridiculous, but wonderful. We sailed around the Solent, discussing root canals between gusts of wind. Oh, Arthur, that's brilliant! A lecture on extractions while bobbing about on the waves! You don't get that kind of thing anymore. Though, on a slightly less glamorous note, we did manage a bargain trip to Prague last month. Fifty pounds for flights and two nights' accommodation. Incredible. Prague's lovely, isn't it? Gorgeous architecture. I’ve always wanted to go back. We went years ago. It's changed, of course. More tourists, but still that medieval charm... It's about finding the right time. I find that applies to everything. Getting tickets for the theatre, for instance. We tried for 'Hamlet' last week, completely sold out. But then you ring the box office, explain you're a couple of old codgers and they miraculously find you two seats right in the middle.

Right then, Fiona. So, we've got a good base idea – these moving image case studies, breaking down complex concepts visually for secondary schoolers. But how do we actually  market  this? It feels like a bit of a niche. I think "niche" is an opportunity, actually. There’s a massive push for visual learning now, particularly since… well, you know. Post-pandemic, attention spans are shorter, engagement is harder. Teachers are desperate for resources that are actually going to  land  with the kids. The key is targeting. I was thinking, starting with History – that's always a tricky subject to make engaging. History's solid, yes. But it's also got established players. BBC Bitesize, the Open University… massive content libraries. How do we stand out? We’re not going to have the budget to compete with that. We don’t  need  to compete. We need to be different. Think smaller scale, more focused. Instead of a huge overview of the Tudors, we do a really deep dive into the role of women at court. Using primary source imagery, maybe? Create a mini-documentary style thing, showcasing specific documents and artifacts. Quality over quantity, remember? I like that. A "deep dive" approach. Makes it feel more… premium. More valuable. But that requires a lot of curation. Where are we going to source all that stuff? Copyright is a minefield. That's where my connections come in handy. I've got some contacts at the British Library and the National Archives.
