They might be willing to grant us access to some images, especially if we offer them a mention in our credits - a ‘supported by’ type of thing. Plus, there are tons of public domain sources online we can use. We just have to be meticulous about permissions. Right. Legalities. Always the fun part. You know, I was thinking about social media. LinkedIn seems obvious for reaching teachers, but I'm a bit wary of it. It feels... corporate. It does. It's a bit stuffy. But you can do it right. Building a genuine community, not just blasting out promotional posts. I was thinking Instagram might actually be surprisingly good. Short, visually arresting clips from the case studies. Behind-the-scenes glimpses of the research process. Interviews with historians. Little snippets of what we’re working on. Instagram... hmm. I haven't really considered it. It does lend itself well to the visual aspect.

That was glorious, wasn’t it? The air just… different down there. Salty, clean. Felt like breathing for the first time in ages. Absolutely. Needed that, both of us did. You seemed particularly drawn in though, staring out at the water for ages. Lost in thought? A bit. Just remembering. Do you remember Sarah and Tom’s wedding on the beach in Cornwall? Vaguely. Seems a lifetime ago now, doesn't it? Sunburns and seagulls, mostly what I recall. Did they ever actually get that honeymoon they dreamed of, to the Maldives? No, apparently not. Something about Tom's work going mental. He's been pulling ridiculous hours lately, trying to secure that promotion. Sarah was proper down about it, she'd saved like crazy for years. Remember how she insisted on having starfish decorations everywhere? Of course. She was obsessed. Poor Sarah. Hope she’s coping. Didn’t realise Tom was under so much pressure. She told me last week, during that terribly awkward ladies’ lunch at The Willow Tree. Honestly, the way Penelope prattled on about her new Range Rover... it was practically a competition of who had the most expensive taste. Honestly, I nearly walked out. Anyway, Sarah seemed… brittle, you know? Like one wrong word and she’d just shatter. Penelope, always a delight. Did she even acknowledge Sarah’s situation at all? Oh, she offered a fleeting “Oh, that’s a shame, darling.” Followed by a lengthy monologue about the fabulous upholstery on her new car. You couldn’t make it up. It’s just… frustrating, isn't it? Seeing people struggle, and others being completely oblivious. It is. It really is. Makes you appreciate… well, makes you appreciate the simple things, I suppose. Like a bracing walk by the sea and decent company. Exactly! And a complete absence of Penelope. I was thinking about sending Sarah a little care package. Something to cheer her up. Do you think she'd like that? Definitely. A little reminder that people are thinking of her. What were you thinking of putting in it? I was pondering some Cornish clotted cream fudge – she’s always been partial. And maybe a little aromatherapy oil, something calming with lavender. Something to help her relax when Tom’s being a stress case. Oh, and a good book. Something purely escapist. I was thinking  Rebecca , actually.  Rebecca ! Good choice. Classic. Remember we read that when we first started seeing each other?

Right, look at this frock! Honestly, it’s a bit… much, innit? Like a peacock exploded on it. Much is an understatement, Tilly. It's maximalist chaos. Though, I do kinda like the colour, that electric blue. It’s just… overwhelming. Reminds me of those neon signs in Soho. It's giving me Vivienne Westwood vibes, actually. Early 90s, when she was really pushing the boundaries. It’s not  good , per se, but it's certainly… a statement. Westwood, eh? Didn't she do all them political statements with the safety pins? I always thought that was a bit much. I mean, wearing your politics is one thing, but that was just… uncomfortable looking. It was brilliant, really. Provocative. Started a whole revolution in fashion and culture. This… …this feels more like a student trying to  pretend  to be provocative. True. It lacks the authenticity of Westwood. It’s trying too hard. I’ve been thinking about trying a more deconstructed look myself, though. I was looking at some Simone Rocha designs the other day, and I’m completely obsessed with those ruffled sleeves. Ruffled sleeves? Nah, darlin'. That’s a bit too frilly for me. I like somethin' with a bit of grit, ya know? Like Doc Martens and a good leather jacket. Can't go wrong with that. Keeps ya warm too, which is handy 'round these parts. You lot down south don't know owt about proper cold weather! Oh, we manage. Although, I did buy a rather lovely cashmere coat last winter. Grey, quite classic. Practical, but doesn't scream "I'm freezing!" I need something more… playful. I’m teaching Year 2, after all. Can’t exactly go in looking like I’m attending a funeral. Although, I  did  see a really cute corduroy pinafore dress the other day. Maybe with a chunky knit jumper over the top? Corduroy? Now, you’re talkin'! Proper sensible, that. Reminds me of me mum's wardrobe. Were always fightin' over her corduroy skirts. But a pinafore... that's a clever move. Proper cute. You could pair it with some good chunky boots, like I said. I don’t know… pinafores feel a bit… childish, don't they? For a grown woman? Then again, the whole “grandmillennial” aesthetic is having a moment. My mum’s totally on board. She’s bought like six floral tea dresses. Exactly! It's about finding the balance, isn't it?

Ugh, finally home. School was mental today. Mrs. Davies went on and on about the French Revolution again. Seriously, who needs to know that much about guillotines? Sounds engaging enough! You seemed a bit down when you left this morning. Everything alright? And let me guess, lots of photos taken? Yeah, loads. I was trying to get some shots of the old pier. It’s looking properly derelict, you know? All grey and sad. It felt… dramatic, I suppose. I'm trying to learn about capturing atmosphere, Mr. Ellis said it was key. The pier is sad, yes, but it has a history, a story. That’s what you need to capture. Tell me about the photographs, show me. And biscuits first? Yeah, thanks. Okay, so… Here’s one. Not great, I know, too much light. And this one is blurry. But… What do you think of this one? That’s… really good, actually, love. The way the gulls look like ghosts. It evokes a feeling, definitely. You've got that atmosphere Mr. Ellis was talking about. You’re starting to see things differently. Are you enjoying that photography class? Costs a lot, but I think it’s worth it if you genuinely like it. I do, Mum. I really do. It’s… it’s a way to see the world, I think. Different. It makes me feel a bit less… anxious, actually. Anxious? About what? School? College applications are coming up. Not just school. Everything, I guess. Like… what if I’m not good enough? At photography, at college, at… anything? It’s stupid, I know. It's not stupid at all. Everyone feels like that sometimes. Remember when I was applying for my postgraduate course? I almost didn't go. I was terrified I'd fail, that I'd be out of my depth. But I went, and it was the best thing I ever did. You are brilliant, Lottie. Really. Don't let a little fear hold you back. It’s just… nerves. Easy for you to say. You’re amazing at everything. Oh, heavens, no. I’ve had my share of failures, believe me. Remember that pottery class? My mugs looked like lopsided blobs. And work… it can be a nightmare some days, dealing with grumpy customers and endless paperwork. But you learn from it. You pick yourself up and keep going. Mrs. Higgins called in sick today, her cat had… well, let's just say it involved a vet and a lot of worried phone calls.

Cor blimey, Freelancer, good to see ya. Bit of a kip this place is, innit? Not like my Doris’ place, that was always spick and span. Mind you, she was a whirlwind, she was. Oh, Arthur, don’t be daft. It’s just lived in. And you always say Doris had far too much fussing going on. More like a military operation, that house. Tea, Arthur? And a biscuit? I've got ginger snaps, shortbread, and those chocolate ones you like. Ginger snaps will do nicely, Maureen. Been a long day, a long day. Can’t seem to get a proper shut-eye these past few weeks. Thoughts just keep racin’ round in me ‘ead. This application form, for one. Gadzooks, it’s like somethin’ out of NASA. They want to know me middle name, apparently. Never 'ad to declare that before, did I? Right, hello both! Sorry I’m late, marking essays took longer than expected. Look at this, Freelancer. Printed it on the new printer. A robin. Still needs a bit of sanding down, but it’s the principle. Fancy, innit? 3D printing a bird. Oh, David, that’s lovely! Really it is. It needs a bit of colour, though, doesn’t it? A nice terracotta for the breast. I was thinking about that. I’m playing with different filaments. Listen, Arthur, about that application form. What’s it for, anyway? The council thing? Aye, the council thing. ‘Elpin’ folks in need, they call it. Been multiplyin’ like rabbits, these forms. And the questions… they poke and prod, don’t they? Like a doctor examin’ a dodgy knee. It’s just trying to get a fuller picture, Arthur. They need to know you're eligible. Don't let it stress you. Let me have a look when you're finished and I can spot any obvious errors. You know, I had a right nightmare with Brendan when I was childminding... absolute terror. Climbed the fence and ran off to the shops for sweets, every single day. Little scamp. Brendan, eh? Reminds me of young Trevor down the road. Used to steal apples from old Mrs. Higgins’ tree. Reckon she’s got a right row goin’ on with 'im now. Speaking of which, there’s a blimin’ cockerel next door, keeps me up all hours with its crowin’. Like a foghorn, it is! You’re not alone there, Arthur.

It’s just… a lot to take in, isn’t it, Peter? After all these years. All these years of just… existing, really. And now, suddenly, a whole new life thrust upon me. It is, Margaret. It’s a big change. But a good one, surely? Bringing Amelia home? You've spoken about her for decades. It’s been a primary source of your worry, hasn’t it? The distance, the feeling you were missing out. Worry is… a polite word for it. It’s been a gnawing ache, Peter. And expensive, the transatlantic calls! She always insisted I didn't spend too much, bless her, but still… knowing she was so far away, forging her own life in Canada… it felt… fragmented. Like a piece of me was missing. She’s a strong woman, your Amelia. Made her own way. And she wants to be closer to you now. That speaks volumes. Most young adults, once they've got their feet under them, don't exactly leap at the chance to move back to their mother's. No, she doesn’t. She’s built a lovely life there. A good job, good friends... a fiancé, practically! Though, he doesn't seem overly thrilled about the move, does he? That's another layer of complexity I hadn’t quite anticipated. Men and their… reluctance to abandon comfortable routines. It’s a timeless phenomenon. Don't worry about him too much. Amelia's made her decision. And he'll have to adapt. Easy for you to say, being a retired teacher with a rather tidy pension. It’s not exactly easy for me, Peter, to suddenly become a…a hostess. I used to have a routine, solitary but peaceful. And now? I’m clearing out my spare bedroom, trying to figure out what furniture to get rid of, fretting about whether I can even  afford  adequately sized sheets. I know it's not easy, Margaret. Financial planning hasn’t exactly been your forte. But we’ll navigate it. We'll look at the budget together. I can cover some of the initial costs of furnishing the room, don't worry. And it's not about extravagance. It’s about making her feel welcome and comfortable. That's all that matters. It’s more than just finances, though. It's... the responsibility. Suddenly, I'm responsible for guiding another adult, providing a home, being something other than the slightly eccentric, elderly woman who lives down the street.

Bit gloomy today, isn’t it? Reminds me of a particularly drizzly lecture I gave on Romantic Poetry last week. Students were practically wilting. Brighton always has a bit of a grey cast, doesn’t it? You can't complain, though. Could be Glasgow right now. Been following the fallout from the Scottish referendum discussions. Quite the kerfuffle, eh? Absolutely. It's fascinating, really. Though I’m not sure 'fascinating' is quite the word people are using. The level of division... it's a bit worrying, to be honest. I’m trying to steer clear of social media; it’s all just shouting matches. I know exactly what you mean. The news is bad enough. I was chatting with Mrs. Peterson at the shops yesterday – she's utterly convinced it's going to trigger the collapse of the Union. A bit dramatic, I think, but you can see where the anxieties are coming from. Still, the younger generation seemed pretty split. What's your take, academically speaking? Well, from a political science perspective, it’s a huge case study in nationalism and identity. The emotional weight of it all is hard to quantify, though. I’ve got a few students who are deeply affected, personally. One of them's family is directly involved, you know, on both sides of the argument. It’s tricky to navigate that in the classroom. It must be. Speaking of tricky, how did the interview for the Head of Department position go for you? I heard you were a frontrunner. That’s… complicated. It went alright, I suppose, technically. The presentation seemed to land well. It’s the panel, you know? Always a bit of a minefield. Professor Davies was particularly… incisive. Really drilled down on my experience with curriculum development. I felt a bit like a lab rat under his microscope. Davies, eh? He always was a tough one. Remember when he tried to get rid of the library system back in '98? Said it was “a relic of a bygone era.” Oh, I’d forgotten about that! He was quite the character back then. Anyway, I’m not holding my breath. There’s a rumour they’re seriously considering Evelyn Reed – you know, from the Sociology department? Reed? Interesting. She's got the academic credentials, certainly. But does she have the admin chops? Running a department is a whole different beast from publishing papers.

Right then, let’s see if we can actually make this mousetrap game work. Daniel, are you sure this design is stable? It looks rather precarious. It  should  be, love. I saw a similar one on a workshop online. The crucial thing is the tension on this string. Too loose, and it won't snap back properly. Too tight, and the whole thing will collapse. Leo, could you hold that block steady for a moment? Yeah, yeah. It's boring though, isn't it? Why are we even making a mousetrap game? Can't we just, like, play video games or something? Because it's a challenge, Leo! And it'll be brilliant. Imagine the look on your face when you finally trigger it! Besides, Mum said it’s good to build things, not just stare at a screen all day. Honestly, you lot! A mousetrap game. Just like your grandfather used to make. Remember those, Margaret? Hours of entertainment he got out of us. Though he did occasionally set one off himself. Oh, he did! That was the year he tried to explain the principles of physics using a rogue spring and a strategically placed apple. It ended with him covered in apple sauce. This is slightly more refined than Grandpa’s contraptions, I think. Less… fruit-based mayhem. Though, I wouldn't put it past Leo. Hey! I’m careful. Mostly. Keep telling yourself that. Speaking of mayhem, I was reading about the school exchange program. Apparently, the American kids are  obsessed  with sugar. Absolutely obsessed. The supervising teacher was practically begging for healthier snack options. Well, that's America for you, isn't it? Everything in excess. I remember when I went to New York with work – the sheer size of everything… the portions in the restaurants! It was overwhelming. And the noise! I felt like I needed a week just to decompress after. I know what you mean. My cousin spent a year in Chicago. He came back saying it was like living in a permanent rush hour. Everyone’s always on the go, always doing something. No one seems to appreciate just… stillness. My friend Chloe’s mum went to California. She said the kids there get, like, free range everything. Free range chicken, free range eggs, free range  fruit . It sounds insane. Our fruit comes in plastic packets from Tesco. Free range everything! Honestly, it’s astonishing.

Honestly, darling, you won't  believe  what I've found. Absolutely incredible! I'm practically buzzing. Let me guess, another haul from that silk market we passed? You know your willpower is showing cracks when you've got three bags before even having a cup of tea. It’s not  just  the silk market, though they did have some lovely things. It’s…it's a whole experience! And yes, there's silk, but there's so much more. Come and have a look. I need your honest opinion, you know me. Honest? That's what you always say, and then you dramatically disagree with me anyway. What is it this time? A jade dragon brooch? Another embroidered shawl? Cheeky! No, nothing like that. Well, there  is  a little something sparkly, but that's beside the point. First, look at this! Linen, darling! Pure linen. And it’s  perfect  for the heat. I was moaning just yesterday about how melting I was feeling in the humidity. That's… unexpectedly sensible. You usually go for something a bit more… flamboyant, shall we say? Lots of ruffles and a vibrant colour palette. I know, right? But I was thinking about practicality. About how much time I spend in lecture halls, chasing students down corridors. Something comfortable and breathable. Plus, the cut is just gorgeous. It has this really flattering drape, and look at the detailing on the sleeves – tiny little embroidered flowers, almost imperceptible. It’s understated elegance, don't you think? It  is  lovely. Really. It suits you. And the colour is…warming, actually. It brings out the brown in your eyes. You're right, it’s far more sophisticated than your usual collection of technicolour creations. See! I knew you’d like it. And it was a steal! Only 180 yuan. Considering the quality of the linen… It's practically criminal. 180 yuan? You’re sure it's genuine linen? These markets… they can be a bit…creative with their descriptions. I got it from that older woman, Mrs. Chen, remember? The one who spoke no English and just smiled a lot? She seemed utterly trustworthy, and she was showing it to some very well-dressed local ladies. Plus, it feels amazing. Light as a feather. Then, look at this! Denim? In this heat? Are you  trying  to spontaneously combust? Don’t be ridiculous! It’s a really soft, lightweight denim. Almost like a twill.

Well, that was a feed. Proper roast, that. And a grand game of rugby too, wouldn’t you say? Absolutely thrilling finish. That last-minute penalty… Jaysus! Yeah, Dad, it was! I was proper stressed. Thought we were gonna lose for a second there. Did you see Murphy’s tackle? That was epic! It was exciting, alright. Though I didn’t understand half of what was going on. All the rucking and mauling… a bit brutal, isn’t it? Oh, rugby, dear. Always has been a bit of a rough house. Though, I must say, the skill of the players now is remarkable. When I was a wee girl, it was mostly just shouting and a lot of mud! Though, minds you, we enjoyed it all the same. Jimmy, did you get the cards signed for Oisin's birthday? Almost forgot, Moira. I did, actually. Got everyone to scribble a wee something. Aoife did a fantastic drawing of a dinosaur, and wee Finn managed to write “Happy B-day!” He’s getting there, isn't he? Show you later, Liam, you’ll get a kick out of it. Cool! Dinosaurs are awesome. Do they teach rugby at your school, Nan? Rugby? Dear boy, when I was teaching, we had netball and a bit of rounders. No rugby for the girls, back in my day. Boys had their rugby, though. Plenty of it! The whole town would turn out for the matches, you know. It was the heart of Glasgow, really. Still is, I'd imagine. Liam, sweetheart, dear, are you getting sleepy? It’s getting late. You’ve got a big day tomorrow, haven’t you? Not really, Mum. I've got history. That's… okay. Could be worse. But I’m not  that  tired. Let him be, Sarah. He's got some energy to burn off yet. Reminds me of myself at that age! Staying up late, staring at the stars... Do you ever do that, Liam? Sometimes, Dad. When it’s clear. We've got that app on Mum's phone, you know, the one that tells you what stars are what. An app for the stars! Goodness me, the world changes so quickly. When I looked at the stars, I just used my imagination. I’d make up stories about them. There was that bright one, I always thought it was a giant’s eye watching over us.

Honestly, Lizzie, watching my niece try to form words is just…mesmerizing. She's only seven months, but she's already got this little ‘goo-goo’ thing down for anything she wants. It’s fascinating from a linguistic perspective, obviously, but also just, you know, adorable. You've got your hands full with little Thomas, haven't you? Last I heard he was attempting to climb the sofa. Oh, you have no idea. Climbing, grabbing, generally being a tiny, adorable menace. He's discovered gravity, apparently. And yes, the “mamamamama” is a frequent demand. It’s exhausting, but the smiles… the smiles make it all worthwhile. Are you thinking about starting a family eventually, then? Eventually, maybe. I keep telling myself I've plenty of time. Though Mum's been dropping not-so-subtle hints. "You're not getting any younger, darling!" you know the drill. But honestly, right now, with the research project and the flat move… it feels a bit too much. Speaking of which, how’s the unpacking going? Did you find your favourite rug yet? Don’t even get me started on the flat move. It’s been chaos. Box after box. I think I've unearthed relics from my childhood I'd completely forgotten about. Found my old Tamagotchi! The rug… it's somewhere under a pile of books, I think. I'm trying to organize it room by room. The kitchen’s functional, at least. I’m dreading the bedroom. It’s the one that really needs doing. Oh, I remember those Tamagotchis! Right peak of childhood. Don’t tell me you still have it! I was thinking about decluttering my own flat before the move, actually. Maybe we should have a clothes swap? I’ve got loads of stuff I never wear. Mostly slightly pretentious London-centric things. A clothes swap! Yes! Absolutely! I’ve got a load of stuff I haven’t worn since I finished university. Far too much floral. And I’d love to have a look at your stuff. You always have such interesting finds. It's a better option than just donating it all. Definitely better. Less guilt involved. My sister's currently using my old wardrobe as her emergency baby clothes repository. Little Leo’s outgrowing things so quickly! It’s a never-ending cycle. She's starting to get really stressed about it all - with work and the baby… it’s a lot.

Right then. So, you’re saying you actually  studied  linguistics, Liam? Seriously? Bit posh for Bedford, innit? Posh? Nah, not really. Just… academically inclined, I suppose. Yeah, did a degree in it. Found it fascinating, really. The way language evolves, the regional variations… it's all interconnected. Like, you know, your accent – proper Eastern Eng, right? - it tells a story about where you come from, your family history… Don't start dissecting me, alright? I just talk like this. It's how me mum talks, how most folk round here talk. It's home, ain't it? Sounds daft putting it like that. Did you ever try to, like,  correct  people's accents when you were teaching? Correct people? Blimey, Liam, you sound like a right…well, a right grammar Nazi. Least you can do is appreciate a bit of local flavour. Bit of Bedfordshire grit in the speech. Speaking of grit, did you see that McGregor fight on Saturday? Proper scrappy. I did catch a bit of it. Though honestly, the commentary was more entertaining than the fight itself. Always seems to be a bloke yelling about striking and angles. Anyway, no, never tried to "correct" accents. That's a bit ridiculous, isn’t it? Trying to erase someone’s identity. It's about understanding, not judging. True, true. But some accents are a bit… challenging, aren't they? Like, sometimes you hear someone and you genuinely have no idea what they're saying. You’d say that about old Mrs. Higgins from down the road, wouldn’t you? Sounds like she's got a mouthful of gravel. But she's a lovely woman, makes the best apple crumble you've ever tasted. Exactly! It's about the person behind the accent, not the accent itself. It’s about communication. Which reminds me, I’ve been meaning to ask – you’re still trying to sell that old mountain bike, aren’t you? Yeah, still got it. Nobody wants a rusty, slightly bent Trek. It's got character though, innit? Proper vintage. Reckon I should just stick it on eBay? eBay’s a minefield. So many time-wasters. Have you tried putting something up in the local Facebook group? "Bedford Buy, Sell & Swap?" That's where most stuff gets moved around. Good shout. Might be more targeted. I'm thinking of selling some old textbooks myself. Got loads collecting dust. Thinking of swapping 'em for a board game, actually.

Honestly, I don’t know why I bother trying to make a remotely healthy dinner on a weeknight. It's always a race against the clock, and then I just end up eating half of it standing over the sink. You’re being dramatic, Liv. It smells amazing, actually. What is it? Something with lentils, right? Yep. Lentils and sweet potato. At least  something  vaguely virtuous. It’s just… the traffic was absolutely horrific tonight. Took me nearly an hour to get back. I was seriously contemplating giving up and just getting a pizza. An hour? Seriously? That's ridiculous. What happened? Another accident on the A1? Worse, I think. Seemed like everyone and their dog decided to commute at the same time. I was tailgated by a van playing incredibly aggressive polka music. Polka! Who even listens to that anymore? Only people with questionable taste, I suspect. You should've just honked. Didn't you have your window down? I did, but honestly, the thought of engaging with someone who clearly hasn’t slept in a decade wasn’t appealing. It’s making me rethink the whole driving situation, you know? What do you mean? Well, the cost of everything is just insane these days. Petrol, insurance… even parking! And then there’s the wear and tear on the car. I’m seriously starting to think about getting rid of it. Getting rid of it? But how would you get around? Public transport is… well, you know. Exactly! It’s a trade-off. Less money spent on the car, more spent on bus passes and probably a lot more time. I was looking at those electric scooters, the foldable ones. Apparently, they’re quite good for short commutes. Those things look a bit… precarious. Especially on London roads. Are you sure? I mean, your dad would have a heart attack. Probably. He’s still convinced my Mini is a death trap. But think about it. If I save, say, £300 a month on car expenses, that's a significant chunk of change. We could actually start saving properly for a deposit on a place. Okay, now you're talking. That  would  be amazing. But honestly, Liv, ditching the car seems… drastic. I rely on you for lifts sometimes, you know. Remember that time I had to lug all my kit for the football tournament across three bus stops in the pouring rain?

Right then, love. Grandparents are due any minute, aren't they? Seems like only yesterday we were wrestling with Christmas decorations, now it's them wanting a cuppa and a sit-down. Did you get the biscuits out, Ethan? The proper ones, mind, not them cheap digestives your Uncle Barry likes to inflict on folks. Aye, Gran. Chocolate Hobnobs. Got a whole packet. And I tidied up a bit. Not perfect, but it’s…presentable? Presentable’ll do, pet. It’s not Buckingham Palace, is it? Though sometimes it feels like it needs a good scrub. Your Grandpa Arthur's got that habit of leaving his newspaper draped over everything. Honestly, a bird could nest in it. Don't you be moaning about Arthur’s paper, Elsie! It keeps a draft out, it does. And I like reading about the allotments. They’ve got some prize marrows this year, apparently. Big as yer head they are! Marrows… used to grow ‘em meself. Back in the day. Used to win a ribbon at the St. Augustine’s fair, I did. Best in show, twice! See, Ethan? Arthur’s got more to talk about than you do, glued to that phone! Grandpa, that's brilliant, really! Two ribbons! I can’t believe it. What year were those prizes, love? Oh, goodness me, Elsie. Decades! Must have been the fifties, or early sixties. Times were simpler then. People had time for marrows and fairs. Was St. Augustine’s a big fair then, Grandpa? Like, with a funfair and everything? Aye, lad! Proper funfair. Swings, a roundabout, a coconut shy. Your grandma used to win at the coconut shy, she did. Always got a teddy bear. Oh, stop it, you two! You’re making me blush. I mostly just went for the toffee apples, if I’m honest. Sticky fingers for hours. Right, someone needs to check the kettle, it's probably gone cold. Ethan, would you be a dear? Do I have to? Can't I just…finish this level? Ethan! Now, no backchat. It’s showing respect to your grandparents. They’ve travelled all the way to see us. And your Grandpa’s got that weird twitch when he’s thirsty, you know. Don’t want him getting agitated. Restless, Elsie. I get restless. Not a twitch. Though my hip's been playing up somethin’ awful today. Oh, Arthur, love. Are you alright? Did you take your tablets?

Right, pirates sorted for now. Leo, you were a  remarkably  convincing Captain Blackheart - all the 'Arrr's and the swagger! And Poppy, your parrot was brilliant, honestly. Proper squawky. I did a  really  good squawk, didn't I, Mummy? Can I do it again? Squawk! Squawk! Polly wants a cracker! I buried the treasure, Mummy! Deep! Really, really deep! You certainly did, darling. A very impressive treasure map too, all those crossed lines and little islands. Now, come on, let’s get some lunch. You two have been running around like… well, like pirates! I’m making pasta with cheese. Everyone happy with that? Cheese! Yay! Can I have extra cheese, please? A REALLY big pile? We'll see about a  really  big pile, Leo. Let’s not be greedy. Now, after lunch, we're talking Shakespeare week. I'm so excited! Shakespeare! Is he a pirate? No, love, he's a playwright. He wrote stories. Really famous stories, lots and lots of years ago. And next week, we’re going to Stratford-upon-Avon! Remember? To see a play. Will there be swords? Like pirate swords? Possibly! It depends on the play. But it’s going to be lots of fun. Learning about knights and kings and… well, lots of rhyming! Rhyming is hard. It can be! But you’re both brilliant at rhyming. Let’s see… “Poppy is bright, Poppy is light…” See? You did that! I did! “Leo is strong, Leo plays long!” “Pirates say ‘Arrr,’ going very far!” Excellent! You're both little poets. Now, speaking of exciting things… Mrs. Davies emailed me about a circus workshop. Speaker_2 & 3: Circus! Yes! But it’s not just  any  circus. Apparently, it's in a  real  circus tent! With sawdust and everything! They’re doing a stop-motion animation workshop too. Wouldn't that be amazing? You could make your own pirate movie! A real circus tent?! With lions? Probably not lions, darling. But maybe acrobats and clowns and… jugglers! Possibly even a unicyclist! And think of the stop-motion! You could recreate your pirate adventure. With moving treasure and everything! We could even use the Easter pictures we took. Remember, with the little bunny ears? We could stick them on the pirates! That would be so funny! A pirate with bunny ears! And I could animate Blackheart fighting a giant carrot! A giant carrot, eh? That’s quite the adversary.

Honestly, David, you won't believe what happened to poor old Arthur. He was telling me just yesterday. Apparently, he tried to sail from Jeddah to Cyprus… in a rather small dinghy, I might add. Arthur, you say? Well, that doesn’t surprise me in the slightest. Arthur always did have a certain…optimism regarding nautical capabilities. Did he make it? Absolutely not! He was apprehended by the Saudi authorities. Can you imagine? Arrested for improper sailing! Apparently, there were a few…protocols he hadn’t quite adhered to. Something about permits and customs declarations. Arrested! Good heavens. Must have been quite the scene. Jeddah? That's a long way to be sailing a dinghy without the proper paperwork. Reminds me of a student I had in Manchester, convinced he was going to become a camel racer. Untapped market, he said! Camel racing, you say? Reminds me of the time I was in Dubai for a conference. Absolutely fascinating place, though the lack of decent dental magazines was quite distressing. All this talk of boats... sailed a bit myself, you know. Small boats, naturally. Nothing adventurous like Arthur's attempt. Proper notices to mariners and everything. You taught in Saudi Arabia, didn't you, Margaret? What was that like? I’ve always been curious about the cultural differences, especially regarding… everything really. It was… an experience. Certainly a unique one. Teaching English to young women in a segregated environment. Very strict rules. You couldn't even be seen with male students outside of the classroom. But the students were incredibly bright, and eager to learn. The support staff were lovely, always ready with a cup of sweet tea. Though, finding a decent glass of wine wasn't exactly easy. Ah, yes, the alcohol situation. A universal challenge for the British abroad. I spent some time lecturing in Cairo. The local ingenuity in obtaining beverages was… remarkable. Let’s just say I developed a taste for very strong hibiscus tea. I remember trying to acquire a bottle of scotch in Bahrain once. It involved a complex series of transactions and a rather nervous-looking shopkeeper. Worth it, of course. A good single malt can smooth over any cultural awkwardness. You’re all sounding like a band of intrepid smugglers! It’s quite remarkable how much effort we Brits put into procuring a simple drink. I remember in Japan, you practically needed a permit just to buy sake.

Honestly, Jan, the bathroom situation is driving me mad. Liam's left hair gel everywhere  again . It’s like he thinks the sink is a personal storage facility. And Sophie's got her beauty products scattered across the windowsill. It’s a bombsite. Ah, teenagers. It's just what they do, love. Remember when you were a teenager? It wasn’t exactly spotless in your room, was it? That’s hardly the point, is it? I was tidier than  this . I actually made my bed. Regularly! This is a daily battle. I've put up signs, reminders… nothing seems to work. I even threatened to lock them out, which, of course, didn't go down well. What's all the shouting about? Sounds like World War Three in here. Your bathroom, Liam! Your appalling, hygiene-challenged bathroom! I cleaned it yesterday. Sort of. "Sort of" involves leaving half-empty tubes of toothpaste and a collection of rogue socks clinging to the shower curtain? He's a typical lad, love. They just think things magically disappear. Speaking of disappearing things, did you ever find those tickets for the football? I was looking for them earlier. No! And I swear, I put them in a safe place. Which, apparently, is in another dimension. Still, the football seems a bit lower down the priority list at the moment compared to convincing my offspring they live in a shared space and not individual palaces. Speaking of palaces, Mr. Harrison said we could all go on the school trip to the National Space Centre now. He’s looking for volunteers to help supervise. Should be good, yeah? Loads of astronauts and stuff. Maybe I'll see if they have any cool stuff for my project. Oh, that’s brilliant, Liam! Really? That’s a fantastic opportunity. Absolutely go for it. It's good experience. You could even mention to Mr. Harrison about your interests in explorers and stuff. That's lovely! You’d be a great help, Liam. Remember how you used to be obsessed with Neil Armstrong when you were little? Yeah, but now I'm more interested in Elon Musk. He's actually  doing  stuff. Armstrong just landed on the moon once. Cheeky. So, you’re thinking of volunteering then? You know a bit of pocket money wouldn’t go amiss for helping out, do you think? Maybe. But it’s the experience, really.

Right, I’m officially bored. Another hour of this Croatian countryside, and I’m gonna start talking to the sheep. They’ve gotta be more interesting than this. Now, now, Elara, be nice. It’s beautiful, isn’t it? Look at them hills rolling away. Reminds me of home, a bit. Just… sunnier. And with fewer rain clouds permanently hanging over ‘em. It’s alright, I suppose. Could do with some Wi-Fi. This signal is rubbish. The lack of consistent digital connectivity across Europe continues to be a significant impediment to modern productivity. Especially given the increasingly mobile nature of… . Though, I agree, the scenery is rather pleasant. Almost… Tuscan. Tuscan? Dad, seriously? This is Istria. It’s  truffles , not pasta. Honestly, you'd think you were still presenting a business proposal. Want to talk about synergy while we're at it? Well, the aesthetic similarities are undeniable. And speaking of truffles… have you tried the truffle pasta at that little place in Rovinj we went to last night? Exquisite. Chef Giorgio is a genius. He is, that's true. Best pasta I’ve had in years. Remember when you used to refuse to eat anything with mushrooms on it, John? Used to give me the devil's own job at Christmas dinners. That was… a phase. Palates evolve. Though I still find the earthy flavour somewhat… assertive. Perhaps if accompanied by a lighter sauce. You’re weird, Dad. You are not wrong, Liam. Anyway, truffles are amazing. Speaking of amazing, I was reading about stem cell research. Apparently, they’re getting closer to reversing age-related diseases. Imagine! No more dodgy knees for you, Mum. Oh, don’t you start tempting fate, Elara! My knees are perfectly serviceable, thank you very much. Although, a bit less creaking wouldn’t go amiss. They’re bad enough when I'm on my feet all day at the hospital delivering babies. Actually, talking about weird… you should see some of the things I've seen. Delivering babies. Quite a different world from spreadsheets and stakeholder analysis. Do you ever miss it, Helen? Some days. It was hard work, no denying that. Long hours, stressful situations. But it was  real , you know? You were bringing life into the world. It felt… important. More important than… …complicated profit margins. Ooh, burn! Mum’s hitting you with the big guns, Dad. I contribute to the global economy, Elara.

Honestly, this quinoa is drier than the Sahara. Did they forget to add any dressing? They always do. Classic CUP lunchtime experience. I learned to bring my own sriracha ages ago. Want some? Oh, please! You’re a lifesaver, Tom. Seriously. It's makes all the difference. So, tell me, how's the marketing campaign for the new historical linguistics textbook going? You seemed pretty stressed about it last time we spoke. Much better, actually. We cracked the audience targeting. Turns out, a lot more undergraduate history students are accidentally stumbling onto our stuff than we initially thought. It's all about those Youtube channels dissecting ancient languages, you know? Reaching them through targeted ads on those platforms is proving really effective. Anyone want another coffee? I managed to wrestle a croissant out of the kitchen. They were practically fighting over them. Yes, please! Black, if you don’t mind. You’re an absolute star, Liam. I'll take a latte, if you're feeling generous. Thanks. So, what's the buzz? Tom seems to have conquered the world of historical linguistics advertising. Just plugging away, Liam. It’s the clever algorithms, really. I just steer the ship. What about you? Still battling the documentation for the updated database? Sounds… thrilling. Thrilling is a  very  generous word. Let’s just say I’m intimately acquainted with the nuances of SQL syntax now. Apparently, a rogue semicolon was the bane of Project Chimera’s existence for a week. It was… dramatic. A rogue semicolon? That’s the most Cambridge thing I've ever heard. It’s like something out of a PhD sitcom. Tell me about it. Professor Davies nearly had a coronary. I swear he aged five years in that one week. It turned out that a junior researcher had slightly modified the schema... didn't check if the changes were accurate and well... it was a mess. Davies, eh? He always had his heart set on that database, didn't he? Says it will revolutionize the way they catalogue ancient texts. Absolutely. Researching changes in language through digital archives is the cutting edge, isn't it? That's precisely  why  I'm coordinating the data acquisition project for the East Anglian dialect survey. We’re trying to build a comparable, albeit smaller-scale, resource. That sounds fascinating, Elara! Are you finding much difference between the modern dialects and records from, say, the Victorian era?

Oh, this is lovely, isn’t it? Just…peaceful. So much better than being stuck in Cambridge, you know? All those…people. And the damp. Honestly, Poland feels so fresh. Aye, it is. Bit of a change from Bury, that’s for sure. Though even Bury’s got its charm, doesn't it? This road's a little bumpy though, isn’t it? You got the suspension sorted on this camper? Sorted as it’ll ever be, love. It’s a vintage thing, you know. Character. And a few rattles. Don't worry, it'll survive. So, you’ve got all your papers in order for the border, have you? Passport, visa… everything? I wouldn't want any bother, not after yesterday's slight detour. Mum’s been on at me for weeks about the visa. Nearly had a meltdown. I’ve got everything, don’t worry. Printed three copies of each, just to be safe. And my Polish phrasebook is ready to go.  Dzień dobry  and  proszę  are going to be my best friends, I reckon. You going to try and brush up on yours? Oh, I used to be quite proficient, you know. Years ago. Before… everything. But it's faded a bit, I'm afraid. I mostly stick to “Where is the nearest  kawiarnia ?” I’ll rely on you to do the heavy lifting with the Polish. Are you nervous about meeting Kasia’s family? A little, yeah. Kasia’s been raving about them, obviously, but you know what it's like. Sometimes things aren’t as perfect as they seem online. I’m mostly just hoping they don’t think I’m some clueless northern girl who's barged her way into their lives. Nonsense, darling. You're a lovely girl, and Kasia would never invite you if she didn't think you'd be welcome. Just be yourself. They’ll see that you’re genuine and kind, and that’s all that matters. Besides, they’re Polish. They've seen everything. They appreciate a bit of good humour. That’s a nice thought. So, you’ve got a plan for the rest of your time here after Tarnow? Kasia said you were thinking about heading south? I am! I’m thinking Krakow, Zakopane… maybe even a little bit of Slovakia. I’ve always wanted to see the Tatra Mountains. It feels… liberating, you know? To be able to just…go.

Honestly, look at that badge! It's just…an assault on the eyes, isn’t it? Another bloody insurance company plastered all over the shirt. Makes ya sick, it does. It’s the modern game, love. Can’t fight it. Every club needs the cash, don’t they? Though, I do agree, some sponsorships are just…visually jarring. That bright yellow on a navy blue background? No good. Jarring is putting it mildly! It looks like a child’s drawing. Remember when it was just the club crest? Proper proud, it felt. Now it's like a walking billboard. And don't even get me started on those sleeve sponsors – absolutely ridiculous. Aye, it’s changed a lot. I was reading something the other day about how much a shirt sponsorship deal can be worth now. Insane numbers. Millions. Used to be a local brewery or something, you know? Now it’s global tech giants. Millions! I know! It's unbelievable when you think back to the days of Arnott’s Pies sponsoring Sunderland. Sweet memories, though. They didn’t break the bank, did they? And the strip was always decent, even back then. Proper red and white, not some Frankenstein creation. Speaking of strip designs, what do you think of Manchester United’s away kit this year? Saw a picture of it earlier. That purple… it's bold, I'll give them that. Purple? Seriously? That’s… questionable, to say the least. It looks like a space alien’s football kit. I mean, they've had some dodgy ones over the years, haven't they? But purple? It's a brave choice, I’ll give 'em that, but not a good one. I’d rather have a beige kit, honestly, than that purple monstrosity. Beige? Now  that  would be a statement. You've got a point, though. It’s just… not right. It needs…something. Maybe a nice, subtle stripe? Something to break up the blandness. Aye, a stripe. Or a nice, classic collar. Anything but that single block of purple. Gets right on your nerves, doesn’t it? It's like they’re deliberately trying to provoke a reaction. Maybe. Though, it'll probably sell loads. People buy into the hype, don't they? Blame the influencers. Don't remind me. They’ll be wearing it even if it clashes horribly with the home kit. Speaking of buying things…are you hungry?

Honestly, Dad, it’s just… relentless. Another day, another two hours spent online, filling out forms, tailoring my CV for jobs I’m not even sure I  want , let alone qualify for. It’s soul-crushing, innit? Tell me about it. You think your lot’s hard? Try staring at the bloody wall for eight hours a day. Try having the DWP breathing down your neck every week. At least you're trying, love. I've lost the will. Don't say that, Dad. You have to keep trying. Mum’s worried sick. I’m worried sick. And, come on, that online course you started, the one for data entry? You were really enthusiastic about it! Enthusiasm fades, doesn't it, Annie? Like that George Foreman. Remember that thing? Mum was convinced it was going to revolutionise our dinners. Three burnt sausages later and it was gathering dust in the shed. Same with this course. It’s all just… promise, and no delivery. Like everything else. Okay, that's a bit dramatic, isn’t it? It’s not the same. You're intelligent, you could be good at it. Have you looked at the job listings again? There were a couple yesterday that seemed… plausible. Plausible until you read the requirements. "Five years experience in data management"... five years! I barely managed to finish school, Annie! And the clever clogs who write these descriptions clearly haven't spent a day in the real world. They wouldn’t know a spreadsheet from a sarnie. You’re impossible. Listen, before I get completely bogged down in job applications, can we talk about something else for a bit? I’m still fuming about that eBay order. What now? Another faulty phone charger? Worse! That vintage vinyl I bought for Gran? The seller said 'excellent condition.' It’s scratched to buggery! Honestly, I’m half tempted to record the conversation when I try to get a refund. Just to have proof. You know, evidence. Recording people without their consent? That can't be right, can it? It’s probably illegal. I know, I know! But I’m so frustrated. It's just another thing. Speaking of which, have you seen the gas and electricity bills? It’s absolutely scandalous! How are people supposed to cope? Tell me about it. I nearly choked on my tea when I saw Margaret next door’s. She's got three kids, running the heating like it’s going out of fashion.

Honestly, the traffic getting here was just appalling. Sat nav took me down this ridiculous little lane, barely wide enough for a bicycle! I swear, these apps are deliberately trying to confuse people. Oh, you and your sat navs, Sarah! You youngsters and yer technology. Used to be you’d just ask someone for directions. Much simpler, innit? Though, I understand. Trying to get around Peterborough these days is a nightmare, even without the fancy gadgets. All those new estates sprawlin’ out. When I were a girl, you knew every lane and every shortcut. Not like now. All these roundabouts…confusing the life out of people. Remember when they put that one in near the King's Dyke? Caused such a kerfuffle! It's a constant source of frustration. I was late for a meeting this morning because of it. Speaking of frustrations, did you see that article about the plane crash in Spain? Dreadful. Absolutely dreadful. So sad, love. Awful thing. Makes you think, doesn't it? Makes you appreciate the simple things, like a nice cuppa and a bit of a gossip. Absolutely. Though, I do need to catch up on some emails later. Being an account manager, you’re always on call, it seems. Still, I wouldn’t trade it. It's rewarding when a deal goes through. Account manager...what’s that, dear? Sounds important. Does it involve numbers? It does, mostly. I look after big clients, making sure they're happy with the services we provide. It’s all about building relationships. Sounds complicated. Me, I just like a bit of elbow grease and a good tidy-up. Always a satisfying feeling when something’s sparkling clean. Right, I'll just pop and check the bathroom, and then I’ll start on the kitchen. Anything you ladies want while I’m in there? Fancy a biscuit? I picked up some shortbread from the Co-op. That sounds lovely, thank you, Di. Perhaps a digestive as well? Oh, yes please! Digestive would be lovely. And a little splash of milk in my coffee, dear. Coming right up. You know, Mrs. ANON mentioned she was having trouble with some warts on her hands. Nasty things, warts. Oh, really? That’s a nuisance. I had a few years ago, tried freezing them off myself with one of those kits. Didn't work terribly well. Ended up going to the doctor eventually.

Honestly, this whole term is just… a lot, innit? Like, my brain feels like playdough someone’s been stomping on. Tell me about it. Mr. Davies practically set the Biology test as a deliberate attempt to induce collective panic. Did you even  understand  half of it? Mitosis? Meiosis? It’s just a load of squiggles and labels! Squiggles and labels is right! I spent the whole time panicking that I’d mixed up the phases. I’m pretty sure I put Anaphase before Metaphase. Not the end of the world, I guess, but still… I’m gonna be googling it tonight, that’s for sure. What were you drawing? Just practicing shading. I’m trying to get the light reflecting off the apple  right . It's for Mrs. Peterson's still life assignment, you know? She’s really pushing us to focus on observation, which is brilliant, actually. It's way better than just copying pictures. Yeah, Mrs. Peterson’s wicked. She actually makes Art… well, arty. Remember last year when Mr. Finch tried to get us to sculpt using only egg boxes and tape? Don’t remind me! Mine looked like a lopsided pigeon that had lost a fight with a vacuum cleaner. Honestly, I’m much better at drawing than sculpting. Definitely. So, are you still doing the trainee teachers shadowing thing? How's that going? It's… interesting. The guy I'm shadowing, Liam, is trying really hard, bless him. But he keeps calling us "students" instead of “pupils.” It's a little awkward. And he tries  way  too many jokes. Like, really,  really  bad puns. Oh, god. I hate people who think puns are hilarious. Remember Mr. Hargrave's terrible jokes in English last year? “Why don’t scientists trust atoms? Because they make up everything!” I nearly died of embarrassment. Oh my gosh, yes! It was brutal! Liam’s are slightly less awful, but still… he was explaining the French Revolution the other day and just randomly threw in, "It's like a really, really bad croissant.” No! Seriously?! A bad croissant?! I swear! I couldn't keep a straight face. I had to pretend I was coughing. The kids were all staring at him, like, "What on earth?" He’s doomed, isn’t he? A really bad croissant? Probably! But you know, he seems to really care about the kids, so I’m trying to be supportive.

So, you were saying about your… auntie Moira? The one who joined a convent? That's right. Auntie Moira. She was always a bit… intense, you know? Always studying, always questioning. We all thought she'd become a lawyer or something. Then, suddenly, she’s off to become a nun. It was quite a shock for everyone. Nun! Nun! Yes, darling, a nun. A very nice lady who helps people and prays a lot. What made her do it? I mean, it's not exactly… common, is it? Loads of people go to uni, or get jobs… but becoming a nun? Well, she said she was searching for… truth. A deeper meaning. She said the world felt… empty. A bit like… you know  The Matrix , but without the cool kung fu. So, she thought being a nun would be like… unplugging from the Matrix? Something like that, I suppose. She said it was about finding a different kind of reality. A reality based on faith. Funny, isn't it? My mum, her sister, she can't even understand it. Thinks Moira’s gone a bit mad. My mate, Ben, was talking about Scientology the other day. He said his uncle joined. Apparently, it’s all about… well, I didn’t really understand. Something about aliens and saving the world. Oh, Scientology. Right. My neighbour down the road got heavily involved in that for a while. Spent all his savings on courses and auditing. Didn’t seem to make him any happier, if anything, it made him more… irritable. It’s all a bit… cult-y, isn't it? Cult-y? What's that mean? It means… it's a group that tends to isolate people from outside influences and can be quite controlling. They try and convince you that  they  have the only true path. Like Auntie Moira and the nuns? That’s different. The Catholic Church, as old and flawed as it is, has been around for centuries. There's a structure, a history… Scientology is much newer. It has a very… strong personality behind it. Spoon! More! Alright, alright. More potatoes coming right up, my love. The thing is, people seek answers, you know? They want to feel like there's a purpose to their lives. Sometimes, they get drawn in by things that promise quick solutions, even if those solutions aren’t… genuine. My gran’s really religious.

Right, so, are you  sure  this is the right way, Liam? Because it feels like we’ve been driving around these bloody roundabouts for an eternity. I swear, every roundabout in this county looks exactly the same. Relax, Chloe. It's just a bit of a detour. The A1 was a nightmare - complete standstill. This is actually faster, trust me. And besides, enjoy the scenery. It’s…pleasant. Pleasant? It’s fields, Liam. Fields and more fields. Back home, we’ve got proper views. The sea, the bridges…a bit of industrial charm. This is all just…green. And quiet. Too quiet. Makes me nervous. Nervous? You, nervous? You’re the one who jumps at shadows when we watch horror films. Speaking of which, did you finish that new series on LoveFilm? The Icelandic one? 'Katla'? Aye, finished it last night. Brutal, wasn't it? The ending... Oh, don't even get me started. Reminded me of some of the Old English sagas, that bleakness, you know? All doom and gloom. Professor Davies would’ve loved it. He’s obsessed with Beowulf. Honestly, sometimes I think he  is  Beowulf, just a bit rounder. He does have a certain…gravitas. It's amazing how much detail he gets into about the language. I still don’t understand why he insists on us translating it ourselves instead of using the glossaries. It feels needlessly difficult. It’s good for us, though, isn't it? Keep the grey matter working. Though sometimes I wonder if he's deliberately trying to age us all prematurely. He keeps going on about “the youthful vigour required for truly understanding the alliterative verse.” Makes us all feel ancient. You’re not ancient! You’re barely older than me. Though, I suppose, at twenty-four, we are getting to that age where people start… dismissing us. I was at a conference last week, and this bloke, no older than fifty, kept talking down to me, assuming I didn't know anything about structural engineering. It was infuriating! The ageism is real, innit? Honestly, it's everywhere, isn't it? My nan was saying the other day how awful she feels being ignored in shops. People assume she’s daft just because she’s older. It’s rubbish. You know, speaking of awful, did you see what Piers Morgan said about Taylor Swift? He’s just… exhausting. Don't even get me started on Piers Morgan.

Right, so, like, are we  sure  this is the right way? This road is getting narrower and narrower. It’s barely wide enough for the car, never mind a caravan. Honestly, Dad, you're a brave man driving this thing through these lanes. Calm yersel’, love. I've driven worse in Bolton, trust me. And this is the scenic route, remember? The brochure promised incredible views. Besides, Colin insisted it’d be ‘character building’ for us all. Absolutely. You've got to experience the  real  Istria, not just the tourist traps. This winding coastal road is what it's all about. And the roads in London are a joke compared to this. Can we just hurry up? I'm buffering, and I'm missing half the Sons of Anarchy re-watch. Jake finally explained the whole Jax and Tara thing, and now I'm lost again. Sons of Anarchy? Seriously, Liam? We’re surrounded by breathtaking scenery and you’re thinking about motorcycle gangs? They’re complicated motorcycle gangs. And it's good! It's got, like, art and… and motorcycles. And drama. It’s way better than that pottery class you dragged me to last year. Speaking o' art, did you see that little gallery we drove past earlier? All those paintings of olive trees… absolutely stunning. Reminded me of yer grandad’s garden, Sarah. Remember how he used to potter around with his herbs and lavender? Yeah, I do. He’d always be trying to get me to help him, but I was always off with my mates. He made the best mint tea, though. I wonder if they sell good olive oil around here? I’ve been wanting to try some proper Istrian olive oil. There's a fantastic market in Rovinj. We should head there tomorrow. Fresh produce, olive oil, wine… all the good stuff. And apparently, some amazing seafood restaurants. We could treat ourselves. A market sounds lovely. I was thinking, maybe we could find a campsite near Motovun? I saw pictures online, and it’s supposed to be gorgeous, all perched up on that hill. A bit of fresh air, a bit o' peace and quiet. A campsite?! No way. Camping is like, medieval. I’d rather stay in a hotel with Wi-Fi. And don’t even  mention  caravans. They're the worst. You’re such a drama queen, Liam. A bit of camping wouldn’t kill you.

Right, so, Chloe's properly gone mental, hasn't she? Sending me these voice notes all day - like, fifty of 'em. Just ramblin’ on about… well, mostly about that new game. “Cosmic Conquerors,” she calls it. Sounds a right daft name, to be honest. Fifty? Seriously? Chloe's always been intense when it comes to games, but that's a new level. She’s been glued to it since it launched. I think she's trying to get you to play with her. Cosmic Conquerors? Is that the one everyone's been talking about? The one with the ridiculously complicated economy? I tried watching a streamer play it, got lost within five minutes. It's like a second job. Nah, it's dead good. Got me proper hooked for a bit. You can build your own space stations and raid other players. Proper bossin’ stuff. Though, I had to give it up, didn’t have enough time with work. See! Told ya it was a right nonsense name. Bossin’ stuff? Honestly, El, you’ve been watching too many YouTube videos again. But Chloe’s obsessed. She was going on about some anal… oh, sorry, I shouldn’t have said that aloud. It’s game jargon, you know. Something to do with strategic resource management. Oh, Bethany! You and your Yorkshire bluntness! Anal as in… strategically allocating resources? That's hilarious! Chloe’s probably dissecting the resource allocation algorithms. Don’t worry, Bethany. I understand. It's just... a bit much for me. Any game that requires a spreadsheet to play properly isn't for me. I’d rather reread Pride and Prejudice, thanks. Speaking of spreadsheets… remember when Liam tried to live-stream himself playing Cosmic Conquerors and his internet kept cutting out? He spent an hour explaining the optimal build order, then the screen froze. It was a classic. Oh, God, that  was  a classic. He was proper red-faced. He blamed the router, naturally. Poor lad. Though, you have to admire his dedication. Building a whole space empire from his bedroom in Harworth. He should've recorded it. That would have been gold. Imagine, sped up, captioned with his frustrated commentary. I think he did, actually. I saw a clip on one of those "Gaming Fails" channels. It was the highlight of my week. The look on his face when the internet died was priceless. Honestly, these lads get so worked up about these games.

Aye, this library coffee's gettin' worse, isn't it? Tastes like dishwater they’ve dyed brown. Remember the cafe down on Chapel Street? Proper bacon butties, that were. You're always reminiscing about bacon butties, Dave! I’ve never known you to miss a chance to mention them. Though, I have to agree, this coffee is a bit grim. I brought a banana, at least. Keeps the hanger at bay. Hanger? You’ve got some posh words, Liv. Just means you’re peckish, doesn't it? I've got a packet of biscuits, anyone want one? Jaffa Cakes. Don't judge. Jaffa Cakes, eh? Can’t say no to a Jaffa Cake. Though, they're a bit too sweet for me first thing. Makes me want something savoury, like… proper chip shop chips, with gravy. Now  that’s  a lunch. Chip shop chips with gravy... Oh my god, you're making me crave that! My Nan used to take me to Alty’s every Saturday after football. The smell alone was worth the visit. They’ve changed since then though, haven’t they? Everything's gone a bit… processed. Alty’s? That's a throwback! My dad used to take me to Tony's in Rochdale. Best mushy peas in the world. Seriously. They weren't that watery, pale green stuff you get everywhere now. They had… body. I’m not even kidding. Food memories are proper strong, aren’t they? Tell me about it. My mam used to do this fantastic steak pie. Not one of those pastry-heavy things, mind you. Proper, juicy, chunky steak, with a light, flaky crust. I've tried to recreate it a couple of times, but it never comes out the same. There’s just something… special about a mam's cooking. It's the love, isn’t it? I think that’s what makes the difference. My mum’s lasagna is legendary. Everyone begs her to make it for birthdays and Christmas. She refuses, though. She says it’s too much effort. Which is ridiculous. Classic mum move! Mine’s the same with her Eccles cakes. Says they're 'too fiddly' but she’ll happily spend three hours scrolling through Facebook. Priorities, eh? What’s been your favourite food discovery lately, Liv? Anything adventurous? Hmmm, adventurous… I tried that Korean fried chicken place on Tib Street last week. Banging! Seriously crispy, gochujang sauce, proper sticky and spicy.

Right then, David. You were saying about this… TikTok thing? Sounds like utter madness, doesn't it? Never understood the appeal of folks filming themselves dancing. Radcliffe wasn't exactly a hotbed of choreographed routines, you know. More like avoiding puddles after a heavy rain. It  is  a bit bonkers, isn't it? But the reach is incredible, Mark. The library's social media engagement has been… well, almost non-existent, let's be honest. I’m trying to convince the Head of Department we need to at least  explore  it. Think of it: short videos about rare manuscripts, quick tours of the special collections… a bit of fun amidst the Dewey Decimal. G’day, fellas. What’s all the excitement then? Sounded like you were wrestling a particularly stubborn catalogue. Social media, you say? Oh, I’ve dabbled. Instagram’s been alright. Showcased some of the Victorian ephemera we have – those old postcards are surprisingly popular. Gets a good little following from history buffs. Victorian postcards? Right. Now  that  sounds interesting. Better than someone miming to a pop song, anyway. Though, my niece tried to get me to do a "challenge" on Instagram last week. Involved a rubber chicken and a dramatic reading of Wordsworth. I politely declined. Gave her a stern talking to about respecting her elders. A rubber chicken and Wordsworth! Oh, Mark, you're a legend. See, that’s the kind of content we could do. "A Librarian's Lament - When the Shelf Placement Goes Wrong." Short, sharp, relatable. Think of the memes! Memes, eh? We had a rogue koala once – got into the rare books room. Now  that  would’ve gone viral. Imagine the headlines: "Koala Considers First Edition." The University authorities weren't thrilled, mind you. Had to spend a week explaining why there were eucalyptus leaves in the Beowulf manuscript. A koala? In a rare books room? You're pulling my leg, you are. No, she's serious. Happened a few years back, apparently. We saw the pictures. Pandemonium, apparently. That’s better publicity than any carefully planned campaign, isn’t it? Absolutely. Unscripted authenticity. People respond to that. Although, I suppose a rogue rubber chicken might cause a similar kind of chaos. You'd have to be careful it doesn't damage anything. Libraries are  very  particular about paper preservation. I can imagine. So, this TikTok... Are we talking about proper accounts and posting regularly?

It’s quite the set-up you have here, David. Very…corporate. Not quite how I pictured a hospice CEO’s office, to be honest. Less glass, more…comforting colours, perhaps? Though I suppose that’s a discussion for the architects, isn't it? Well, Eleanor, it’s a reflection of the organisation I run now, not what I  imagine  a hospice CEO’s office should be. Fundamentally it’s still about financial stability, which dictates a certain aesthetic, I’m afraid. But you're right, the new build needs to be… different. Beyond the practicalities, it needs to  feel  like a place of solace. So, the tape – the initial presentation for the board – where do you think we’re at? I was reviewing the draft business case again last night. I’ve been giving it a good chew over too, David. The financials look solid, certainly, but I’m still slightly uneasy about the rationale for Tunbridge Wells. It's not exactly underserved, is it? We've got Eastbourne, Hastings… why here? We need to hammer that home in the presentation, make it undeniably persuasive. It can’t just be said we saw a “gap in the market.” They’ll tear that apart. Agreed. The consultant's report highlighted a significant shortage of palliative care beds specifically  within  the M25, and Tunbridge Wells offered a prime, accessible location. Good road links, relatively affluent catchment area, the council are supportive… I know it looks a bit…out of the way for some, but the data backs it up. The recruitment challenge is the biggest hurdle, admittedly, and that’s why the nursing package needs to be absolutely stellar. What about the consultation? Have we started the community engagement? We've had the initial meetings with the local GP practices. Generally positive feedback, though Dr. Sharma at Pembury was quite vocal about the potential strain on the local acute hospitals. He's worried about them being even  more  overburdened when they discharge patients who could benefit from hospice care. We need to address that head-on. Perhaps integrate a dedicated liaison nurse into the local hospitals to facilitate smoother transitions? Good suggestion. We absolutely need to quell those concerns. We don’t want to be seen as adding to the existing pressures. It’s about working  with  the system, not against it. I’ve been talking to St. Thomas’s Hospice in London – they've got a surprisingly robust relationship with their local NHS trust.

Right then, look at this one! Remember this, Dave? From Sarah’s hen do in Brighton? Cor, we were a right state weren't we? Good heavens, yes! You've still got glitter in your hair, love. And I'm wearing that ridiculous Hawaiian shirt. Honestly, where did we get those ideas? Sarah had a good time, though. She did well to marry Tom. Oh my gosh, Auntie Claire! You are  sparkling . Is that the Electric Blue cocktail? I remember hearing stories about those... Electric Blue indeed! They were potent little numbers, weren’t they? Definitely fueled the karaoke. And you, darling, were far too well-behaved for that crowd. Always the sensible one. Got an update on that job interview, have you? Not yet, no. Interview was yesterday afternoon. Head of Communications for that sustainable fashion brand, Bloom & Thread. It felt… good, actually. Really positive vibes. But this waiting is killing me. I’ve refreshed my emails about fifty times already. Sustainable fashion, eh? Sounds right up your street, that does. You always were keen on buying ethically. Remember that whole campaign you organised at university about fast fashion? A proper crusade that was. It feels like a lifetime ago. Uni seems so… small now. I just really,  really  want this job, you know? It’d be amazing, a proper step up. You’d be brilliant, love. Absolutely brilliant. You’ve got the talent and the drive. Stop fretting, you'll get the news when you get it. Now, are you hungry? I'm thinking we'll have a roast veg bake with some halloumi. What do you reckon? Sounds lovely, Claire. Though, I'm rather partial to a bit of gravy on mine. Always have been, always will be. Reminds me of me Nan's cooking. She used to make the  best  gravy. Never told anyone her secret, though. Just said it was a pinch of this and a dash of that. Speaking of family, look at this one! Grandad on the pony at Ascot. He looks so dashing! Did he ever actually win anything? Oh, Grandad! He was a character, wasn’t he? Never won anything significant, bless him. More like a casual gambler, really. He did once manage to back a horse called 'Lucky Star' – couldn't believe his luck! But mostly, it was just the excuse to wear a fancy hat and drink champagne. Ascot was his favourite.

Right, so, you’re  sure  you’re up for this then, Liv? Because I’m tellin’ ya now, I've heard whispers about ‘Smile’. Apparently, it's proper unsettling. More than just jump scares, ya know? Like, it gets under yer skin. Honestly, Chloe, you build things up so much. I’ve seen trailers. It looks…intense, sure. But 'unsettling' doesn’t automatically mean 'terrifying'. I’m ready for a bit of a fright. Besides, it's the perfect weather for a scary film, innit? Rain lashing against the windows, the wind howling… sets the mood. Aye, tha’s true. Proper atmospheric. But remember ‘The Ring’? That one, I couldn't sleep for a week! Kept expecting that horrifying girl to pop out from under me bed. This ‘Smile’ business sounds like somethin’ similar, only… more psychological, apparently. Not just a creepy video tape, but a curse. A cursed smile! How morbid is that? You’re catastrophising already. It’s just a film, Chloe. They write these things to be spooky, to get a reaction. It's not going to actually curse us. Although, I do love a good curse narrative. It’s like a fairytale, but with more gore. Gore’s one thing, Liv, but the clever stuff, the stuff that messes with yer head… that’s proper scary. Remember that dream I had after watchin' 'Sinister'? About the cornfields and the… the static on the TV? I still get shivers thinkin’ about it. Oh, God,  Sinister ! You had me waking up in cold sweats for days after that one. The music… the found footage aspect… it was brilliantly creepy. But honestly, I think you just have a more vivid imagination than me. I appreciate the atmosphere, the suspense, but I'm not easily spooked. Don’t be so sure. You jumped a mile when that pigeon flew past the window earlier! That was a  very  sudden pigeon, Chloe! And it startled me, it didn’t traumatise me. There's a difference. Are you sure you haven't been watching too many true crime documentaries again? They do have a way of warping your perspective. Maybe a little. But I like knowin’ stuff, ya know? Even if it is a bit grim. Right, well, are we doin' this then? Dim the lights? Popcorn ready? I’ve even got a blanket for when you get all jumpy. Player-hater! Yes, let’s do it.

Right then, Grandad. Just winding down for the night. You’ve been remarkably chipper today, considering. Did you manage to watch the snooker? Chipper? I suppose I was. That young Judd Trump, eh? A whirlwind. Though, I still think Ronnie O’Sullivan is the real deal. A bit temperamental, of course, but magnificent when he’s on form. Did you record it, love? I did, yes. Thought you might want to see it again. So, tell me, how was your email check? Any spam trying to sell you miracle cures again? Always. At least twice a day. Offered me a villa in the Bahamas for a pittance. As if! I nearly showed you one, actually. Absolutely dreadful. All lime green and plastic furniture. Not like our old settee, no. That was proper leather. Remember that? Vaguely. It was  very  brown, wasn’t it? And slightly sticky in the summer. We need to do something about the furniture in here, you know. It’s all a bit… faded. I was thinking of looking on that… what’s it called, Wayfair? I saw a lovely little oak side table online. Wayfair? Sounds like something from a science fiction film. Online shopping. Honestly. Back in my day, you went to the shop, you touched the wood, you haggled with the salesman. Now, it's all flashing pictures and clever algorithms. It's rather disconcerting. It's convenient, though. And you can read reviews. Remember when I tried to explain Airbnb to you? Those holiday rentals? Paying someone to stay in their house? When you could just book a proper hotel? It seems a bit… precarious to me. Though, I suppose people are making a bit of money from it. Young people, mostly, struggling to make ends meet. Exactly. It’s a side hustle for a lot of folks. Actually, Auntie Susan was telling me about renting out a room in her cottage in Cornwall. Making a tidy sum. Speaking of making sums, did you ever look at that pizza delivery app I showed you? That... glowing rectangle! All those choices! Pepperoni? Hawaiian? What’s ‘vegan’ even mean? Give me a simple cheese and tomato any day. Used to get a decent pizza from Luigi's down the road in Wolverhampton. Proper Italian, he was. Not these chains. Right, old school pizza. I get it. I think I’ll order one in tomorrow. We could have a movie night.

Och, this is grand, isn’t it, Hamish? Just… grand. Proper peace and quiet. City life drains ye, doesn’t it? Even for a seasoned communications manager like myself. Aye, it does, Alistair. Drains ye dry. Though, I’ve found marking essays on the bus can be a strangely meditative experience. Less peaceful, mind you, with the screaming bairns and the busker butchering Oasis, but meditative nonetheless. Did you finish that Murakami you were telling me about?  Kafka on the Shore ? I did. Finished it last night. Right before drifting off. Honestly, Hamish, it fair burrowed under my skin. The whole weirdness of it, the cats, the talking fish… It was brilliant, wasn’t it? Proper unsettling, too. Reminded me a wee bit of a Lewis Grassic Gibbon novel, that sense of dreamlike reality interwoven with the ordinary. Have ye read any Gibbon? Aye, of course.  Sunset Song . Classics for a reason. Though I’ve always preferred  Sweet Dreams . So much sharper, I think. More brutally honest about the realities of rural life. Murakami… he’s got this knack for capturing that feeling of displacement, though. I’ve just finished “Norwegian Wood”. Quite different from  Kafka , less fantastical, more… melancholy. A real mood piece. I've heard good things about that one. It's on the list. My list is longer than the River Forth at this point, though. I was thinking, we should really get ourselves organised, shouldn't we? Like a proper reading group, just the two of us. We could dedicate a few evenings a month, discuss a book properly. No distractions, just… analysis and maybe a dram or two. I’d be up for that, Alistair. Sounds lovely, actually. We could even rotate themes. One month fiction, next month non-fiction. Could get quite… intellectual. Though, knowing us, we'll end up spending half the time arguing about the accuracy of the author’s depiction of ramen noodles. Aye, most likely! That’s the charm of it, isn’t it? Now, speaking of travels and other delights... Remember that trip we took to Japan ten years ago? The cherry blossoms in Kyoto? It still feels like a dream, doesn’t it? Like a perfectly preserved memory. The gardens, the temples... And the food! I’m convinced I gained a stone just from eating takoyaki. Do you remember trying to navigate the train system? Absolutely baffling at first, but then you got the hang of it.

Right, so, I've finished the draft cover letter. What do you think, Mum? It feels…flat. A bit lifeless, somehow. Let me have a look, love. Don’t fret. Most first drafts do feel a bit…not quite right. Which firm is it for again? The one near Shoreditch? Yeah, 'Archimedes & Blake'. Really prestigious, you know? Contemporary design, sustainable practices… it’s exactly what I want to be doing. That's why I'm trying to make the letter shine, but I'm struggling to convey my passion without sounding gushy. Hmm. It’s well-written, technically. No typos, good use of vocabulary. But you're right, it  does  read a bit…formal. A bit like you’re reciting facts rather than explaining why you  really  want this. See this bit? "Possessing a strong foundation in structural engineering principles…" Bit dry, isn't it? Yeah, I thought so. It felt like I had to list all my qualifications, didn’t it? Like a CV in paragraph form. Exactly. They already have your CV, darling. This letter is about showing them who  you  are. What excites you about their work. Remember that project they did, the community centre in Hackney? The one with the green roof? Oh, yes! Absolutely stunning. The way they integrated the natural elements… It was so innovative, and genuinely beneficial for the local community. There you go!  That ’s what they want to hear. Not just that you know about structural principles. Tell them you were inspired by that Hackney project. Tell them you admire their commitment to sustainable design and think your postgraduate research into passive solar heating could be valuable. Passive solar heating… Okay, yeah, I could weave that in. But I worry about sounding… conceited. Like I’m suggesting I can do better than them. No, no! It’s not about doing better. It's about showing you’re aligned with their values and have something to contribute. It’s about enthusiasm. Remember when you were little, and you’d tell me all about your Lego creations? You didn’t apologise for being excited; you just  told  me! This is the grown-up version of that. You always did have a way of putting things into perspective. It's funny, isn't it? I overthink everything with this job, but with Lego, I just built. Well, building a career is a bit more complicated than Lego, love.

Blimey, look at that drizzle, eh, Arthur? Proper Norfolk weather this is. Just like I used to see on the drive to work back when I was… well, you know. Aye, Harold. Drizzle it is.
