Blimey, Nan, this is proper weird. Leprechauns wear boots? I thought they were, like, little shoe-less fellas. It's a bit of artistic license, love. Don't you worry about it. It’s meant to be fun, isn’t it? Your mum found it in a charity shop. Said it reminded her of you and your imagination. Aye, it’s a charming wee story, even if the footwear is a bit unorthodox for a leprechaun. Though, I suppose in Ireland, you'll find all sorts! Remember old Mrs. MacIntyre, claiming to have seen a fairy riding a badger? Fairies riding badgers? That’s mental. Still, the pictures are good. Who drew them? They’re lovely, aren’t they? I don’t know who did, it just doesn’t say. But look at this one, of the little leprechaun hiding behind the shamrock. It reminds me of Finn when he was little, always trying to sneak extra biscuits. Finn? My Finn? He's, like, a massive teenager now, practically a man. He wouldn't hide behind a shamrock. He'd be, I dunno, playing Fortnite or something. Time flies, doesn't it? Seems like yesterday I was teaching your mum in primary school. A bright, clever girl, always asking questions. She reminded me a bit of myself, actually. Driven. She had a fire in her belly. She does, doesn’t she? You know, sometimes I think about how different things would be if… well, if your dad had stuck around more. It'd be easier, wouldn’t it? Getting Finn to understand things, to appreciate… well, everything. He does appreciate things. He just shows it differently. He bought me that new controller, didn't he? The one I wanted. Of course, he did, love. He’s a good lad. But he needs stability, you know? He needs to feel…rooted. Like a good family tree. Remember how we used to look at the family tree Mum made, the one with all the faded photos? Aye, a grand tree it was. Going back generations. I remember painstakingly researching all those names, verifying birthdates, marriages… So much history in those few branches. Your great-grandfather, William, was a shipbuilder. Tough man. Didn’t have much, but he worked hard. Are we actually going to look at the tree later? I wanna see if I'm related to anyone famous. Probably not though, we’re all just… Bristol, aren't we?

Right, finally finished marking those essays. Honestly, some of ‘em were… a right mess. Like they hadn’t even  looked  at the reading list. Tell me about it. My tutor's been on my case about the feedback turnaround time. Apparently, I’m supposed to be providing ‘constructive criticism’ within 48 hours. As if I have time to craft literary masterpieces about student essays  and  actually attend my own lectures. Aye, that sounds stressful. I’m lucky, I just get the occasional passive-aggressive email from the head of department if I'm a bit behind. But 48 hours? That's brutal. What are you studying again? Something fancy, weren't you? Archaeology. It  does  sound fancy, but mostly it involves sifting through dirt and trying to convince people that a slightly chipped pot shard is actually incredibly significant. Sounds like me marking essays, to be honest. Digging through depths of… well, not dirt, but questionable grammar and tenuous arguments. So, did you manage to get that vintage market stall sorted? You were saying about wanting to sell some knitted things. Yeah, I did! Got a spot booked for the weekend. Little bit nervous, though, to be honest. What if no one buys anything? I mean, I enjoy knitting, but I'm not expecting to become wildly rich off it. You’ll be grand, love. You make proper good stuff. People are always lookin' for somethin’ a bit different, a bit handmade. Don't you worry your head. Speaking of different… I was thinkin’ about somethin’ earlier. Right, this might be a weird thing to bring up, but… Bring it on. You’ve told me weirder things while eating Yorkshire pudding. Right, well… I was lookin' in the mirror this mornin', and I was thinkin' about… body hair. Body hair? Seriously? That’s what you’ve been wrestling with after marking hideous essays? It's a valid thing to think about! I mean, everyone’s got it, right? But everyone seems to either shave everything off or… don't. There's not much in between. I’ve been thinkin’ about just… letting it be, y’know? On my legs, mostly. I get it. It’s a whole… societal pressure thing, isn't it? I used to religiously shave every other day when I was younger. Felt like I  had  to. Then, last year, I just… stopped. Really? Just stopped? Yep. Couldn't be bothered.

Right, so you're saying you genuinely spent an entire afternoon trying to alphabetize your spice rack? Like, meticulously? Don’t knock it till you’ve tried it, Beth. It was surprisingly… meditative. And, frankly, needed. It was a chaotic mess. Cloves next to cayenne, paprika under parsley… utter anarchy. Plus, it uncovered a packet of star anise I'd completely forgotten about. Unexpected bonus. You're a special one, you are. Meditative spice rack alphabetizing. Only you, Liam. You’d find tranquility rearranging pebbles. Well, someone’s gotta maintain order in the universe, eh? Speaking of order, you were talking about dialects earlier. Did you ever get to explain why the alphabet itself is so… weird? I mean, think about it - 'q' is almost unused, ‘x’ is a nightmare to pronounce, and what’s even the point of 'z'? It's a historical mess. Aye, it is, isn’t it? It’s all leftover baggage from different invasions and languages mixing and mingling over centuries. Like a right bog of history, our language is. The 'q' is a proper relic, hanging on by its fingernails. They tried to get rid of it at one point, I reckon. Exactly! Makes you wonder why we can’t just start fresh, eh? Invent a proper logical alphabet. Easier to learn, easier to use. Less chance of embarrassing mispronunciations. Now you're getting ahead of yourself. It’s comforting, isn’t it? That slightly wonky, unpredictable nature of it all. Like a familiar friend who always does things a bit sideways. Besides, who’d want to lose all the rhyme and reason in poetry? It'd be right dull. Point taken. Though, I still think a standardized phonetic alphabet would make a world of difference. Less confusion. Less misunderstanding. Which, incidentally, brings me to something I was reading about... racism in football. It's… it’s just appalling, isn't it? The vitriol online, the stuff they’re shouting from the terraces. Aye. Horrendous. Absolute disgrace. Makes you ashamed to even be associated with the sport sometimes. And it’s not just blokes, is it? Women are being targeted too. It’s a bleedin’ cancer. I saw that thing on Sky Sports, the one about the abuse Marcus Rashford got… turned me right off my dinner. It’s the anonymity, I think. It emboldens people to say things they’d  never  say face to face.

Right, so the application for the Heritage Lottery Fund is due in two weeks. I’ve wrestled with the ‘community engagement’ section for hours. It feels… performative, somehow. Like ticking a box rather than genuinely reflecting what we hope to achieve with the restoration of the old mill. Oh, darling, welcome to the world of grant applications. Performative is a rather polite word for it. They  want  to see boxes ticked. But you can't let that completely dictate your approach. You need to weave that genuine desire into the performance. Tell a story. People respond to stories. Easier said than done, isn't it? The mill’s history is fascinating—it powered the village for centuries, significant in the wool trade—but tying that to a modern community… well, they mostly use it as a shortcut to the supermarket now. They do, don’t they? Well, you need to find the threads. What are people  already  doing around the mill? Any local artists using the river for inspiration? Any schools showing an interest in local industrial history? Even if it’s tenuous, latch onto it. And remember, ‘community engagement’ isn’t just about generating buzz. It’s about ownership. Making people feel invested in the outcome. That’s true. I was focusing so much on grand workshops and open days I forgot about the smaller connections. Perhaps involving the local history group in documenting oral histories? They’re always keen. Absolutely. And don’t underestimate the power of a simple ‘Friends of the Mill’ scheme. Little and often, that builds trust. I recall with the old vicarage in Kent... Dreadful state, leaky roof threatening to collapse. The grant application landed flat until we got the Women's Institute to organise a bake sale and a guided tour. Suddenly, everyone was invested– they wanted  their  vicarage saved. Raised a surprising amount, too. A bake sale! That's brilliant. It's so much more relatable than projections and structural engineers’ reports. Have you ever had an application rejected purely because the business plan was… unrealistic? Constantly. They’re not looking for utopia, you know. They're looking for a believable path to sustainability. You need to show them, not just  tell  them, how the mill will generate income beyond the initial restoration. Think beyond the obvious. Tourism is good, certainly, but what else? Could you offer studio space for creatives? Classes – pottery, weaving – tapping into that ‘make’ culture?

Right, that’s a proper brew, then. Strong enough to stand a spoon in, like me mam used to make. You still reckon Earl Grey’s the only way to go, do ya? Honestly, a bit weak for me taste, it is. I appreciate a good Earl Grey, yes. It’s… refined. But I’m not averse to a builder’s tea, especially when it's being made by someone who clearly knows what they’re doing. Sunderland strong, I presume? Aye, that's the one. Learned it at the source. So, you were saying earlier about your research... something about semantic drift in, what was it, archaic dialects? Sounds proper complicated. It is, a bit. Essentially, I’m tracking how the meanings of words have changed over centuries, specifically in West Midlands dialects. There's a fascinating example with "smell.” You know, like, a scent. But back in the 16th century, it could also mean ‘to brag’ or ‘to boast.’ The connection is… obscure, to say the least. So, I'm trying to unravel how that evolution happened. Blimey. So, like, words just…shift? Is there a reason for it? Is it just people being daft, or… It's far more nuanced than people being daft, though sometimes it feels like it! There are social factors, geographical isolation, linguistic influence from other areas… a whole web of things. Think about how “like” is used now, mostly as a filler. It's a relatively recent phenomenon, born out of Californian slang that trickled into the UK. That’s mad, innit? I never thought about it like that. My Nana used to say ‘like’ when she meant ‘as if’. Totally different! It's funny, isn't it, how things change. Makes you think about how folk will be looking at our slang in 200 years, thinkin’ we were a right bunch of weirdos. Exactly! It's about understanding the historical context behind language. I’m using a massive corpus of early English texts - stuff like Paston letters and early plays - and computationally analysing them to track these shifts. It's a bit of a beast, to be honest. A beast! That sounds like a right headache. You’re workin’ yourself to the bone, aren’t you? You need a holiday. Seriously. Where are you thinkin’ of going when you finish? Somewhere sunny, I hope. No more rainy Cambridge for a while, eh?

Right, so, school dinners. Let’s tackle this. Poppy, Leo, tell me honestly, are you actually  eating  anything? Not just pushing it around the plate, actually eating it? Sometimes. The chips are good. The sausages are mostly nice! But sometimes they’re… rubbery. Rubbery sausages. That’s a very accurate description, Leo. See, that's what I need to know! Are they generally edible? Because I’m starting to feel like I’m throwing money away every week. They send home half-eaten plates constantly. I like the pasta on Tuesday. With the tomato sauce. But Tuesday is pizza day! I know! But I like the pasta better. Right. Okay. Pizza day is your favourite, Leo. Note to self. Poppy, what about you? Anything you deem worthy of consumption? The yoghurts are good. Orange ones. Okay, orange yoghurt it is. We’ll focus on that. Listen, I was thinking... if you’re not eating much, maybe I should just pack you both lunches. At least then I know you’re getting something you like. But… it’s another thing to organize, isn’t it? Especially with the tennis tournament coming up. Tennis tournament?! I’m going to win! I practiced my serve! I’m sure you will, darling. Big tournament on Saturday, remember? We need to make sure you’ve got your white shorts and everything. And a good lunch, of course. Maybe a little picnic? Can we have sandwiches? Cucumber sandwiches? Cucumber sandwiches? Really, Poppy? For a tennis tournament? You'll be playing in the sun! I want sausage rolls! Like Granny makes! Yes, Granny’s sausage rolls are legendary. Speaking of Granny, are you two looking forward to seeing her next weekend? She's really keen on you both coming over. She's promised to make that rhubarb crumble you both love. Yes! Can we play in her garden? And see the cat? And she always lets me build a tower with the cushions on the sofa! Higher than I’m allowed at home! Well, I’m sure she won't mind a cushion tower, will she? It'll be lovely to see her. It’s just… running around to Granny’s, the tennis tournament, and trying to feed you both properly… it’s all a bit much sometimes. The school sends these notes home about healthy eating and balanced diets, then serve rubbery sausages! Did you ever go to the circus, Mummy?

That film, “The Banshees of Inisherin,” wasn’t it just… beautifully bleak? I mean, the scenery was stunning, of course, but the story. So simple, yet so devastating. Did you both find it as affecting as I did, David? Affecting? Aye, I found it a bit… well, gloomy, lass. A man refusing to speak to another. Seems a bit daft, doesn’t it? All over a fiddle tune. Though the scenery  was  lovely. Reminded me a bit of the Chilterns, actually, in the autumn. Daft, maybe, but brilliantly observed, wouldn’t you say? It’s about legacy, about what we leave behind, and the fear of being forgotten. Especially poignant now, I think, with everything going on. And the performances were incredible. Colm Meaney, honestly, stole the show. Absolutely. And it just felt so… honest, you know? Unlike so much of what we see these days. Reminds me of that debate I went to at King's the other week – about teaching history. It was fascinating, although utterly exhausting. All these academics arguing about whether to focus on ‘grand narratives’ or micro-histories. History, eh? They were messing about with history when I was at school. Dates and battles, mostly. Not much about ordinary folk. Though I did enjoy learning about the Romans. Always liked that lot. Building roads and baths, sensible chaps. Sensible, perhaps, in a conquering sort of way, Dad. It's funny, though, that debate. It really highlighted how fractured the national curriculum is at the moment. It's often criticised as being too broad, too shallow. Trying to cram everything in, without allowing for real depth. Exactly! And it’s not just the content, it’s the teaching methods too. This professor was arguing for a more ‘inquiry-based’ approach, encouraging students to question everything. It sounds lovely in theory, but it’s incredibly difficult to implement in a class of thirty Year 8s! I end up spending half my time just managing behaviour. Year 8s, you say? My goodness. When I was a lad, you were expected to have some manners. A bit of respect for your teachers. Nowadays… Times have changed, Dad. Though I agree, a little respect goes a long way. Listen, speaking of education and the future… I was just thinking about my niece, Eleanor. She's starting to apply for universities. She wants to go into advertising, naturally, a wee bit biased, I suppose.

Cor blimey, this damp’s got right into me bones, it 'as. Been a right miserable day, 'asn’t it? Could practically taste the fog comin' in off the marshes this mornin'. It has, Arthur. Positively dreary. Though I did manage to get the washing in before it started really pouring. Remember the summer of '76? Now that was a summer. Dry as a bone, it were. Not a drop of rain for weeks. You youngsters probably wouldn’t appreciate it. Constant rain seemingly suits you. The Met Office gets it all wrong, doesn't it? Always predicting sunshine and we get deluge. Always, David. They're a hopeless bunch. Typical Westminster mismanagement, really. Though, thinking about summers, I recall my grandfather used to tell stories about rationing during the war... dry summers, of course, meant poorer harvests and even stricter rationing. Hard to imagine now, isn't it? Rationin'. I remember a bit of it, mind you. I was just a lad, but me mother used to queue for hours just for a bit of sugar and butter. They said it was the ‘shut yer gob and get on with it’ generation, weren’t they? Never complained, though. Not like today. It's true. My mother talked incessantly about the wartime sacrifices. Losing her brother, Albert, in Italy... she never really got over it. He was so young, barely nineteen. Lovely boy, apparently. Never knew 'im myself, of course. My father fought in North Africa. Didn’t talk about it much. Came back a changed man, I think. Quiet, withdrawn. Just… different. Took him years to adjust, if he ever truly did. Built up a successful business after the war, though. Started small, just selling timber. Became quite the local employer. It’s amazing how many families were touched, isn’t it? My father was a policeman during the Blitz. He used to tell me stories about the sirens, the blackout, the sheer terror people felt. Imagine being responsible for keeping order amidst all that chaos. Police, eh? Had a bit of bother with ‘em meself, once. Years ago now. Thought I was nicked for pilfering an apple from old Mr. Grimshaw’s orchard. Never did, thankfully. Bloke 'ad a soft spot for me, he did. Always let me 'ave a few fallen apples to feed the chickens. Arthur! You and your chickens. Are they still going strong, then? Still peckin' away, they are.

Right then, so, Northampton. Last time in this car heading this way for a while, isn't it? Feels… weird. Bit melancholy, actually. Aye, it does a bit. Mum’s place, eh? Been a good twenty-odd years, hasn't it, since your mum and I bought that little bungalow? Seems like yesterday we were arguing about the shade of beige for the kitchen cupboards. Beige! God, that was awful. I remember wanting really bright blue, and you guys were adamant beige was "sensible." Still, it's been a lovely base for us, hasn't it? All those Christmases… Lovely, yes. Though, I still reckon you hid more presents in that airing cupboard than a department store. You were a tricky one, you know. Always plotting. Guilty as charged. So, about the movers... Have you spoken to them again? Just to confirm everything's still on track for next Tuesday? I'm a bit stressed about that deadline, you know. Between setting up the new place and finishing up my contract at the language school... Spoke to them this morning. They’re booked in, Tuesday’s the day. They seemed reliable enough, gave me a good quote too. Don’t you fret, love. You've done enough fretting already. Are you sure you’re feeling alright? You seem a bit… drained. Just tired, really. Trying to pack my life into boxes is surprisingly emotionally taxing. Plus, I’ve got that persistent cough. I think it’s just a cold, but… A cough, eh? You need to be careful. Last thing we need is you getting poorly right before the move. Remember what the doctor said about your allergies? The air quality up in Manchester is different. Yeah, I remember. Trying to factor that in with my finances, actually. Allergy medication isn’t cheap. That's one of the things I’m worrying about, you know? Balancing the mortgage with everything else. It’s… a lot. Don't you worry about the mortgage. We talked about this. You're doing the right thing, getting your own place. Builds independence, gives you a bit of breathing room. We’ll help out with the initial payments, you know that. Always have, always will. Remember when I was trying to save for my first car? You were forever “helping” me – which usually involved ‘borrowing’ my pocket money. Oh, don't remind me! I thought I was being clever, actually.

Right, let’s tackle this. Mum's birthday is next Saturday, and we need a plan. I'm feeling a bit overwhelmed already, to be honest. Don't be, Auntie Sarah! We'll get it sorted. It’s just a bit of organisation. So, food first, yeah? You were talking about maybe a roast? I was. But I’m not sure if a full-on roast is too much. She gets tired so easily now, doesn't she? And it’s a lot of work for me. Perhaps something a bit lighter? Maybe chicken with roasted vegetables? Less carving, easier to eat. Yeah, chicken's good. Can we do, like, lemon and herb? She loves that. And what about potatoes? Roasties, or mashed? Mashed, definitely. Much easier on her jaw. And green beans, I think. Brighten everything up a bit. Oh, and stuffing! She always likes stuffing. Right, chicken, mashed potato, green beans, stuffing. Got it. Dessert? We need to think about something she'll actually enjoy. Remember last year with the trifle? She barely touched it! Don't remind me! Too much cream, apparently. We need something simpler. Maybe a crumble? Apple or rhubarb? Apple. Definitely apple. With custard! And can we get those little candles for it? The sparkly ones? Good idea! I’ll add that to the list. Right, seating plan then. This is always tricky. Uncle George gets grumpy if he’s not near the window. And Grandma needs to be somewhere she can hear everyone easily. Right, so George by the window. Grandma... How about next to you, Auntie Sarah? You can keep an eye on her. And I’ll put cousin Emily on her other side - she's good at chatting. That sounds sensible. Though, it does make me think… I was clearing out some of the cupboards the other day, and I found a box of old photographs. I really should get them out and show Grandma. She might enjoy looking through them. Oh, that's a lovely idea! We could do it after dinner, while we're all having coffee. It might bring back some nice memories for her. Yes, it might. Although, sometimes those memories… they become a bit muddled, don't they? It's hard to watch. I read an article the other day about the early signs of dementia. It's quite worrying, actually. I know. It is. It’s just… we have to focus on making her happy now, right?

Right, so, this dentist… honestly, Chloe. He looked like he’d never seen a wisdom tooth in his life. Just prodded about with this little hook thing, makin’ a right mess o’ me gums. Oh, you are being dramatic, Maisie! It's just a bit uncomfortable. My mum said getting hers out was like being abducted by aliens. Abducted by aliens? Seriously? Mine felt more like a badger attack, to be fair. And the cost! They’re bleedin' expensive, aren’t they? Not like back home, where the NHS… well, you know. At least you can  try  to get somethin' for free. Here, it’s just… straight out of your pocket. Tell me about it. Everything's more expensive here. And the language barrier doesn’t exactly help when you're trying to haggle over a cavity filling. Speaking of holes... did you finally get that one on your molar checked out? The one you were moanin’ about before we left? Aye, reet. Got it filled! Thankfully. It was startin’ to proper throb. Dentist was a right character, though. Kept tryin’ to tell me about the benefits of flossing with seaweed. Seaweed, Chloe! Like I’m gonna be brushin' me teeth with that. Only in France! Honestly, my parents are driving me mad already. They sent the longest email this morning. Apparently, my dad spent three hours arguing with the council about the garden fence. Something about it being 2cm too high. 2cm! Typical dad behaviour. Mine’s currently obsessed with getting a ‘smart thermostat’ installed. Says it’ll save us a fortune. I’m thinkin’ it'll just give him somethin’ else to tinker with and yell at when it doesn’t work properly. My dad is the same. Utterly convinced he's an expert in everything. It’s exhausting. Are you even remotely thinking about heading back to uni next week? Everything's a bit of a muddle, isn't it? My lease is ending, I’m supposed to be lookin' at new places… It is a right mess. I’m still tryin' to sort out the house situation. Mum's been fussin' something awful. Says she needs me to come back and “help with the dogs” for a few days before move-in day. Which, let's be honest, is code for “sort out a mountain of laundry and eat several dinners of overcooked Yorkshire puddings.”

Right, I’m thinking this lactose-free chocolate cake recipe is actually quite good. A bit drier than the regular one, naturally, but with a good buttercream, no one will notice. You two like chocolate, don't you? Chocolate! Yes! Can I lick the bowl, Mummy? Please? Absolutely not, darling. It’s still got eggs in it. Remember what happened last time? You ended up covered head to toe. But you  can  help me decorate it later. Maybe we can use some of those little jelly beans. Is it the dragon year? It is, sweetheart! That's exactly right. Chinese New Year's nearly here. Do you know what a dragon symbolises? Powerful? Like a knight? Very good! Powerful, lucky, and strong. Lots of red and gold, fireworks, special food… and giving lucky red envelopes with money inside. Money! Can I have a red envelope? Of course, you can, my love. But remember, that’s for luck and to share the happiness. We'll think of someone we can give one to as well, okay? Speaking of which, we were talking about doing acts of kindness, weren't we? Remember that list we started? The kindness list! I wrote "give flowers to Mrs. Higgins!" She looks sad. That's a brilliant idea! You're right, she does look a bit down. We could do that tomorrow. What about you, darling? Any thoughts on our kindness list? Maybe... maybe we could let Mr. Peterson have all the Chess pieces? He’s always asking to play. Mr. Peterson? You mean the retired accountant from next door? The one who's always wearing that tweed jacket? Yeah. He said he lost his set ages ago. We could give him ours. That’s… surprisingly thoughtful, that is. I always thought you two were just using those pieces as pretend money! Remember the other day when you were using them to buy imaginary sweets? “One knight, please, for a lollipop!” They  are  good money. I bought a whole castle! They are, aren't they? But giving them to Mr. Peterson... that's a really kind thing to do. It would really cheer him up, I reckon. He seems a bit lonely sometimes. Alright then, we’ll add “Loan Mr. Peterson our Chess pieces” to the kindness list. That’s really very sweet of you, love. What else can we do? Can I dye my hair blue?

Honestly, Mum, school's just… draining. Mrs. Davies keeps going on about symbolism in  Alice in Wonderland . Symbolism! Like, a talking rabbit is  obviously  symbolic. What else is it supposed to be, a rabbit that can talk? Well, she’s trying to get you to think deeper, love. It’s a classic for a reason. Remember how you used to dress up as Alice for World Book Day? You had the most amazing blue dress. Yeah, well, Chloe dressed as Hermione and everyone thought she was so clever. My Alice costume was just… a dress. She made it look like she understood the whole “looking glass” thing. Don’t be daft. Your costume was brilliant. And you  did  understand the story. You were completely captivated by it. Remember how you insisted on having a tea party afterward with all your stuffed animals? Don't remind me. Barnaby the bear got jam all over his face. Anyway, it’s not the same as understanding literary theory, is it? And seriously, the week’s been awful. That awful crash near the pier… did you see it on the news? I did. Dreadful, wasn’t it? Right outside the bakery. I hope everyone’s alright. Poor drivers, must have been terrifying. Did they say what caused it? They think it was icy. It happened right after that freezing rain we had on Tuesday. I was walking home from basketball practice then, and I nearly slipped, Mum! Gave me a proper fright. You’re a good basketball player, you know that? You’re getting really strong. Just be careful out there. Anything else happening at school? Still obsessed with that band, 'Static Bloom'? Oh my god, yes! They're releasing a new single next week. I’ve pre-ordered the limited edition vinyl - it's turquoise! It’s so cool. I saw a video online of them rehearsing. Finn, the drummer, has this amazing scar on his arm. It’s like, a really long, jagged one. It's kinda... awesome. Awesome? A scar? That sounds quite painful, darling. Honestly, you teens and your fascination with the unconventional. It reminds me of when I was your age. I had a little scar on my knee from falling off my bike – I thought it made me look like a rebel. You, a rebel? Mum, you used to read Austen! Don’t underestimate the subversive power of a good romance novel!

Honestly, Arthur, it's just exhausting. Last night’s meeting with the Sunbeam Valley group... all so earnest, so worried. They've got these solar farms proposed for prime agricultural land. It mirrored so much what you were telling me about the Willow Creek situation, doesn’t it? Just… scale difference, really. Absolutely, Margaret. The core anxieties are the same. Loss of landscape, potential impact on wildlife, the feeling that decisions are being rushed through. You were very good with them last night, you know. Pointing out the importance of scrutinising the ecological impact assessments. They were hanging on your every word. Ecological impact assessments! Don't get me started. Willow Creek's assessment was riddled with inaccuracies. Apparently, the report claimed there were no nesting skylarks in the area when I’ve been watching them for thirty years! These companies, they pay good money for reports that fit their narrative. Precisely. And the council… well, I'm not going to name names, but Councillor Davies seems awfully keen on pushing these applications through. Says it’s "progress," “sustainable energy,” all that nonsense. Doesn’t seem to factor in the displacement of sheep farmers and the visual pollution. They’re all too enamoured with the glossy brochures and the promises of jobs, aren’t they? The Development Control Committee is a minefield. You’ve got your local planners, pressured by the council, swayed by the energy companies... it's a complex web to navigate. And the Planning Appeal! That’s the real kicker. They refuse it, and then the company lodges an appeal with the national planning inspectorate. The costs involved in fighting that are astronomical. You need specialist legal advice, expert witnesses... That’s what I tried to emphasize to the Sunbeam Valley group. They need to be meticulous. Every 'i' dotted, every 't' crossed. Do your research. Understand the relevant planning policies inside and out. Find independent experts who can challenge the company’s claims. Absolutely. It's not enough just to say "we don't like it." You have to demonstrate  why  it's detrimental, using facts and solid evidence. Do you remember that case in Kent, years ago, with the biomass plant? They got away with it because the local opposition was disorganised and didn’t have their facts straight. The politics of it all are the most frustrating. It’s not just the local level, either.

Right then, Eleanor. This is… a lot, isn’t it? All these little diagrams and road signs. Remember when I was learning? They didn't have all this fancy colour coding back then. Just a simple book and a bit of grit, if I'm honest. Dad, you learned to drive in a Morris Minor! That’s practically prehistoric. And you did it on country lanes, not the M6. Things have changed. This booklet helps. Break it down, one section at a time. We can go through it together later. Don't overwhelm the poor girl, Arthur. It's stressful enough learning to drive as it is. Eleanor, love, you’re doing brilliantly, aren’t you? I remember when I was doing my test. Nearly swerved into a lamppost trying to parallel park. Absolutely mortifying. The examiner just sighed and said, 'Well, that was certainly  a  parking attempt, wasn’t it?' Still passed though, thankfully. Thanks, Mum. Yeah, it’s okay, I think. I managed a decent three-point turn in the Tesco car park yesterday. Almost. I stalled it twice. Stalling is perfectly normal, Eleanor. Don’t let it put you off. I used to stall Brenda’s Mini regularly. She wasn’t too pleased, I can tell you. Brenda? Was that your first girlfriend, Dad? A youthful indiscretion, that’s all. Anyway, back to the matter at hand. This insurance business… it’s daylight robbery, isn't it? I got a quote for myself last year, and it was extortionate. Sixty quid a month just to drive to the garden centre! It  is  outrageous. You’re young, Eleanor, so you’ll be hit with the higher risk tariffs. Mum and I were looking at travel insurance the other day – similar story. They know us oldies are desperate for a holiday! I've been comparing quotes online. It’s mental. Learner driver insurance is even more ridiculous. Mum, remember you were saying you might go to Cornwall next week? That’s the plan, dear. Just a little break. Been working too hard. Need some sea air. Little cottage near St Ives. Peaceful. I'm already wishing I was there. What about you both? Any plans for the week? Besides Dad terrorising the theory test book? I am not terrorising! I am… engaging with the material! And as for plans, beyond helping Eleanor, I’m hoping to finish tidying the shed.

Honestly, Dad, the parking in Brighton is an absolute nightmare. I spent twenty minutes circling just to find a space the other day, and when I did, it was a double yellow. Could’ve sworn I saw a parking enforcement officer lurking, eyes gleaming. Brighton, eh? Always was a bit of a madhouse. Remember when your mum and I went down there for a weekend in ‘68? Couldn’t find anywhere to park the Mini, ended up a mile and a half away. Walked the whole way! Gave us blisters, it did. Blisters are the least of it. You’re paying a fortune for the privilege of driving around in circles. I'm seriously considering getting rid of the car altogether, just rely on buses and trains. Except getting to the stables with all the kit… that's impossible. Stables still going then? Good, good. Always liked horses. Reminds me of seeing the Grand National on the telly back in the fifties. Black and white, of course. You had to really concentrate, couldn't miss a thing. Exciting stuff. Did you have a bet on this weekend’s races? A little flutter, yeah. Nothing major. Trying to be sensible these days. It's always tempting though, isn't it? Especially when you see a horse with a good name. This one's called "Royal Ascent", sounds promising. Names can be deceiving. It’s the form that matters, love. The form. Always been the form. Used to know a man, down the pub, reckons he could predict the winner just by looking at the horse's legs. Said it was all about the tendons. Never quite believed him myself. Right. My betting strategy is a lot less scientific. I just pick a colour I like. Speaking of betting, I did see something on Facebook the other day about… well, people are using it to organize food banks. Supporting each other. Facebook, eh? Can't get my head round that thing. Too much scrolling, not enough real conversation. And those notifications! Ping, ping, ping, all the time. Distracting. Remember when a phone call was an event? Now it's just relentless. I know! I have them all muted mostly. But it's good for connecting with people, seeing what’s going on. Plus, the local stables group uses it to organize rides and share news. It's easier than posting flyers on the village notice board these days.

Honestly, I still can’t believe Professor Davies marked me down on the Hamlet essay for “over-reliance on modern interpretations.” Like, what's the point of studying Shakespeare if you can’t apply it to, you know,  now ? He acts like we're supposed to all be reciting the First Folio in Old English. Davies, eh? Sounds about right. He always seemed to relish being a gatekeeper of literary purity. Remember when he nearly had a coronary because someone suggested Romeo and Juliet was about teenagers crashing under the weight of parental expectations? He insisted it was purely about 'courtly love' and the tragedy of feuding families. So very… theatrical. Ridiculous, wasn’t it? It’s easy to fall into the trap of just being sarcastic with Shakespeare, though. It's too ripe for it. I had to reel myself in a few times during the writing process. I almost included a footnote saying, "Yes, I realise the Prince is stating the obvious - just thought you'd like a bit of self-awareness sprinkled in." Oh god, you absolute menace! That would have been legendary. You’d have been expelled. Though, to be fair, sarcasm is practically  in  Shakespeare. He weaponized it. Look at Iago! Entirely driven by passive-aggressive remarks and subtle digs. Exactly! It’s layered. It's not just some dusty old play. Anyway, speaking of skill learning… did you ever manage to get the hang of that golf simulator your dad got? Don’t even ask. It’s a money pit that humiliates me. My dad's ecstatic, though. He keeps saying, "It's all about strategy, lad! You just need to  learn  to win." As if applying business school logic to hitting a tiny ball is going to suddenly make me a golfing prodigy. I’ve sunk more money into range balls than I have into my textbooks this semester. Sounds about right. My grandpa's the same way with Sudoku. He’ll critique your strategy like you're negotiating a multi-million pound deal. He called my last attempt 'a display of reckless abandon'. My grandmother is similar! She’s obsessed with genealogy. Has this impressive chart stretching back to the 1600s. We’re all ‘descendants of Smythe’ apparently. Smythe! It sounds like something out of a newspaper cartoon. Smythe? Seriously? That  is  ridiculously on the nose. My family surname is Hawthorne. So dreadfully cliché, isn’t it?

Right, so, another Monday bites the dust. Honestly, this conference at the Birmingham NEC next week is gonna kill me. It’s HUGE. Like, hundreds of exhibitors, thousands of attendees. I’ve got a spreadsheet bigger than my flat. Birmingham, eh? Bit far for a Monday morning commute, innit? Sounds stressful though. What kind of conference is it? It’s a renewable energy one. All solar panels and wind turbines and stuff. Honestly, I can barely tell the difference anymore. My brain’s completely glazed over from power points and jargon. I just have to make sure the coffee flows and the stands are sparkling. It’s not exactly intellectually stimulating, is it? Sounds glamorous, in its own way. Though I can imagine the pressure. My job's stressful, but it’s mostly in my head. You’re juggling everyone's expectations, aren’t you? Exactly! And then there's the vendors… Don't even get me started on Brenda from "Sustainable Soaps." She thinks her lavender-scented handwash is more vital than the entire electricity grid. Sounds like a character. So, are you getting any downtime at all during the week? Honestly, not much. I'm staying in a hotel near the NEC, so I can at least collapse into a proper bed at night. It's a bit lonely, though. I miss having a proper kitchen, you know? Living in that tiny studio flat in Leeds is fine for a while, saves money, but it’s not exactly conducive to, like, proper cooking. I hear you. London living is… an experience. You realize how much space you value when you’re sharing a two-bed with two other people. And for the price! I’m seriously considering moving out further out once my lease is up. Somewhere with a garden, maybe. A proper kitchen, like you said. That's a good shout. This area’s not bad, though. Peaceful. Not much happens, mind. Which is nice, sometimes. Peaceful is one word for it. Boring is another. I need a bit of a buzz in my life. Though, maybe after Birmingham, some peace  will  be welcome. Moving out further from London is expensive though, isn't it? I'm trying to be good with money this year. Reckon I need to get serious about my diet. I’ve started meal prepping - mostly salads. Very dull, but helps. Salad? You’re brave, lass.

Cor blimey, Brenda, you’re looking right perky today! The light's good in Harrow, innit? Much better than this gloom over Norwich. Feels like November already, even though it's barely August. You too, Arthur. Bit grey on ya, though! Are you still pottering about in that garden of yours? I swear, last time I saw it, it was overflowing with things. Overflowing is right, Derek! It’s become a proper jungle, hasn't it? Been trying to get some order amongst it, bit of a challenge, mind. See, I’ve put up this bamboo - a bit of a gamble, read it can be a right menace, but I fancied a bit of height. And over there… well, you'll see in a minute. . Hello, my loves! Arthur, that bamboo  is  impressive, though I agree, sounds like a handful. Derek, you're looking well, dear. Did you get that shed sorted finally? Nearly finished, Brenda. Just need to put the final screws in. Found a whole box of them I’d completely forgotten about, tucked away in the old toolbox. Amazing, innit? Remember when your dad used to build things, Brenda? Always had a shed full of bits and bobs. Speaking of amazing… did you manage to catch any of that eclipse yesterday? I missed the peak, sadly, was inside having a cuppa, as you do. It was rather lovely, actually. Didn’t get the full dark effect here, but still, the sky turned a gorgeous shade of orange. Made me think about… well, you know, all that space stuff. Black holes and the cosmos and beginnings. Aye, gets you thinking, doesn't it? All that vastness. Always been fascinated by it, I have. Mind you, some of that science is a bit beyond me now. All this talk of quantum entanglement and… and gravity waves. Used to understand structures, bridges, that kind of thing. Now I’m struggling to grasp a black hole. You and me both, Arthur. All this scientific jargon! Remember when they used to just say the planets went round the sun? Simpler times, weren't they? Though, I do like that painting programme on the telly. The one with the fella who paints landscapes. Oh yes! I love that one. . We’re trying to do a bit of painting ourselves, Derek. Little watercolour landscapes. Not brilliant, mind you. Watercolour, eh? Fancy! I’m hopeless at anything artistic.

Honestly, this roundabout is giving me the willies. Three lanes, and nobody knows what they're doing. It's like a Stockton bus station at rush hour, I swear. Bit dramatic, aren't we, love? It's just a roundabout. They’re designed to improve traffic flow. Though, I’ll admit, this one  is  a bit chaotic. Did you see that bloke try to merge from the outside lane? Reckless. Reckless? That’s putting it mildly! He nearly clipped a Fiesta. I swear, people just don’t pay attention. You'd think, being in a car, you’d actually  drive  the car. Back home, we've got smaller roundabouts. More manageable, you know? Proper sensible ones. Smaller ones probably have less traffic. We’re near Guildford, remember? It’s a commuter town. Everyone's rushing somewhere. Anyway, fancy that new Italian place, ‘Bella Notte’? Sarah said it was brilliant. Bella Notte? Oh, aye. I saw something about it online. Is it posh? Because if it's posh, I'm away. I’m not wearing heels and pretending I understand truffle oil, you know? Remember that place we went in Winchester last year? Honestly, I felt like an alien. Mon Dieu this and fleur de sel that… Alright, alright. No need to get dramatic again! It’s not  that  posh, apparently. Just good food. I was thinking we could go on Saturday? After we look at that house in Farnham. The house? Oh, right! The one with the… the wonky chimneys? You’re sure it’s worth a look? Farnham is proper far out though, isn't it? Like, miles. We could’ve just taken the bus from Guildford. It would’ve been cheaper. The bus would take forever. And it's a potential investment, love. We've talked about needing more space. Plus, it has a garden. I’m thinking the cat could use a bit of outside time. Aye, Mittens does seem a bit stir-crazy lately. Still, that garden better be big enough for her to chase pigeons without me having to intervene. Honestly, those pigeons in Guildford are fearless. They practically land on your head. We’ll sort it out. I’ve already checked the train lines near Farnham. Good connections to London. We could pop down for a show now and then. Have you ever been to Salisbury Cathedral? Salisbury Cathedral? Nah. We don’t do much cathedral-going back home.

Cor, listen to that! Do you know what that is, Margaret? Sounds like a proper chaffinch, doesn't it? Right cheery, they are. It does sound cheerful, yes. Could be a goldfinch, though. They have a similar call, a bit more…clipped, I think. It’s getting difficult to tell sometimes, isn’t it? Things are blending together. Aye, it is. Used to be I could tell 'em all at a glance. Spend hours out in the garden listenin'. Used to get me dad out too, bless him. He were a dab hand at bird identification. Proper encyclopaedia, that man was. He could name every weed in the garden, too, which weren't much use to me, mind! My husband, David, was the same about plants. Could talk for hours about the Latin names. He’d be horrified if I just called a rose a…well, just a rose! It's a common failing, isn’t it? Me, I’m just grateful if it looks pretty. Speaking of things that wake you up…my alarm clock! Dreadful thing. Went off at precisely 6:15 this mornin’ to the sound of a rooster crowing. Proper jarring, it was. Thought I’d jumped out of me skin! Oh, dear! I hate those novelty alarm clocks. I stick with a simple ticking one. It’s much gentler. Though, having said that, I often wake up at 5:30 anyway. Used to be to get the kids off to school, now it’s just…habit, I suppose. Aye, routine. Keeps you goin'. Right, let's talk birds again. I've been meaning to put out some proper suet pellets for the tits. They’re gettin’ lean, poor little things. Saw a robin struggling to get a worm out the frozen ground yesterday. Broke my heart. The squirrels have been marauding my feeders again! It’s a constant battle. I bought one of those cages, you know, supposed to keep them out, but they're surprisingly clever. They figure it out within a day. Oh, the little blighters! They have a right of way, don’t they? It’s just… frustrating when you’re trying to feed the birds, innit? Right, I have got to book a dentist appointment. My gums are playin’ up again. Nasty ache. Oh, dentists! I loathe them. Had a nosebleed just last week, right in the waiting room! Mortifying. Just started to relax, thinking maybe it wouldn't be too bad, then… splutter!

Honestly, Sarah, it’s lovely to see you. It feels like ages since we properly caught up. Last time was, what, Emily's christening? Remember how chaotic that was? Little Toby nearly pulled the cake over. Oh, I do! Toby was a whirlwind, wasn't he? And yes, it's been far too long. Cambridge is a treat though - much nicer than rushing around Dorchester on a Saturday. This café is lovely. So, what’s been keeping you busy? Still battling teenagers and Shakespeare? Battling is a good word for it. Yes, still teaching. Year 10 this year – GCSEs looming, the usual stress. But I'm hoping to do some yoga retreats this summer. My back has been absolutely killing me. You know, I’ve been trying that hot yoga place – the one near the river – and it's actually incredible. Really eases the tension. You should try it. I’ve been meaning to. My shoulders are permanently knotted. I'm often dealing with incredibly stressful situations at work, you know, and it all just builds up. Social work… well, it’s relentless sometimes. But truthfully, it’s rewarding too. It’s just... draining. I can imagine. You’re carrying so much weight for others. Speaking of difficult things, how's… everything? With the IVF? It was… intense. We did three rounds, you know? The final one, thankfully, worked. Leo is nearly two now. It’s the most amazing thing, of course, but the toll it took on both of us... financially, emotionally... it was a lot. It’s hard to explain to people who haven't gone through it. They see this little boy, happy and healthy, and don’t realise the sheer effort and heartbreak that went into getting him here. I can only imagine. It takes such bravery. I’m so incredibly happy for you, truly. It’s wonderful. I’ve been thinking a lot about… well, it’s probably a bit silly, but I've been thinking about writing a book. A book! That's fantastic! About what? Shakespearean teenagers? No, not quite. It's more...a collection of short stories, really. Little vignettes about life, you know? Things I've observed over the years. I've got a notebook full of ideas, and it just feels like now is the time to actually  do  something with them. A proper creative outlet. It would be nice to not be defined by my job, I think.

This is lovely, Anon. You’ve really made this place your own. Much brighter than it was when you first moved in, isn't it? Aye, that it is, love. Bit of elbow grease and a splash of colour, that's all it took. Glad you approve. Kettle’s on, fancy another biscuit? Got some ginger snaps this time. Oh, go on then. Ginger snaps sound perfect. So, Anon mentioned you were a teacher too? What did you teach? History, primarily. A bit of geography thrown in for good measure. Birmingham schools needed a decent history teacher back in the day, apparently. Used to love it, actually. Seeing young’uns' eyes light up when they got something, a connection to the past… that was the best bit. Though the paperwork! Don't even get me started. Drove me round the bend. I can imagine! Bureaucracy is a nightmare, even in language teaching. We’re drowning in assessment forms and curricula changes. It feels like we spend more time  planning  to teach than actually teaching sometimes. I teach French and Spanish, mostly to adults. Trying to get them to remember the subjunctive is… a challenge. The subjunctive! Oh, I remember hearing about that. A proper headache, that one. Always thought it was a bit overcomplicated myself. They keep messing with that language, don’t they? Every time you learn something, they change it. Exactly! It's like a moving target. Though, I do love seeing my students’ progress. One of them, a lovely older gentleman, is planning to visit his daughter in Lyon next year. He can finally hold a conversation; it's just brilliant. Good for him! That's what it's all about, isn’t it? Opening up a new world. You know, my daughter, Sarah, she's a solicitor now. Top firm in London. Smart girl. Keeps me on my toes, she does. Always asking about pensions and investments... That's wonderful. Solicitors must be  swamped  these days, what with everything going on. Speaking of which, have you seen anything on the news about the recent burglaries in the area? It's quite unsettling, isn't it? Aye, dreadful, that is. Poor Mrs. Henderson got her jewellery taken. Happens far too often, round here. Seems like the police are stretched thin. Used to be you could leave your doors unlocked, back in my day. Can’t do that now, can you?

Right then, this chilli's proper good, Annie. You've outdone yerself, lass. Proper hearty stuff, just what I needed after a day fiddling with hydraulics. Glad you like it, Liam! It’s my nan's recipe, you know. She reckons it’s the secret to surviving those grey Sunderland winters. Bit warmer than Leeds, I’d imagine? Speaking of surviving, anyone else feeling like a bit of Fleet Foxes to combat the post-chilli nap-inducing effect? Found this beauty rummaging through a charity shop in town. Fleet Foxes? Seriously, Klaus? You know I only listen to stuff with a solid bassline. Though, I have to admit, that chilli  does  smell rather good, Annie. Anything left for tomorrow? Got a presentation to prep, horrifyingly. Of course, there's loads left! I made enough for an army. And Klaus, don't get your knickers in a twist. Fleet Foxes are good for the soul, you need a bit of chill sometimes! Liam, you're nodding. You agree? Aye, I get ya, Annie. Folk gettin' all wound up down here. Honestly, down South, everyone's forever rushing. Up North, we take our time. Proper enjoy t'simple things, like a good bowl of food and a bit of mellow music. Though, Fleet Foxes... It's a bit much for a Thursday night, innit? "Helplessness Blues" is a masterpiece, Liam! Think of it as… restorative engineering for the ears. Helps you re-align your priorities. Like, do you  really  need to optimize that pressure valve to within a tenth of a millimeter? Right, right, you and your fancy engineering philosophy. I was just thinking about that job on the housing estate. The drainpipe's gone knackered again. Proper mess, they are. Kids clambering all over it. Housing estate drains… That’s far from my world of sustainable infrastructure projects, I’m afraid. Though, I do appreciate the importance of reliable drainage. No one wants a flooded basement beneath a luxury eco-home. Moving on from drains! Klaus, you were saying about charity shops? Did you find anything else interesting? I'm always on the lookout for vintage band tees. Actually, yes. Found a first edition of “Suspiria” on Blu-ray. The original Goblin soundtrack  alone  is worth the price of admission. You lot need to experience Italian horror at its finest. "Suspiria"? Sounds… intense. I’m more of a Wes Anderson man myself. "The Grand Budapest Hotel" is pure cinematic joy.

Honestly, this weather's a joke. July, and it's proper miserable. Remember last summer? We were practically melting. Remember that trip to Cornwall? Oh, God, yes! I think I spent most of it with a giant floppy hat glued to my head, trying not to spontaneously combust. It was brilliant though, wasn’t it? The surfing was surprisingly good. Brilliant, and expensive! My bank account hasn’t fully recovered. Although, the pasties were worth it. I’m still dreaming of a proper Cornish pasty. You lot always manage to find the expensive things to do. I was in Brighton a few weeks ago - loads cheaper, and the arcades are still as gloriously tacky as ever. I won ten pounds on one of those claw machines. Ten pounds? Beginner's luck, mate. I've spent a fortune trying to win a giant fluffy unicorn. Still no luck. Speaking of spending money... anyone been to that new gym, "Titan Fitness," yet? The one down by the river? I went last week! It’s…intense. Seriously, intense. All those bodybuilders grunting and looking like they’re about to bench press a small car. I felt a bit out of my depth, to be honest. Did a spin class, though. Nearly died. Sounds terrifying. I’m sticking to yoga for now, thanks. It’s much more my speed. Less chance of accidentally getting crushed. Are they even doing the summer kids' camp this year? Little Leo would be obsessed with it. Yeah, I think they are. Sarah from the council mentioned it. It's got a coding workshop this year, which I think Leo would adore - he's already trying to build his own little games on the tablet. Should I look into it? Definitely. It'll keep him busy, and you'll get a couple of hours peace. Although, knowing Leo, he’ll probably build a robot that takes over the world. Don't give him any ideas! It’s a miracle he hasn't managed to disassemble the toaster yet. I'm trying to get him into music – a little guitar, mostly. He keeps trying to strum it like a drum. Very...enthusiastic. Honestly, it's a relief when they just want to play with Lego. Actually, talking about music - have you guys heard the new Arctic Monkeys track? I’m obsessed. It’s got that slow, swaggering feel, you know? Yeah, it’s decent.

Honestly, this ref is having an absolute shocker, isn't he? Like, how many times can he get it wrong in one game? It’s ridiculous. Yeah, he’s not having a great time. Textbook case of trying to be too clever, I reckon. Reminds me of Professor Davies, always trying to overcomplicate things. Should just let the game flow, shouldn't he? Flow? Flow?! He's strangling the flow! See, that was a clear foul! Right there! On Henderson. Blinded him completely. You’re getting quite animated, love. It's only the first half. Though I agree, that  was  dubious. Still, Liverpool are dominating possession. They'll create chances. Possession doesn't win you games, does it? Goals do. And we’re not looking like we’re gonna score any anytime soon, not with that defence lacking any sort of bite. Remember when we were kids, and Dad used to drill it into us – "Attack, attack, attack! Defence wins championships but attack entertains!"? He always said that, didn't he? He was obsessed with football. Still is. Speaking of reminiscing, did you ever finish watching that documentary about George Best last week? Nah, I got distracted. It was good though, right? Proper sad, really. All that talent, gone to waste. Makes you think, doesn't it? It does. About responsibility, wasted potential…all that. Similar to some of the research I'm looking at, actually. Brilliant minds applying themselves to completely unproductive ends. Heavy stuff for a Saturday afternoon watching football, isn’t it? You and your PhD. Need to relax a bit, you know. Speaking of relaxing… Easter's coming up. Have you thought about what we're doing? I was thinking maybe a walk in the Fens? It’s surprisingly nice out there, when the weather cooperates. Plenty of birds to spot, nice open spaces… a bit of peace and quiet. I could do with some peace and quiet. The Fens? Seriously? That sounds…flat. Don't get me wrong, I appreciate nature and all that, but I’d rather be somewhere with a bit more  oomph . Maybe somewhere we can get some decent fish and chips? I'm craving some proper Northen fish and chips. None of that fancy, soggy batter nonsense. You are hopeless! Fine, we can get fish and chips. But we're doing the Fens walk  sometime . It’s good for you to get out of the city.

Jaysus, look at this one. Liam, isn’t it? About eight years old, I’d say. At that bloody fun fair in Weston-super-Mare. Remember that, Moira? Oh, bless him! He looks terrified but also massively excited. Weston-super-Mare… goodness, that was a proper day out, wasn’t it? Remember that awful carousel? The one that kept stopping. Poor little thing clinging on for dear life. Aye, a right deathtrap, that one was. But he wouldn’t let go. Said he was going to ride it 'til he threw up. Kids, eh? Fierce characters. And look at his wee face, covered in candy floss. Weston-super-Mare. Used to take my wee laddie there every summer. The smell of the chips, the sea breeze… lovely memories. Though, I must say, those fun fairs were always a bit… chaotic. Didn’t trust those rides half as much as I trusted a good phonics lesson. You’d always make sure they ate proper fish and chips, wouldn't you, Nan? Not just the greasy sort. Always said it was important for growing boys. Liam wasn't too keen, I recall. More interested in those sticky lollipops. Speaking of growing boys… did you see the photos Daniel sent over from the London Marathon? The lad ran it, the clever b     d. No! Really? I haven’t seen them yet. Oh, I'm so proud! Did he do well? What was his time? He did grand, Moira. Not a record breaker, mind you, but a solid finish. Under four and a half hours, I think he said. He was absolutely shattered afterward though, apparently. Legs like jelly. But beaming. A marathon! That’s a remarkable achievement. It takes real dedication. I taught a boy once who was determined to run the Highland Games marathon. Never managed it, sadly, but he kept trying. Admirable spirit, that lad. He's got ambition, our Daniel. Remember how he used to badger you, Liam’s dad, to build him a treehouse? He was relentless, that one. Nearly drove you mad. Aye, he did. Near enough. But he got his treehouse. A proper fortress it was, too. Had ropes and ladders and everything. Thought he was Tarzan, he did. Now he’s running marathons. It’s a grand thing to see, aye. It is. He’s growing into a fine young man. Just like his brother. Do you remember when they both wanted that Star Wars Lego set for Christmas?

Right then, ladies! Dig in. I made a big batch, thought we’d all appreciate a proper comfort food dinner. It’s not quite Mum’s, but…well, nothing ever is, is it? Oh, this looks lovely, Sarah. You’ve done brilliantly. Smell’s gorgeous. Reminds me of my Nan’s, actually. She used to make a right mess of the mashed potato topping - always lumpy, but it tasted divine. Aye, she did, didn’t she, love? Always a bit of flour sticking to the sides of the bowl. Never could get the hang of it, bless her. Though her gravy… that was something else. You could stand a spoon in it. See? It's the gravy that makes it, isn't it? Or at least, the memories attached to it! Speaking of memories, I was just thinking about those little plastic bead sets we used to have as kids. Remember those, both of you? The ones you’d string together to make bracelets? Oh my goodness, yes! The Floral Beadlets! I had a massive tin full. Spent hours twisting those things into patterns. Remember the colours? The pinks and yellows and the… horrible orange, which nobody ever wanted. Yes, dear, I remember. Used to trade them at school. A blue bead was worth a fortune! My little Dennis would be after them constantly, trying to get a blue one off me. Cheeky monkey. Dennis was a sweetheart. Mine just wanted to build elaborate cities with Lego. Hours and hours. I’d try to help, but he always insisted I had to build the "shops," which invariably were just grey bricks stacked on top of each other. He was a very particular child. Children are, aren't they? My Emily got obsessed with those little porcelain dolls – the ones with the painted eyelashes. She’d line them all up on her bed and tell them stories. I used to worry she was talking to herself too much. That’s a classic. My nephew has the same thing with dinosaurs. He's convinced they're real and they're planning a secret invasion. It's quite endearing, really. This is lovely, dear. Makes a change from that microwave muck they sell these days. Do you ever read real books anymore, Sarah? Or do you just bother with those…eBooks? It’s a bit of both, really. eBooks are brilliant for travelling, you know?

Mmm, that's nice, that is. Proper pickle, this. Not that watered-down stuff you get in the supermarkets these days. Remember Mrs. Higgins down the road used to make her own? Proper fiery it was, could set your tongue alight. I do remember Mrs. Higgins. She was a character, wasn't she? Always had a pot of something bubbling on the stove. Her gooseberry fool was legendary. These sandwiches are lovely, Arthur. You’ve outdone yourself. Just a bit of effort, love. Can’t have you eating nothin' but dry crusts now, can I? Though, come to think of it, I haven't had a proper pickle sandwich like this in ages. Gets a bit monotonous, doesn't it? Same thing day in, day out. It does, doesn't it? Though I find a routine is comforting, in a way. Keeps things… predictable. Especially with everything going on in the world. You hear somethin’ on the news, and you just want a bit of normal, don’t you? Want a good cup of tea and a sandwich. Aye. The news… don’t watch it much anymore. Too much doom and gloom. Gives you a right ache in your chest, it does. Remember when they used to have those nice nature programs? Attenborough and all that. Peaceful, that was. David Attenborough. He's a national treasure, isn’t he? My grandchildren are obsessed with him. Little Leo keeps asking me if I’ve ever seen a blue-footed booby. Blue-footed booby! Where does he even hear these things? Little tykes do pick up on things, don't they? My nephew used to go on about dinosaurs at three years old. Knew all their names, he did. Tyrannosaurus Rex, Triceratops… drove his poor mother mad. It’s wonderful, though, isn’t it? Their curiosity. They see the world with such… fresh eyes. It reminds you to look at things differently. I try to encourage it. They come over and ask me about everything, you know. “Granny, why is the sky blue?” “Granny, where do birds go when it rains?” That’s good of you. Always good to encourage 'em. Though, sometimes I think they ask questions just to wind you up. Remember when my youngest, young David, kept asking, "Why is water wet?" Drove his mother round the bend! She had a proper go at him. Oh, they do, don't they?

Right, so, Chloe was saying she’s thinking of getting a pug. A pug! Can you imagine, Liv? Little wrinkly face, snorting everywhere. My little nephew, Finn, would absolutely adore it, but I think my sister would be pulling her hair out. A pug's a commitment, aren't they? Lots of shedding, apparently. And breathing issues, if you believe everything you read online. But they  are  undeniably cute. You know, I’ve been looking into getting a dog myself. Something a bit calmer than a pug. A golden retriever, maybe? Golden retrievers are gorgeous, Liv. Total softies. But you’ve got to be prepared for the walks! London parks get pretty packed, especially on a weekend. I had a near miss the other day with a particularly energetic corgi. Sent my coffee flying! Oh, goodness! Poor you, Maisie. You’d think people would have a bit more control over their dogs, wouldn’t you? It’s the same with the kids at school, really. All this boundless energy. You’re constantly trying to redirect them. I can imagine! Teaching must be exhausting. How’s little Leo doing? Still obsessed with dinosaurs? Absolutely fixated! He drew me a picture of a T-Rex the other day. It was amazing, really. Scarily realistic for a five-year-old. I have it stuck on the fridge. Speaking of art, did you see that exhibition at the Tate Modern last week? The one with the… well, I’m not sure what to call it, but the interactive installations? Vaguely? I’ve been drowning in deadlines. The new campaign for that gin brand is proving surprisingly tricky. Apparently, ‘sophisticated botanical blend’ doesn’t exactly scream ‘excitement’ to marketing. I’m playing with all sorts of wordplay. It's draining, to be honest. I’m dreaming of a holiday. Oh, copywriting. Sounds intense! You always were the clever one, Maisie. Speaking of holidays, I'm thinking of going to Cornwall this summer. Somewhere quiet, with a beach. Need some serious recharging after this term. Have you ever been, Chloe? Cornwall! Lovely. My nan lives down near St Ives. Absolutely gorgeous there, proper cream-tea-and-sea-air vibes. I try to go down every couple of months. The traffic getting there is a nightmare, though. Last time I went, it took us nearly four hours. And then  my  car decided to throw a tantrum right outside her house.

Right then, so you were saying, Annie, about this street… It’s got a bit rough, hasn’t it? Used to be lovely, all those little terraced houses with the flower boxes. Now you get… well, you get what you get, don't ya? Tell me about it, Herr Doktor! Proper gone downhill. Used to be Ms. Doherty across the way, lovely woman, always had a pot of jam on the boil. Now it’s… I don’t wanna talk about it, honestly. Just not the same feel, is it? The kids, they're running wild. Not saying they're all bad, mind, but there’s not the same respect, y'know? And the bins… overflowing all the time. Makes you feel a bit… unsafe. It's not  that  bad, is it? I mean, I walk past here a few times a week on my way from the office. It's just…noisy. Lots of shouting. Noisy's an understatement, love. Living next to the school helps, gives you a sense of what young people are like these days. And you’ve got the traffic, naturally. I'm worried about young Finn, actually. His mum’s always fretting about him, he's forever out on his bike, isn't he? Mum just worries. It’s what mums do. I'm fine. I know where I'm going. Finn’s a good lad, though. Bit quiet, but good. At least he's reading! Keepin’ himself out of mischief. My little Liam, he's all TikTok and Fortnite. Drives me round the bend! He says I’m ‘cheugy’, can you believe it? Cheugy? Another one of these internet words. The language evolves faster than I can keep up! I was trying to explain the concept of irony to my class the other day, and it was like talking to a brick wall. They want instant gratification, instant meaning. No patience for nuance. Reminds me a bit of… well, some of the political discourse nowadays. All this yapping about ISIS, and folks just agreeing and disagreeing with zero understanding of the complexities. Don't you think that's a bit… much to bring up over tea, Mr. Schmidt? Just drawing a parallel, love. Point is, complexity is being lost. Just like in literature. Nobody reads Dickens anymore. They want superheroes and wizards. Speaking of which, Finn here’s engrossed in Harry Potter, eh? Good choice.

Nepal, you say, Penelope? Really? It’s a bit… ambitious, isn’t it? For us, I mean. Remember that walking tour of Tuscany? I thought  that  was a stretch after my ankle gave me gyp. Oh, don’t be such a worrywart, Margaret! It won’t be all trekking, you know. There are beautiful cities, wonderful temples… and apparently, the coffee is quite good. Though, I must say, this coffee here is rather delightful. Did you get that new blend from the Farm Shop? Yes, I did. The lamb sausages too, of course. Couldn't resist. They’re far superior to anything the Village Shop offers these days. Honestly, it's gone downhill. Young Timmy seems to think people want pre-packaged everything. Remember Mrs. Higgins? She knew exactly which cuts of meat you wanted. You’re talking my language! The Village Shop used to be the heart of the community. Now, it’s just… impersonal. Farm Shop's the only way to go. And speaking of food, Penelope, you’re looking absolutely radiant! Are you already planning your menus for Nepal? I’ve heard the local cuisine can be… challenging. Challenging is one way to put it! I’m trying to be sensible. Gluten-free, mostly, of course. You know I can’t risk it. Though, goodness knows how I'll manage when I have the little one over for tea. Apparently, having a baby these days is a minefield of allergies and whatnot. My sister's already giving me pamphlets on organic, hypoallergenic everything. My goodness. When my children were small, it was jam and bread, dear. If they didn’t like it, they got nothing. Simple as that. Though, I do recall my mother-in-law… now  there's  a story. Her journey during the war. You wouldn't believe it. She started in Siberia... Oh, tell us! I’ve only heard snippets. Well, her family were… let’s just say they weren't looked upon favorably by the Soviets. They managed to flee, eventually ending up in Africa, meandering through several countries along the way. Imagine, a young girl, leaving everything behind, reliant on the kindness of strangers. No gluten-free options in those days, I can assure you. Just whatever you could get your hands on. My father-in-law always said she could make a feast out of dandelion roots. Extraordinary! My grandfather, on the other hand, spent the war years rationing sausages.

Right, that's reet grand. Proper cuppa. Needed that, honestly. This whole Cambridge thing is drainin' me. You look knackered, Liv! Long day at the conference? Did everything go okay with the keynote speaker? Last I heard he was being a right diva. Aye, a right diva is right. Professor Davies. Don’t get me started. Kept rantin' about the catering, the lighting, the  temperature  of the room. Like he's royalty or summat. And the venue... honestly, ANON chose the most awkward, cramped space in Cambridge possible. I reckon he did it just to wind me up. Oh, the drama! You handle these things so well, Liv. I’d be in tears. Honestly, my boss, Mr. Henderson, is enough to drive a person mad on his own, let alone adding a temperamental academic to the mix. Thanks, Maisie. Means a lot. Bit of a juggling act, it is. But at least it's payin’ the bills, innit? What about you, Chloe? Still battling paperwork mountains in your production gig? Don’t even ask. We're launching a new product line next month - biodegradable picnic blankets - ironically enough, given that Henderson keeps lecturing me on sustainability while simultaneously insisting on using single-use everything in the office. It's a nightmare. Deadlines are tighter than my jeans after Christmas dinner. Biodegradable picnic blankets. That’s reet clever, tha’s got a good job then. Sounds like a world of difference from catering to stuffy professors. It is proper grown-up stuff, Chloe. I’m still basically a glorified filing machine at my end. Mr. Abernathy wants everything alphabetised, colour-coded, and laminated. He’s convinced it improves productivity. It mostly just gives me a headache. Laminated? Seriously? That’s… intense. It’s the little things, isn’t it? Like finding a stapler that actually works. That’s a victory. Aye, tell me about it. Try findin' a decent Yorkshire pudding here. It’s like searchin’ for gold dust. Anyway, enough about work moanin'. What have you two been up to lately, besides stressin' yourselves ragged? Well, I went to that pottery class I mentioned last week. Turns out, I'm spectacularly bad at it. My vase looked like a wobbly potato. But it was surprisingly relaxing, actually. Got me thinking about something a bit more creative to do. That’s lovely, Maisie. You need a creative outlet. I’ve been trying to run a bit more.

Honestly, David, I’m fuming. Did you see the plans for the library? They’re really going ahead with it, aren't they? Demolishing it to build… another block of flats. Honestly, more flats! Plumstead can barely cope as it is. Saw them, yes. Utter madness. Another concrete box dominating the skyline. They call it ‘modernizing the area’. It’s just greed, plain and simple. I can’t believe they’re letting it happen. So, you’re serious about the petition? Absolutely serious. I’ve started a draft. It’s surprisingly hard to articulate the sheer ridiculousness of the whole thing in a formal letter. "The proposal to demolish a vital community resource to facilitate the construction of luxury accommodation is demonstrably detrimental…" Blah, blah, blah. It just feels inadequate. Right, the bureaucratic language. Always a challenge. Maybe we need to focus on the  impact . The kids’ reading groups, the elderly computer classes, the quiet space for students. Show them the human cost. Exactly! I’ve got some photos from the kids’ reading hour last week. Little Leo was absolutely mesmerised by the dinosaur book. How are they going to replace that? With a concierge and a gym? Precisely. Speaking of replacement, how are those night shifts at transcription going? Still exhausting? They are. Honestly, I’m starting to question my life choices. Proofreading legal documents at 2 am is not my idea of a good time. I'm attempting to use the "memory palace" technique my niece told me about to help. Apparently, you create a mental space - a familiar house, perhaps - and place each key piece of information in a specific room. Then you just ‘walk through’ the house to recall everything. A memory palace? Sounds a bit… intense. You’re turning into my niece, then. She’s obsessed with brain training apps and obscure mnemonics. I tried one that involved assigning colours to numbers, it just gave me a headache. It’s surprisingly helpful, actually. I’m assigning different rooms in my old primary school to different legal terms. It’s oddly comforting, revisiting those memories. Helps me focus, too. Less likely to drift off and misspell ‘subpoena’. Well, as long as it’s working. I've been completely swamped with paperwork here. Borough Council decisions are becoming increasingly baffling. Apparently, they're considering removing the planters from High Street. The planters? The ones Mrs. Davies painstakingly planted with those lavender bushes?

Cor, this brew’s a bit weak, innit? Brenda didn’t put enough leaves in, I reckon. Still, better than nothin’. Lovely bit of Victoria sponge though, she’s got a real knack for that, that one. Aye, Brenda does make a good sponge. Though, mind you, I still prefer her lemon drizzle. Remember that lemon drizzle she made for Doreen’s birthday? Nearly caused a riot, everyone wanted a second slice. Oh, don’t exaggerate, Arthur! It was a nice cake, that’s all. It’s lovely to see you both. So, has anyone been out and about much lately? I saw a pair of goldcrests in my garden yesterday, tiny little things, weren't they? Absolutely adorable. Goldcrests, eh? Didn't see ‘em myself. Been mostly pottering about, tidying up a bit. It's horrifying, the amount of clutter one accumulates, even when you're not  doing  much. You’d think retirement would be all sunshine and roses, wouldn’t you? Bit more dust and paperwork, more like. Tell me about it! I’m fighting a losing battle with the magazines in the shed. Been promising meself I’d sort ‘em out for… well, for years now. Still got some from ’83 in there! Thought I might build somethin' with the wood, but that's another project for another lifetime, I suppose. You should just be ruthless, Arthur! Throw it all out! Seriously, decluttering is so therapeutic. I had a clear-out last month. Got rid of half the china. Half! My daughter nearly had a fit. Said it was family heirlooms. Don’t get started on families and heirlooms, Brenda. That's a rabbit hole best left unexplored. Speaking of families, have you heard anything from Sarah and Tom? Promised to ring last week. Haven’t heard a peep. Probably busy with the little ones. Little terrors, they are, but lovely little terrors. Remember when Emily drew all over the kitchen wall with crayon? Nearly gave Sarah a heart attack. Oh, yes! And then blamed the cat! Classic. It reminds me, I saw a leaflet through the door the other day, about the Jehovah’s Witnesses. They’re quite persistent, aren’t they? They called round recently. Pleasant enough, but… Persistent is putting it mild. Like wasps in summer. You can’t escape ‘em. Personally, I don’t hold with it, but each to their own, I suppose.

Right then, Mum, Dad, settle in. I’ve made a fresh batch – proper dark chocolate, the way you like it. And David’s just put the kettle on. It smells wonderful, Anne. And thank you, dear. Long journey from Tokyo, wasn't it, Mother? You must be exhausted. It  is  rather good, Anne. Though a touch more salt, perhaps? Still, it’s a thoughtful gesture. Tokyo was… an experience. The sheer scale of everything. And the politeness! You could bounce a ball off the people. Always were a observant one, Margaret. Remember that trip to Venice? You spent half an hour just watching the pigeons. Pigeons are fascinating, Arthur. A tiny, feathered microcosm of the city itself! Besides, Venice was dreadfully overcrowded. Still, the gondolas were something. So, Dad, how was the flight? Any turbulence? I was worried about you, knowing how you get. Perfectly smooth, actually. Although the vegan meals... Honestly, Anne, I'm worried about the future. Carrot and lentil loaf. Who  wants  that on a seven-hour flight? You’re incorrigible, Arthur. I’m quite happy with the carrot and lentil loaf. It's a necessary evil, you know. Less impact on the environment. Speaking of necessary evils, did you hear about the new restaurant down the street? "The Gilded Spoon." Dreadfully pretentious name, but apparently, their mashed potato is divine. They use truffle oil, you know. I haven’t! Really? I’ve been meaning to try somewhere new. The budget's a bit tight at the moment, though. I'm still dealing with some of the fallout from that last transcription project. They outsourced some of it to India – apparently to save money.
