Honestly, the quality was shocking! I ended up having to correct more than I transcribed. That’s infuriating, Anne. It’s the same everywhere. Cost-cutting at the expense of quality. It’s happening here too in the admin department. They’re talking about streamlining… which usually means getting rid of people. Streamlining! It’s just a euphemism for ruining things, isn’t it? Back in my day, at the school, we ran things properly. No outsourcing nonsense. Loyalty, dedication – those were the values we instilled. Academies have changed everything, Margaret. A complete different world. All about targets and paperwork. No room for a bit of character building. I remember… …Young Timothy Harrison. Bright lad, but terrible at rugby. Spent all his time in the library.

Right then, Doris, you were saying about this Sat Nav of yours. Went walkabout again, did it? Walkabout is putting it politely, Arthur. Told you I should’ve stuck with that old paper map. More reliable, that was. At least you knew where you were, even if it did take an hour to find Mill Road. This fancy thing sent me down a field track! Nearly got stuck in the mud, I did. Brenda was fumin’. Brenda's always fumin’ about something, love. Remember when she tried to put sugar in the diesel tank of that delivery van? Oh, don't remind me! The poor driver cleared off quicker than you can say 'Norfolk’! Still, Brenda’s got a good heart, she does. Just a bit… excitable. Excitable's one word for it. Look, Doris, I still reckon the algorithms are flawed. They’re just not thinking about the practicalities, are they? A field track isn't a road, regardless of what the blinking box tells you. Back in my day, as a civil engineer, we considered  everything . Ground conditions, gradients, drainage... Sat Navs? They’re just assuming a flat, paved surface everywhere. It's funny, isn't it? We used to rely on landmarks, remember? “Turn left at the old oak tree…” Now it’s all beeping and flashing directions. Speaking of things changing, did you both hear the latest on council tax? They're putting it up again! It's outrageous, simply outrageous. Don’t get me started! Where’s all the money going, I’d like to know? Potholes everywhere, and they want  more  of my pension? I used to have a bit left over for a packet of biscuits, now I'm scrimping just to keep the lights on. It’s the same everywhere, isn’t it? They bleed you dry. And the government... don’t even get me going on the government. Promises, promises. All talk, no action. That new housing development down by the river... seventeen houses, posh as you please. Who do they think's going to afford those? Certainly not folks like us. It’s just not fair, is it? Buying a house used to be a dream for young couples. Now it’s a lottery. My granddaughter, Sarah, she’s trying to get on the property ladder. Bless her heart, she's working two jobs and still struggling. She's a good girl, Sarah.

Right, so about Liam's tablet. It’s still giving me grief. The warranty’s expired, of course. Typical. Just as I was thinking of getting him a new one for his birthday. Did you manage to get the virus off? I told you, dodgy websites, didn’t I? I swear, teenagers and the internet... it's a minefield. Aye, well, the virus itself was handled, more or less. But now it’s booting up slow as molasses and freezing constantly. I reckon it's a hard drive issue, but getting a new hard drive in these things is… fiddly, to put it mildly. And a bit pricey considering I’m not sure how much longer the rest of it will last. Honestly, Michael, you're such a wizard with computers. I wouldn't even know where to begin. Remember that old laptop of mine? Completely bricked after just a year. I just threw it out. Aye, well, throwing it out was probably the sensible option, Sarah. Some things aren't worth the hassle. But young Liam, he’s already attached to that thing. He’s got all his games on it and his online stuff. It would be a right drama trying to replace everything. I’ve got all my saves on it too! And my Minecraft world! I was  just  starting to build a proper castle! There you go, see? Drama already. Look, I could try to wipe it and reinstall the OS. It might give it a bit of life, but it’s a gamble. What do you reckon, Sarah? Liam, are you up for wiping everything off and starting fresh? Don’t want you getting all weepy. He’s distracted by building… whatever that is. Looks like the Leaning Tower of Pisa. Michael, do you think it’s worth the effort? Wouldn’t it be easier just to… Don’t you say it, Sarah. Don't you  dare  suggest a new one. My wallet is still recovering from the new rugby jersey. Rugby? Are we watching the Ireland game this weekend? Please say we are, Dad! Aye, we are. Got the tickets sorted. Reckon we should head over a bit earlier this time? The pubs fill up fast. Maybe grab some food before? Sarah, what are you thinking for dinner tonight? I was thinking fajitas, but I’m out of that decent salsa. Fajitas sound lovely. But honestly, with little Eoin causing chaos everywhere… …anything that doesn't involve a million dishes would be a victory.

Right, that was excellent. Honestly, best Margherita I’ve had in ages. You two cleared your plates, didn’t you? Practically inhaled it! It was yummy, Mummy! Can we have it again tomorrow? Pizza! Yes! And chocolate pudding! Chocolate pudding every day isn't exactly a balanced diet, is it, love? We'll see. We'll see. Speaking of things being balanced… did you two manage even a single second of a handstand today like I suggested? I tried! But I fell over. Leo laughed. You did! It was funny! Like a wobbly tower! Right, well, practice makes perfect. It's all about core strength, you know. Think of it like building a really strong base. What’s two and two? We need a strong base for handstands  and  for maths! Four! Four! Excellent! See? You’re building that mathematical base already. Now, we were talking about communication earlier, weren't we? Remember how I said sometimes words aren't enough? Like when I was sad about my drawing getting ripped? Exactly. Sometimes a hug, or just sitting quietly together, says more than any words could. Because sometimes, feeling understood is the most important thing. It's like, when you see a really,  really  big lake, you don’t need to describe how vast it is, you just  know . Right? Like Loch Ness. Nessie! Is she real? Well, nobody’s ever  really  proven she exists, have they? Loads of people  think  she does. Loads and loads of people. It's a mystery, isn’t it? A giant mystery hiding in a huge, deep lake. Imagine… it’s dark, it’s cold, and then  splash!  A monster! Maybe! Or maybe it's just a big wave. Or a log. But it’s more exciting to imagine it’s a monster, don't you think? It's all about how you communicate your ideas. You can  say  there's a monster, but showing someone a picture, or acting like you're a giant sea serpent… that's a much better way to tell the story! ROAR! I’m Nessie! I’m very, very big! You’re tickling me, Nessie! See? That's communicating! You're telling a whole story without saying a single word except for "ROAR!" Now, about that fairy garden we were planning... we have the perfect little pot for it, remember? We could use moss for the grass and those sparkly pebbles we found at the beach.

"This truffle pasta, honestly, it's unreal. I didn’t think I’d ever taste anything like it. Proper posh grub, innit?" "Posh or not, love, it's delicious. Reminds me of that little place in Bury, The Moorcock, they used to do a mean truffle risotto. Though, this is... more refined, wouldn't you say, John?" “Refined is a good word, Susan. It’s got a certain… elegance. A lot lighter than anything I’d expect to find in Bury, that's for sure. And the wine? Excellent pairing.” He takes a sip of his wine, nodding approvingly. "Much better than the stuff they serve in Canary Wharf, that's for certain." “Can I have some more bread, Mum? And is that really truffle? Like, proper truffle from a pig digging it up?” "Aye, lad, proper truffle. Not that artificial stuff they sometimes use. Bit of a luxury, this, eh? Speaking of digging things up, remember old Mr. Henderson down the street and his prize-winning pumpkins?" “Oh my god, yes! He was obsessed. Honestly, he'd be having a heart attack looking at this price tag! But thinking about school, they're trying to get us to do a whole project on food technology. It’s so boring. They showed us how they make fake cheese, and I nearly chucked up." "Fake cheese? The world’s gone mad. At least this pasta is genuine. Though, I suppose even growing truffles now involves some technological intervention, doesn't it? Controlled environments and all that." “Aye, they’re all at it. Used to be simple, wouldn’t it? But then again, things change. Remember when we flew to Gran Canaria? The queues at Manchester Airport were a nightmare. Now you’re lucky to even get a decent cup of tea at the gate. And those immigration officers! One of them looked like he was questioning me about running a smuggling ring." “Did you smuggle anything, Grandma?” He grins mischievously. “Don’t you be daft, lad. Just had a dodgy suitcase full of souvenir mugs. They were suspicious of the mugs, surprisingly. Seriously, though, I was thinking about that documentary we watched last week about Ebola. Makes you think, doesn't it? How quickly things can change.” "It does. Though, honestly, sometimes I just need to escape it all. I’ve been getting into photography, you know? Trying to capture the light here.

Cor, this tea’s a bit weak, innit? Not like Mrs. Higgins used to make it. Proper brew, she did. Anyway, that letter from the debt collectors… didn’t like that one bit, did ya, Marjorie? Proper cheek, demanding all that after all these years. Honestly, Arthur. It’s just the way of things now. They’ll chase anyone for anything. Remember that PPI claim? Had to fight tooth and nail to get that sorted. It’s a racket, the whole lot of it. It is, Marjorie, utterly. These firms, they’re built on preying on vulnerable people. I had a similar issue with a supplier years ago. Went through a solicitor, of course. Ended up costing me a fortune, but at least they backed off. You really should speak to someone about it, Arthur. Or at least write back and tell them you're on a very, very fixed income. I read an article about that in  The Spectator  last week. They were saying these debt collection companies are being reined in a bit more now. There’s supposed to be more oversight. Might be worth looking into, Arthur. I'll bring it round next time. It had the details of some consumer rights organizations. Oversight, eh? Don't make me laugh! They'll find a loophole somewhere, they will. Still, thanks, David. A bit hopeful, mind. It's just... it feels like they're always after something. It's disconcerting. Speaking of which, did you remember to confirm with Sarah about the party? The one next Saturday? Right you are, dear. Nearly forgot. Sarah’s away that weekend though, isn't she? Visiting her daughter in Brighton. That’s a shame. It put a real dampener on things, didn’t it? Still, we can reschedule. Perhaps in a couple of weeks? I’ve got that Italian wine I wanted to try. Yes, the party  was  looking a bit sparse without Sarah. It's alright though, we’ll manage. Though she does make the best Victoria sponge. Where have you been getting your tomato seeds, Arthur? I saw such a lovely variety in Thompson & Morgan’s catalogue. Oh, that's right! Actually, Mrs. Peterson down the road gave me some. Proper fella, she is. Gardening’s her life. Said these were “Early Girl” variety, extra good for sandwiches. She's a champion grower, that one. You and your sandwiches, Arthur! Remember when you used to sing in the choir at St. Peter's?

Right, that’s the last lot through for today. Honestly, the frustration levels were palpable in that last case. Seems everyone's feeling the pinch, doesn’t it? Aye, you're tellin' me. You see it in their faces, lass. The worry lines are deeper these days. I've never known it like this, no. Fuel prices alone… it’s criminal, near enough. Criminal is a good word for it. I was reading an article the other day about the impact of climate change on food production. It felt like a direct link to the cost of everything. Basic economics, really, but it's just… bleak. Climate, eh? I remember when you could rely on the seasons. Not like this now. Blistering summers, floods in the autumn... I was just down visiting my daughter in Inverness, and they’ve had more rain than I’ve ever seen. Messed up the hills something proper. Thankfully she’s got a wee garden tucked away, and she’s managed to keep some vegetables going. That’s wonderful. I'm trying to do my bit with a small garden myself, but slugs are the bane of my existence. It’s a constant battle. I’ve been teaching my students a bit about sustainable living, trying to make them aware. Honestly, though, sometimes I feel like I’m shouting into the void. Don't you fret about that, dear. Every little bit counts. My grandson, Rory, he’s showing a real interest, clever lad. Studying environmental science at university, he is. Makes you feel a bit hopeful, doesn't it? What about your lot? Are they taking it in? Some are switched on, definitely. Others… well, let's just say teenage apathy is a powerful force. I try to make it relevant, link it to things they care about. Like, how climate change impacts travel, or their favourite brands. It’s a challenge. Speaking of travel, I'm hoping to get away somewhere this summer. Somewhere… warm. Oh, a holiday! That'd be lovely. I haven’t managed one in a few years. Courts been busy. Retirement’s not quite the dream I thought it would be, I tell you. A bit of extra money helps, of course, but the loneliness…that gets you. I can imagine. Are your children nearby? My eldest's in Manchester, my daughter in Inverness, and the youngest’s got himself a flat down in London.

Honestly, it’s just been one of  those  days, hasn't it? But, you know what? I feel…happy. Really happy. Doesn’t seem to fit, does it, after wrangling thirty Year Sixes all day? Happy like sunshine? Exactly like sunshine, sweetheart. Warm and bright. Like when we went to the beach last summer. Remember building that enormous sandcastle? With the moat! And the little flags! Did we get ice cream too? We certainly did, didn’t we? Two scoops each! That was a happy day, wasn't it? You both were covered in sand. I was a sandy mermaid! I was a dinosaur king! Roar! You were indeed. It’s silly, isn’t it? Sometimes the simplest things make you happiest. Though, I was reading an article today about how happiness is linked to financial security. Apparently, once you’re above a certain level, more money doesn’t necessarily make you  more  happy. More money? Like,  lots  of money? More than Daddy earns? Perhaps even more than Daddy earns, darling. Enough to buy a castle! Would you like a castle? A castle! With a dragon! A big, scary dragon! Maybe not a scary dragon, darling. Perhaps a friendly one who guards the treasure. Right, let’s make a rhyme to go with it. "A castle so grand, with treasures at hand…" “…And a friendly dragon band!” Brilliant! See? Making rhymes makes me happy! "A castle so grand, with treasures at hand, and a friendly dragon band! And a swimming pool… full of candy!” Full of candy, you say? That's quite a wish! But what I was trying to say is... having loads and loads of money would be nice, wouldn't it? We could go on more holidays, buy you both all the toys you wanted... But then would you still play with me? Oh, sweetheart. Never. Money can’t buy our time together, can it? That’s the  real  treasure. Don't you think so? Can we build a castle out of blankets now? Absolutely! Let’s raid the linen cupboard! But first, let’s finish our rhyme. "A castle so grand…” “…With treasures at hand…” “…and a friendly dragon band! And lots of cuddles, hand in hand!” Perfect! Absolutely perfect. That's the happiest rhyme I’ve heard all day. And the happiest family too, I reckon. Now, blankets… let's build! Can the dinosaur be the dragon?

Honestly, Mrs. Davies’ careers talk was a complete waste of time. "Be a good accountant!" Like that's groundbreaking advice. Everyone says that. Yeah, it was a bit… predictable. Though, I did like the guy from the engineering firm. He made it sound pretty exciting, the bit about designing sustainable bridges. Bridges? Seriously? That’s like, the most classic engineer thing ever. I’m looking for something… I don’t know… disruptive. Something that actually changes things. Like what? Inventing cold fusion? That's the kind of 'disruptive' you mean, right? Okay, maybe not  that  disruptive. But something with a patent, you know? Something you can actually  own . I was reading about this kid, like, barely older than us, who invented a new type of algae-based packaging. Got a patent and now he's saving the world  and  making money. That's the dream. Algae packaging, huh? Smart. My uncle – he’s in Slough, works in logistics – he’s always moaning about all the plastic waste. He says it’s a massive problem for the supply chain, not just the environment. Exactly! See? Problem, solution, patent, profit. Rinse and repeat. It’s a formula, isn't it? It just needs the initial spark. Have you got any genius ideas bubbling away? I’ve been messing around with augmented reality stuff. Trying to develop an app that overlays information onto a real-world environment – like interactive museum tours, or practical guides for… well, anything, really. Augmented reality? That's cool! Is it just a gimmick, or could it actually be useful? I think it could be genuinely useful. The problem is the tech is still so… clunky. And the battery life. You'd need to find a way to make it super efficient. That's the challenge. It’s a long way off a patent, mind. It's mostly doodles at this point. Still, doodles can lead to breakthroughs. My dad keeps talking about investing in tech startups. He says it’s the future – AI, biotech, AR. Says China's already miles ahead in some areas. My mum worries about China. She says they're snapping up all the resources and then flooding the market with cheap goods. It’s putting British businesses under pressure. She's a bit of a protectionist, to be honest. I get that. But it’s also an opportunity, isn’t it? If you can understand the Chinese market, you could potentially reach billions of customers.

Honestly, Sarah, I'm still a bit miffed about that blue run we attempted yesterday. I know you were saying it was "perfectly fine," but my knees were screaming by the bottom! I feel like I’ve aged ten years. Oh, come on, Debs! Don't be such a drama queen. It  was  perfectly fine. Just a little icy in patches. You were gripping the poles like you were fighting a bear! It's supposed to be challenging, remember? That’s the fun of it. And besides, you're getting better; you were definitely faster than on Monday. Faster doesn’t equal painless! I’m starting to think I should have stuck to the nursery slopes altogether. Remember that time we tried the black run in Morzine? I swore I’d never go near a mountain again after that. Oh, good grief, that  was  a disaster. You nearly ended up in a snowdrift. But you conquered it! And that's what skiing’s about, isn’t it? Pushing yourself, seeing what you can do. This holiday was supposed to be a bit more adventurous than just gentle slopes. Besides, you love a good challenge, you always have. Remember trying to convince Mum to let us dye our hair purple in year eight? Alright, alright, you've got me there. But that was a different kind of challenge. This involves potential broken bones! Have you heard from Liam and the kids? I haven't seen a message from them since we arrived. No, not since yesterday morning. Liam said his phone signal was patchy up on the mountain, and the kids are probably too busy terrorising the instructors. Probably building a massive snowman, judging by their last text. I told him to send pictures! Are you thinking of giving them a call later? Yes, I was. I just want to make sure they're okay, and that Oliver hasn't lost another ski boot. That boy is a menace. It’s terrible being away from them, even for a few days. I miss the chaos, to be honest. Tell me about it. It's lovely having a break, definitely, but I keep thinking about little Chloe and whether she's remembering to brush her teeth. You know how she is. Honestly, sometimes I feel like I'm juggling a million things even when I'm  here . It’s the not knowing, isn’t it?

Honestly, Arthur, this is getting ridiculous. Three rackets this month alone with snapped strings! People are treating these things like toys these days, not the investment they used to be. Well, the cost of materials hasn't helped, has it? These strings are appalling quality now. Used to be, you’d get a decent string that’d last a good season. Now? Bang, snaps the moment a decent rally happens. But we  are  onto something here, Margaret. A repair service… there are people who’d pay for a proper fix, something that lasts. Absolutely. And it's the principles of it! We’re not just slapping new strings on – we're restringing properly, tensioning correctly. Remember Mrs. Henderson’s racket? She was ecstatic when we did hers. Said she hadn't felt like that on the court in years. Remember her complaining about her ear lobe getting caught in the net during the demonstration? A cautionary tale, that. Though, speaking of demonstrations… I’ve been thinking about this cable tie situation. Instead of just replacing the broken string, we could reinforce the vulnerable points with these little beauties. Small, discreet, and surprisingly strong. Cable ties, you say? But wouldn't they look rather...clunky? People want a professional finish, Arthur. Not a fix job held together with plastic. Not clunky if we do it right. Smaller ones, strategically placed. Maybe two, near the top and bottom of the string bed, where it's most prone to shearing. And we’d have to find a colour that blends with the racket’s frame. Black, probably, to be safe. We’d need a box of assorted sizes, really - perhaps a mixed pack to start with. Cost-wise... I reckon a box of 100 decent cable ties wouldn’t break the bank - maybe £15? And then we'd factor in the string itself, obviously. Right. And the string… that’s the other major expense. We need to source something reliable. Remember that synthetic stuff we used for young Timothy at school? It seemed to hold up well enough. Timothy, goodness, that was years ago! I think he's playing cricket now. Are you sure about using synthetic in this application? Primary school rackets are a different beast to the ones used in secondary school - more hard hits. Perhaps something a little tougher? We'd need to research the optimum gauge, tension, and material for different racket types.

Cor, this is a lovely brew, Annie. Proper builder's tea, just how I like it. Mind you, not as good as me mum used to make, bless ‘er. Could put a bit o' magic in a cuppa, she could. You always say that, Arthur. And you always appreciate Annie’s efforts. She puts a lot of thought into it, you know. All this fancy loose leaf stuff. Doesn’t matter to you though, does it? As long as it’s strong. Aye, strong’s the ticket. All this floral nonsense… don’t need that. Give me a good, honest cup of tea and a biscuit. Speaking o' biscuits… are there any digestives left, Sarah? Just a few, Dad. I was saving them for after we'd finished talking about the exhibition. Exhibition, eh? This modern… doodling you’ve been on about. It's not doodling, Arthur. It’s contemporary art. There’s a significant difference. The artist is exploring themes of displacement and memory through abstract form. Displacement? Memory? Sounds like a right load of rubbish if you ask me. Back in me day, art was a painting o' a nice landscape, or a proper portrait. You knew what you were lookin' at! This… …this is just splodges! It’s not  just  splodges, Dad. It’s about evoking a feeling, a sense of something. The colours, the texture... they’re meant to prompt a response in the viewer. Think of Rothko, for example. Those massive blocks of colour? People find them incredibly moving. Rothko? Never ‘eard of ‘im. Sounds foreign. I'm more a Constable man, I am. Constable and Turner. Now  they  knew how to paint a sky. Arthur, you’re being deliberately difficult. Sarah's worked hard on her dissertation on this stuff. It's important to her. It’s alright, Mum. Dad’s entitled to his opinion! But honestly, some of it is quite thought-provoking. This artist, Elara Vance, she uses recycled materials. It's about sustainability too, which is, well, important. She's got this installation, it's made entirely of discarded plastic bottles, woven together to create these shimmering, almost ethereal forms. It's quite remarkable, actually. The way she transforms something so mundane into something so… resonant. It’s not just about the recycling aspect, although that’s a valid point. It’s about the inherent beauty in the discarded, the overlooked.

Ugh, honestly, Chloe from marketing is  such  a nightmare. Did you hear what she said to Liam about his presentation slides? Apparently, they were "aggressively beige." Aggressively beige! Seriously, who even uses that adjective? Aggressively beige? That’s…ridiculous. What’s wrong with beige? It’s calming. It’s neutral. People like neutral! Sounds like she just wanted to be difficult. What’s she even got against Liam? I don’t know! He’s a lovely bloke, Liam. A bit quiet, maybe, but genuinely nice. She just… thrives on power dynamics, I think. Or maybe she's just desperately trying to appear edgy and cool. It's embarrassing, really. Makes the whole office feel like a giant school playground. Sounds about right. Some people just want to watch the world burn, or at least, rearrange the colour palettes. My shift was equally… stimulating. Had a patient convinced she was communicating with squirrels through interpretive dance. Oh my god! That’s brilliant, in a chaotic sort of way. At least it's more entertaining than aggressively beige presentations. Squirrel interpretive dance... I need to write that down. Speaking of chaotic, this kitchen is currently resembling a biohazard zone. Did you manage to tackle any of the mountain of dishes? I did a valiant attempt! See? Still a fair few lurking, though. I was going to leave it ‘til tomorrow but…you're right. It’s staring at me. Honestly, I just want to collapse on the sofa and binge-watch something. Procrastination level: Expert. Same. I was supposed to be finalising those reports for Monday, but I’ve spent the last hour looking at pictures of otters doing yoga. Apparently, it's a thing. Otters doing yoga? Show me! Oh. My. God. Those are  amazing . How did I not know this was a thing? Look at his little downward dog! It’s so perfect. I feel slightly inadequate now. Don’t! You deal with actual human psychological trauma all day. Otters are just being silly. It's perfectly acceptable to find them amusing. Though, it does make me question the English language a little. "Aggressively beige" – what a strange phrase. Who invented that? Right? Like, aggressively. It implies  intent , doesn't it? Beige doesn't have intent. It just  is . It's the linguistic equivalent of putting sprinkles on plain porridge. Just… unnecessary. And, you know, honestly quite judgmental. Imagine judging someone's choices of beige wallpaper.

Honestly, another day, another mountain of spreadsheets. Mr. Davies is on a real tear with the quarterly projections this week. It's like he  wants  to see me age prematurely. Sounds rough, love. Did he at least let you have a decent lunch break? A fifteen-minute window to wolf down a sandwich while simultaneously responding to seven urgent emails. It's a wonder I haven’t developed stress-induced tinnitus. I’m thinking of requesting a standing desk. You know, posture and all that. Standing desks? Right. The peak of workplace innovation. You'll be aching your feet by lunchtime. Look, you need to find a way to switch off a bit more. You're glued to that phone even when you're  here . I know, I know. It's just… ingrained now, isn't it? This constant accessibility. Still, I’m half tempted. Maybe a little exercise built into the daily routine would do me good. Fewer biscuits, too. Speaking of which… Don't start. You promised yourself fewer biscuits. And you know the doctor was saying… Yes, yes. The doctor was saying I should cut back. But a biscuit is hardly the root of all evil. It's a tiny comfort! Besides, everything in moderation, right? Much like a glass of wine after a day wrestling with Davies’ spreadsheets. That's exactly what I’m talking about. It’s become a habit, a crutch. It's not about denying yourself  everything , it’s about thinking about  why  you're reaching for it. Are you truly relaxing, or just avoiding something? That's… a surprisingly perceptive question, considering you spent the last hour watching documentaries about ancient Roman plumbing. Hey! Roman plumbing is fascinating! And it's related… it’s about engineering, planning, problem-solving. It's no different to figuring out how to streamline Mr. Davies’ workflow! Oh, right. The parallels are striking. It’s just… sometimes, you need a little distraction. It’s not  all  about deep philosophical reasoning. Actually, it brings me to something I was reading the other day… about common sense versus intelligence. Oh, here we go. Deep dive time. No, seriously. There was this article arguing that someone can be incredibly intelligent - PhDs, the works - but utterly lacking in common sense. And vice versa, you know? People with little formal education, but a real knack for navigating the world. I get it. There's a big difference between book smarts and street smarts.

Right, well, that was… an adventure. Honestly, Comberton Farm felt like a zoo today, didn’t it? So many little legs running around. The pigs! The pigs were muddy! I petted a pig, Mummy! A big, pink one! I saw a sheep. It had fluffy wool. And it ate grass. Boring. Well, sheep  are  pretty dedicated grass eaters, aren't they, love? But the farmer said they’re very important, providing wool for jumpers and blankets. Remember your favourite blue jumper? That comes from sheep! My blue jumper?! Wow! Did the sheep make my jumper?! Well, not  directly , darling. But their wool is spun into yarn, then knitted into jumpers just like yours. I want pizza. Honestly, you're all the same. Pizza can wait, Leo. We had a lovely picnic at the farm, didn’t we? Remember the sandwiches? And the strawberries? The strawberries were yummy! And I got to feed the chickens! But one chicken pecked me! Did it hurt, sweetie? No, just a little tickle! Then I laughed. I wanted to feed the goats. But you said no because they’d eat my hat. Because they  would  have, Leo! Goats are notorious hat-eaters. It’s a well-documented phenomenon. Besides, we had enough excitement already. Mrs. Henderson from school called today – apparently, there were a few… incidents in class this afternoon. Incidents? What happened? Well, apparently, someone decided to build a rather elaborate tower out of blocks during phonics time. It disrupted the whole class. I built it! It was really tall! It was, was it? And what was the lesson, Leo? What’s more important - building tall towers or learning your ‘a’ and ‘e’ sounds? Towers are fun. They  are  fun. But education is important too, darling. And then there was the… glitter incident. Glitter? Did someone spill glitter? A  lot  of glitter. Let's just say the classroom resembled a snow globe after a rather enthusiastic arts and crafts session. And Mrs. Henderson suspects  someone  may have decided glitter needed to be redistributed to every available surface, including, but not limited to, the teacher’s hair. It was very sparkly! It was a nightmare to clean up. Honestly, I'm half tempted to just ban glitter from the house altogether. What about it, should we? No! Glitter is pretty! We could make sparkly pictures! That’s true, darling. Perhaps we can limit it to supervised sparkly picture-making sessions.

Right, then. Earl Grey it is. Standard, eh? You didn’t fancy a builders today? Feels a bit…celebratory, doesn't it? Like it should be strong enough to stand a spoon up in. Celebratory, are we? It’s just Easter, love. A bit of chocolate, a bit of family, no need for industrial-strength tea. And you know I'm not a fan. Besides, you’ll be bouncing off the walls as it is after all that yarn you've been hoarding. Hoarding is a strong word! I'm  collecting . There's a difference. And it's not just yarn, it's alpaca, merino, cashmere…holds a certain quality, ya know? This new shade of seafoam green, it’s absolutely  perfect  for a shawl. Think I'll start it for Mam. She’s been moaning about needing something warm for the evenings. Seafoam green, eh? Bit stylish for Mam, isn't it? She usually goes for beige. Practical beige. Well, she deserves a bit of stylish, doesn't she? Proper practically stylish, mind. Functional and lovely. Like...like Florence Pugh in a boiler suit. Now  that’s  style. Did you see her at that premiere last week? Stunning. Just… smashing. You and your celebrities. You’ve got a soft spot for Florence, haven’t you? What is it about her, anyway? Everything! Her acting, obviously. But her confidence, the way she owns the room… she seems genuinely happy to be herself. Not a manufactured happy, you know? Like some of 'em. And that hair! Just...perfectly undone. I’ve been trying to recreate it for weeks, but I end up looking like I wrestled a badger. I can imagine. You've got the passion, just maybe not the volume. Although, I did catch a bit of the Olympics the other day. Some of those athletes are defying gravity. It's incredible. Reminded me of that Matisse cut-out exhibition I saw last year. The way he used those shapes… so dynamic, so full of energy. Similar, in a way, to the sheer athleticism. Matisse, right? The ones all cut out? Aye, I saw that in the Tate Modern a few years back. Bold, weren't they? Made you feel like you could just leap off the wall. Speaking of color... I've been thinking about doing a bigger project, not just a shawl. Maybe a blanket. And I was wondering, what do you reckon about incorporating some metallics?

Right then, Arthur. Tell me again why we had to take the Northern Line all the way down? Couldn’t we ‘ave got the Victoria Line like we usually do? It's always less crowded, innit? Now, Maureen, don’t start. The Victoria Line was having “engineering works,” apparently. Big sign up at Euston. Couldn’t miss it. Besides, the Northern Line goes right past the Science Museum, remember? You were all keen on seeing that dinosaur exhibit. Dinosaurs. Right. Just as well I brought me little travel pillow. Felt like a sardine in a tin, I did. Packed in like 'em little kippers from Grimsby. Honestly, London public transport is gettin' worse every year. Remember when you could actually  breathe  on the Tube? You’re exaggerating, love. It wasn’t that bad. And think of the saving! The Victoria Line tickets are always a few bob more. Stretching the pension a bit, you know. Stretching the pension? Arthur, you’ve got a bit of a nest egg yourself, don’t be daft. It’s about comfort, isn't it? Proper comfort. Stood on strangers' feet for half an hour, I did. The lad next to me kept looking at me like I was some sort of… oddity. Probably thought I was lost. He probably just thought you were a sensible woman travelling comfortably. That pillow was a good idea, by the way. So, the Science Museum. What did you think? Did they have some decent bits and bobs? Well, the dinosaurs were alright, I suppose. A bit… dusty looking, to be honest. More like bones in a cupboard than prehistoric beasts. Though that T-Rex skeleton  was  impressive, I’ll give them that. Reminded me of that big one they had at the World Museum back home. We used to take little Liam there when he were a lad. Liam’s getting on a bit now, isn’t he? Last time I saw him, he had a beard down to 'ere. He does. A proper scruffy one, too. Says it’s “artistic.” Still, his mum's fussing over him, as always. Anyway, after the dinosaurs, I was thinkin’ we should've gone to the IMAX. Remember how we talked about seeing that new wildlife film? Ah, yes. But the IMAX tickets were frightfully expensive, love. And after battling that Tube, I just wanted a cuppa and a sit-down. And frankly, the 3D glasses always give me a headache.

Right then, Operation Christmas Dinner. Where are we at? I've checked with Sarah, and the kids are definitely flying in from Singapore on the 23rd. So, we're hosting Christmas Eve and Christmas Day, yes? Aye, that’s the plan. Christmas Eve's always been more relaxed, hasn’t it? Just a proper roast, loads of laughter. Christmas Day – the full shebang. Turkey, all the trimmings, enough food to feed a small army. I’ve started thinking about the sides already. Yorkshire puddings are definitely essential, of course. No Christmas dinner is complete without 'em. Absolutely vital. I was thinking of doing a proper chestnut stuffing this year. I found this recipe online – apparently, you have to roast the chestnuts first to really bring out the flavour. Bit of faff, but supposedly worth it. What about the potatoes? Roasties or mashed? Roasties, definitely roasties. Crispy on the outside, fluffy on the inside. My nan used to make the  best  roast potatoes. She’d soak ‘em in this vinegar water for hours. Secret ingredient, she’d say. Never told anyone exactly what kind of vinegar, mind you. Proper tease she was. Always used to say ‘a good roast potato is a testament to a life well lived’ – which, ironically, she lived a long and absolutely chaotic one! Sounds like her! My mum’s more of a mashed potato person, but I think roasties win out for Christmas. Speaking of chaotic lives, have you heard from Liam and Chloe? Are they still firm on spending Boxing Day with your sister in Shanghai? I spoke to Liam just last week. They're confirmed. Says Chloe’s been teaching their little one how to say “Ni hao.” Which is adorable, right? He did mention something about them struggling to find a decent Christmas tree in Shanghai. Apparently, most of the ones they’ve seen are… well, let's just say they're not exactly the Nordic variety. I can imagine! Everything here's a slightly skewed version of what we're used to. It’s bizarre, isn't it? I saw a Christmas advert on TV the other day – snow, reindeer, the whole shebang – and it just hit me how completely foreign this whole experience is, even though it's Christmas. Reminds me of that film,  Lost in Translation .  Lost in Translation ! Good choice. That film gets right under your skin, doesn't it?

Right, I’m officially beyond knackered. What a day. Lectures were brutal. Professor Davies decided to spring a pop quiz on us about 18th-century agricultural policy. Like, seriously? Who cares? Sounds delightful. At least you have something to complain about that isn’t dough sticking to your fingers. My Saturday was… an experience. Ooh, do tell. Was it the usual Saturday morning rush gone wrong? I’m still traumatised from last weekend’s Americano disaster. Someone actually sent back a perfectly decent Americano because it wasn’t "strong enough." Worse, honestly. This bloke, right? Came in for a sourdough loaf, and when I gave it to him, he starts going on about it being "too crusty." Like, it's sourdough! What did he expect? Fluffy? I tried to explain the process, you know, the starters, the fermentation... He just cut me off and said he wanted a refund. Blimey. Some people, eh? You can't win. Did you give him one? No way! I stood my ground. Told him sourdough is naturally crusty. He huffed and puffed, threatened to write a review… Oh, don't even mention reviews! I was just refreshing. Apparently, someone left a one-star review on 'The Corner Cupboard' last night. Said my oat latte tasted like "sadness." Sadness! Where do these people come from? Sadness! Right. Honestly, the things people write online… I saw a review of that new Italian place, 'Bella Notte,' just down the road. Someone complained the pasta was too… Italian. It’s madness. You put your heart and soul into something, and some random on the internet can just tear it down with a few ill-chosen words. It’s enough to make you want to chuck the whole thing in. I know! Especially when it’s completely unfair. Like, I’ve worked so hard to create a cosy, welcoming atmosphere in the café. It’s not a Michelin-starred restaurant, it’s a lovely little place for a coffee and a chat. But people expect five-star service and then get all dramatic when the milk's not frothed  exactly  how they want it. It’s the Twitter effect, isn’t it? Everyone thinks they’re a food critic these days. I saw a post the other day, someone slating a restaurant for  not  having oat milk. Like, what’s the problem with regular milk? Don't even start me on dietary restrictions.

Right then, everyone, dinner’s nearly ready. Oisin, darling, please don't throw those raspberries on the floor! Honestly, you'd think they were poisonous, the way you're rejecting them. They’re… squishy! Squishy food is the best, Mum. Like those chocolate ice creams we got last week. Remember? The ones with the little honeycomb bits? Yes, I remember very well. You practically inhaled three of them. We'll get more soon, but tonight is about vegetables. We've got carrots, peas, and a side of broccoli. Now, Ben, put your phone away and come and set the table properly, please. Ben, don't be rude! And Mum, are you using the rosemary from the garden? It smells amazing. Broccoli? Seriously? It looks like tiny trees. They  are  tiny trees, Ben. And perfectly good for you. Think of the Popeye factor. Strong muscles! Remember when we went cycling last weekend? You were flagging by the end of the hill. More broccoli, stronger legs. I like orange ones! See? Someone appreciates a good vegetable. This rosemary is lovely, Sarah. I’m so glad I finally planted some, it makes such a difference. I was worried about the birds getting to the bird eggs, that’s why I put that netting up. Did you see them, Sarah, when you were in the garden earlier? I did! There were three little blue ones. Absolutely adorable. We need to be careful they don’t fall out of the nest. It’s so lovely to see them, though. Reminds me of when I was a kid, playing in my grandma's garden in London. She had the most amazing roses. I’d rather have gerbils. They’re easier. You don’t have to make them eat vegetables. Gerbils don't exactly need broccoli, no. But you do! Look, just try one bite. One tiny bite. And if you're still not keen, we'll have some yogurt afterwards. How about that? Yogurt! With sprinkles! Sprinkles are always a good incentive. My little Leo  lives  on sprinkles. Trying to get him to eat anything green is a nightmare. It's just endless negotiating. "Just one bite of broccoli, and then…!" I know exactly what you mean! It’s exhausting, isn't it? Still, it’s all worth it to see them growing up. Though, I do wish Oisin would eat  something  other than raspberries. Honestly, that boy lives on fruit and sheer willpower.

Honestly, the supermarket was a nightmare this morning. Absolute chaos. They’d run out of avocados, can you believe it? And the queue for the self-checkout was stretching halfway across the store. I felt like I was in a rugby scrum. Did you manage to get everything you needed, Sarah? Aye, mostly. They were a bit short on washing-up liquid, but nothing major. The young 'uns were causing a right commotion in the frozen food aisle, though. One of them nearly knocked over a whole stack of pizzas! Honestly, some people have no spatial awareness. But I got the biscuits you asked for. Chocolate digestives, your favourite. Pizzas knockin’ over? Back in my day, you’d get a clip ‘round the ear for less! Nowadays, it’s all just… mayhem. Remember when Mr. Henderson used to run the greengrocer’s down the street? Proper good quality, he had. Knew everything about his fruit and veg. None of this imported nonsense. Oh, absolutely, Nan. Everything felt so much more… considered, didn’t it? Less disposable. I was talking to a colleague the other day about food waste. It’s just appalling, isn't it? We practically throw away a third of what we buy. Speaking of which, I was thinking, we should all go out for a meal next week. Somewhere nice. Perhaps that Italian place we like? Oh, that sounds lovely! It would be a nice change from cooking every night. I’m free on Wednesday, if that works for everyone? And it would be good to get out. My back’s been a bit dodgy lately, you know, from all the bending and scrubbing. Wednesday suits me fine. As long as they’ve got a bit of cod on the menu. Can't beat a bit of good fish, can you? It’s better than all this fancy foreign stuff. Of course, Nan. Fish it is. Right, so Wednesday it is then. I'll book a table. Now, Sarah, have you had a chance to sort out Mrs. Peterson’s medication deliveries? She's been quite distressed about it. I know you're busy, but she really relies on you. I’ve been tryin', love. But the pharmacy keeps messin' it up. They say they’ve sent it, but it doesn’t arrive. I’ve had to chase them twice this week already. It’s a right palaver.

Honestly, this weaning process is proving to be quite the marathon, isn’t it? Little Leo is a whirlwind of mashed carrots and sheer determination. He’s got your stubborn streak, love, you know. He definitely does. It’s a battle of wills at every mealtime! He mostly just wants to fling it across the room, doesn't he? Though, I have to admit, the look on his face when he actually manages to get something in his mouth? Priceless. Yesterday he got a whole chunk of sweet potato stuck to his nose. Oh, bless him! I remember when you were little, you used to wear your dinner like a badge of honour. Broccoli in your hair, peas on your chin… your dad would just roar with laughter. It's a lovely phase, though. A messy one, but lovely. Are you finding the puree textures are going down okay? I read somewhere you need to gradually increase the chunkiness. Yeah, I'm trying. He did reject the lumps yesterday, but today seemed a bit better. I’m trying to follow the NHS guidelines, but sometimes it’s hard to remember which stage he’s supposed to be at. It feels like every website says something different! Tell me about it. Information overload, isn’t it? Remember when we were trying to figure out cot safety rules? I felt like I needed a degree just to put him down to sleep! So, have you heard back from Sarah about the barbecue on Saturday? Not yet. I texted her this morning but no reply. She’s probably just busy with marking. Her class is apparently a handful this term. She said they're all running around like headless chickens. I’m really hoping she can make it though. It would be nice to see everyone. And for Leo to get some proper family time. Absolutely. It’s been a little isolating just us three lately. I was thinking, and I know it's a bit ambitious, but perhaps we could try and get a family get-together going next weekend? Your uncle David’s birthday is the following week, so let's aim for the one before. We could do a roast, I’d love to have everyone around. Oh, that would be wonderful! I'll chase up Sarah and see if she’s free. What about Auntie Maureen? She’s been wanting to see Leo, hasn’t she?

Honestly, I can’t quite believe this is Norfolk. It feels… elevated. Like a proper landscape, not just a flat expanse of fields. Are you sure we’re still in the same county? Quite sure. This is the Brecks. It's a bit of a geological anomaly, really. Remnant of ancient sandy hills, carved out by glaciers. Not exactly the Norfolk everyone pictures, is it? More like a tiny slice of the Peak District accidentally ended up here. It’s extraordinary. I’ve lived in Norwich my entire life, and I’d never ventured this far. It’s so… wild. I’m used to the neat, regimented fields. This feels almost… untamed. And the silence! It's almost deafening compared to the city. Well, that’s the point, isn't it? Escape the concrete jungle. Though, wild doesn't exactly mean untouched. There's loads of forestry work going on around here, managing the pine forests. Part of the reason these hills are even visible now – they were mostly obscured by woodland for centuries. Forestry, right. Practicality. Always practicality. Still, it’s lovely to see. I’ve been reading about the Bronze Age settlements up here. Apparently, it was a prime location because of the slightly higher ground, affording better views and defence. Imagine, standing here millennia ago, looking out… completely different, of course. Fewer sheep, more likely to encounter a wild boar. Probably. Did you spot the flint workings on the way up? They're rather subtle, just pits in the landscape but indicative of how important this area was. The flint was incredibly high quality, used for tools and weapons all over the region. I did catch a glimpse - I thought they were just depressions in the ground! I'm used to thinking of Norfolk as just farming, but there's so much history layered beneath the surface, isn't there? It's like discovering a whole new part of England. Exactly. And the villages are charming too. We could head to Lakenheath later for a pub lunch. It’s got a Norman church, apparently built on the site of a Saxon chapel. A real mixed bag of ages. Lakenheath sounds perfect. Are those houses down there, nestled into the valley? Are they quite old? Most of them, yeah. Many have thatched roofs, though renovations are often required. The exposed location means they bear the brunt of the wind.

Honestly, Liam, another cycling documentary? You’ve got a whole collection of ‘em now, haven't ya? It’s like you’re planning on becoming one. It’s good stuff, El! Inspiring, even. Did you see that bit about the guy tackling the Stelvio Pass? Absolutely mental. Plus, it makes me feel better about my slightly wobbly commute. At least I’m not battling gale-force winds on a mountain pass. Aye, well, battling rush hour traffic on the A1 is its own kind of hell, isn't it? More stop-start than summit climbs, though. Speaking of which, did you hear back about Sarah’s application for that project manager role at GreenTech? Not yet, no. Fingers crossed, though. She was properly chuffed when she told me, wasn't she? Said it was a good fit, opportunity to use her permaculture knowledge. She deserves it, she really does. Always been dead clever, Sarah. Remember when we were kids, beating everyone at Kerplunk? She’d have this laser focus, didn’t miss a beat. Bet she’s brilliant at spreadsheets now. She was a Kerplunk prodigy, that's for sure. And spreadsheets? Probably a natural. I hope she gets it, it would be brilliant for her savings – she’s trying to get that deposit together, isn’t she? Trying. It's a struggle, isn't it? All this house buying malarkey. I’ve been looking at some flats in Durham, but… well, they’re all tiny, and the council tax is a killer. Reminds me of home, but without the sea air. Durham’s lovely though, historically. You could always look further afield, maybe? I know it's easier said than done, though. But you're right, house prices are ridiculous. Feels like you need to win the lottery just to get a foothold. Tell me about it! I nearly choked on me tea when I saw one advertised the other day – three bedrooms, needing a full refurb, and costing more than me mam's entire house! Exactly. It's bonkers. Though, remember when we saw 'Everything Everywhere All at Once'? The bit where Evelyn's daughter had that massive student debt… that felt pretty close to reality, didn't it? Aye, it did. Gut-wrenching, that was. Although a wee bit much, even for me. All the hot dog fingers and raccoon chefs? A bit… weird. Still, the message was sound, innit?

Oh, look at these, Liam. They’re just bursting with colour. Cowslips and primroses all tangled together. It’s proper lovely, isn't it? Reminds me of being a kid, foraging for them with my nan. She’d make a cordial, absolutely divine. It is. Bit windy though, isn’t it? Should have remembered a scarf. Much nicer than the grey of London, though. Really does clear the head. Research deadline looming, you know. That econometric model is being a right pain. Tell me about it. Mine’s the comparative linguistics project. I’m starting to think I’ve bitten off more than I can chew. Trying to map the semantic drift of regional dialect terms for farming practices… it's a rabbit hole, a proper rabbit hole. Especially when you start looking at archaic words. Did you know there were like, twelve different ways of referring to a scarecrow in Norfolk alone? Twelve? Seriously? My model just wants to spit out errors. I’m trying to factor in the impact of government subsidies on cash crop diversification post-Brexit. Want to guess how many variables that entails? And the data… the data’s a nightmare. Half of it’s sourced from Farmers Weekly, and the other half is… well, let’s just say it's ‘optimistic’ to say it's reliable. Optimistic. Yes, that’s a good word for it. My grandma used to complain about the Ministry of Agriculture. Said they didn't understand the first thing about growing anything. All spreadsheets and complicated regulations. She just knew, you see. She  felt  when the soil was right. Something you can’t quantify, obviously. Exactly! You can run all the regressions in the world, but you’ll miss the nuance. Speaking of feeling, did you see the Norwich game on Saturday? Utter shambles. Absolutely dire. Don't remind me. My dad was livid. Kept muttering about the defence. Said it was like watching a team of amateurs. Although, I did think Sargent had a decent first half. Sargent had a decent  moment . The rest were… well, let's just say they wouldn’t be getting a look-in at Arsenal. It's just frustrating, you know? All that potential, wasted. Honestly, sometimes I wonder if the whole Premier League system is sustainable. All that money, all that pressure… does it actually improve the quality of the football? I was reading an article the other day arguing for a regional league system again.

Right, so, parking at Mum's is gonna be a nightmare, isn't it? She's got the WI bake sale on Saturday, and Mr. Henderson's got his vintage tractor club thing going. Honestly, you’d think they planned it. They probably did. Small town life, eh? You'll have to drop me off a block away and I'll hoof it. Don’t want to risk a tow, especially not for the football. Aye, don't be daft. I’ll sort it. I'll park on the street. It's not ideal, but it’ll do. More important thing is, are you actually sure you're coming to the match on Sunday? You were looking a bit…non-committal last week. I'm coming. Really. Just been a hectic couple of weeks with the Davies project, you know? All-nighters and endless spreadsheets. Needed a bit of a mental reset. Sunderland vs. Newcastle… that's my reset button. Good lad. Wouldn’t be the same without you moaning about the ref and shouting at the lads. Speaking of lads, have you been watching Wimbledon? Djokovic is practically untouchable, isn't he? Absolutely dominant. Alcaraz had a tough run, didn't he? But Djokovic…legendary. I was thinking, we should try and hit up the courts again next weekend. You’ve been practicing, haven't you? A bit. Mostly just rallying with my little brother, Liam. He’s getting quite decent, actually. Though he still thinks shouting encouragement at the ball makes it go in. Typical lad. Of course he does! Remember when he tried to put a football in the net with a catapult? Don't remind me! Mum nearly had a heart attack. He was convinced he'd invented a new sport. "Catapult Football," he called it. Honestly. Kids. Anyway, no catapults allowed at the tennis court, I hope. Right, back to arrangements. Have you had any more luck with those flats in Durham? The ones you were looking at near the cathedral? Not really, nah. Everything decent is either snapped up instantly or ridiculously priced. Honestly, you’d think they were selling gold bricks, not one-bedroom apartments. I saw one today that was openly advertising its “historic charm” - which translated to ‘slightly damp and with questionable plumbing’. Sounds delightful. Durham’s a nightmare for property. It's all postcode lottery, isn’t it? And parking…don't even get me started on parking.

Honestly, it’s just relentless, isn’t it? This Depp-Heard trial. Every single detail splashed all over the news. I saw something about faecal matter again this morning. Really… Cor, that sounds grim. I saw a bit about it on the telly the other night. Didn't understand half of it, all the legal jargon. Just seemed like a lot of shouting, really. Though, I do feel sorry for the poor dogs. Imagine being caught up in all that. Dogs are alright, aren’t they? Loyal creatures. Much better than some humans I’ve known. Remember old Reginald next door, Elsie? Used to nick apples off my tree, he did. Bold as brass. Oh, Elsie! You always had the best stories. Apples, was it? Or was it pears? It's all a haze now. Still, Reginald sounds like a character. Much more interesting than Hollywood lawyers, I’d say. Reginald sounds a right rascal! Here you go, Elsie. Nice ginger snap. Thank you, dear. They don’t make biscuits like they used to, you know. More flavour. Less… air. Anyway, speaking of wildlife, have you seen that flock of geese gathering down by the river? Biggest I’ve seen in years. No, I haven't actually. I've been so preoccupied with… well, everything. But geese, that’s lovely. Are they getting ready to migrate? Oh, yes, definitely. They’ve been getting louder and louder, honking their heads off. My grandson, little Liam, he loves watching them. He calls them ‘big honkers.’ He’s a clever little chap, that one. Migration… I remember my husband, George, he used to track the swallows every year. Kept a little notebook and everything. Marked down the date they arrived, the date they left. Called it his "Swallow Log." Utterly useless, of course. Never did anyone any good, but he loved it. That's so sweet. A dedicated Swallow Log! It's lovely to have little obsessions like that, isn't it? Gives life a bit of colour. I have a thing for waxwings, although I rarely see them. They’re just so… elegant. Waxwings? Never seen one. What do they look like? They're quite striking, actually. Greyish-brown, very sleek, with these bright red markings under their wings and on their tails. They look a bit like miniature cardinals. We used to get a pair nesting in the old oak tree at the bottom of the garden.

That pasta bake is absolutely lovely, Anon. Seriously, you’ve outdone yourself. It's exactly what I needed after that morning. Glad you think so! It’s my mum’s recipe, actually. She always makes it for family gatherings. So, tell me all about this morning. You sounded a bit stressed on the phone. Oh, it was… a day. A job interview. For a head of department position at that new language school in Solihull. You know, the one that just opened? The 'Lingua Nova'? I've seen adverts for it. Sounds fancy. How did it go? Don't tell me you froze up like you did at that awful interview for the online tutoring gig last year! Please don’t remind me about  that . No freezing, thankfully. Though, I think I might have come across a bit intense. They asked me about my vision for curriculum development and... well, I just launched straight into a ten-minute explanation involving communicative language teaching, task-based learning, and incorporating digital tools. I think I might have scared them a little. Right, sounds like you. You get so passionate about it. They probably just weren’t prepared for that much enthusiasm. Did you at least talk about assessment? That's always a big thing for those roles. Yes, of course! Briefly, after I’d finished my entire lecture on learner autonomy! Honestly, I feel like I need to work on my delivery, pacing myself a bit. I just get so excited to share my ideas. It’s a terrible habit. And then they asked me about dealing with challenging students, and I started rambling about differentiation strategies, and… it was just a mess! Look, you’re clearly brilliant at what you do, Sarah. You’ve always been. And you’ve got the qualifications to prove it. They were probably just trying to see how you cope under pressure. Don't beat yourself up. Did they say when they'd be in touch? They said they’d be in touch next week. But honestly, I'm not holding my breath. I feel like I could have handled it so much better. It's just… I really need this. My current school is… well, it’s fine, but it’s not inspiring. It’s just… routine. I know exactly what you mean. Sometimes you just need something fresh. Speaking of fresh, have you seen little Leo lately?

Honestly, this is exactly what I needed. A proper catch-up and a cuppa. Work has been absolutely mental this past month, you wouldn’t believe. We’re launching that new line of… well, you wouldn't care about the specifics, but it's involved a lot of spreadsheets and stressed-out suppliers. Tell me about it! Admin at the clinic is always chaotic. It’s just… constant. Paperwork, appointments, chasing up referrals… Dr. Harding keeps promising to get us some decent new software, but it’s been "next quarter" for like, six quarters now. You know? You get used to the madness, but it doesn't make it any less maddening. Oh, the classic “next quarter.” My boss does that a lot. It’s like a verbal shield against actually doing things. So, what  are  your plans for when you eventually escape the horrors of clinic admin? Seriously, you’ve got a postgraduate degree, you could do anything. That’s the thing, isn't it? I  could  do anything, theoretically. Part of me wants to just… go travelling. South America, maybe. Learn to salsa, see some ancient ruins, you know? Just get completely lost for a while. But the other part, the sensible part, is terrified. Terrified of what? Of… everything falling apart. My bank account, mostly. And having to come back and start all over again, probably in a worse position. Mum keeps going on about finding a stable career path, getting on the property ladder. The whole nine yards. Right, the parental pressure. I get that. My nan's always asking when I’m going to settle down and buy a little house with a garden. As if that’s all there is to life! But seriously, South America sounds amazing. You’d love it. And it doesn’t have to be forever. Even six months would do you good. It’s about recharging, finding something that makes you feel… alive, I guess. It  does  sound amazing. I’ve been looking at flights, you know, just browsing. Buenos Aires looks incredible. But then I think about the visa situation, the language barrier… and it just feels overwhelming. Language barriers are easily overcome. Duolingo, a phrasebook, a willingness to look like an idiot for a while. It's all part of the adventure! And visas… well, that’s planning, isn't it? Small steps. What's a really tiny, achievable step you could take today or tomorrow?

Honestly, this wine tastes like vinegar. Proper vinegar. You’d get a better drink outta a puddle back 'ome. Ooh, dramatic as ever, Liv. It's French wine, love, give it a chance! Besides, we're in France, ain't we? Supposed to be soaking up the culture and all that. Culture includes decent wine, doesn't it? This ain't culture, this is a crime against grapes. Anyway, tell us about Liam. Last I heard, he was being all awkward at the market. Don't even start. He was proper weird. Kept saying "Bonjour, madame!" to every single stallholder, even the lads selling sausages. It was embarrassing. I swear, he's trying to be French. Liam’s just trying to impress you, El. It’s a classic boy thing. Remember Tom and the ‘I’m fluent in Italian’ phase? Oh, don’t remind me about Tom! That was a disaster. He couldn’t order a coffee without sweating! Liam's just...different. It’s not the Italian tan and forced accent, it's the obsequiousness. He keeps opening doors for me like I'm Queen Victoria. Sounds like he's overcompensating for something. Maybe he’s realised you’re actually the boss of the relationship. You are, aren't you? Always. Always. Though it’s tiring sometimes, being the one holding everything together. Being a woman in general is tiring, El. Let's not pretend it’s just Liam. Look, you’re worrying too much. He’s probably just nervous, he wants to be thoughtful. Thoughtful would be remembering I hate pain au chocolat! He brought me one this morning. A pain au chocolat! The woman's allergic, practically. Seriously? That’s a tactical error, that is. Right, next time, point blank refuse it and make a big show of leaving it on the table. Make him feel guilty. Yorkshire women know how to handle these things. You and your Yorkshire tactics, Liv. Sometimes, a simple, "Honey, I don't like those" would suffice. Honestly, you two are exhausting. I've been trying to enjoy these macarons, and it’s all been about Liam's bizarre attempts at French charm. Well excuse me for having a boyfriend who’s attempting to morph into a Parisian stereotype! It’s infuriating! And it's not just Liam, is it? It’s everyone. Chloe’s gone all starry-eyed over that new bloke she met at the gallery.

This chicken’s lovely, isn’t it, James? You’ve really outdone yourself tonight. Just a simple roast, love. Nothing fancy. Glad you're enjoying it. Though you're eating like you're on a diet. More potatoes? Don't you start! It’s just…trying to be sensible, that's all. The market research report needs proofreading and I need my brain working properly. Can’t be fueled entirely by carbs. It's awesome, Mr. Patel! Seriously! Can we have this every Sunday? We’ll see, Liam. Depends on whether your mum lets me in the kitchen again after last week’s… incident. Incident? You call setting off the smoke alarm "an incident"? You nearly gave me a heart attack! It was a rogue onion! Honestly. It exploded. I was just trying to caramelise it. Caramelizing onions is hard. Remember when Dad tried to make French Onion Soup? The kitchen smelled like burnt rubber for days. Oh, don’t remind me! That was a disaster. Right, so, Liam, how was hockey practice this afternoon? Did you score any goals? Yeah! One! And I almost had another, but the goalie blocked it. He’s really good. Well done, you! I'm so pleased. You're getting so much better, aren’t you. Are you still thinking about trials for the regional team? Definitely. Mr. Davies says I’ve got potential if I work on my skating. Potential for falling over, more like. Just joking, Liam. Very funny, Finn. Finn, put that phone down and engage! We're having a family dinner. How are your friends? Still seeing a lot of Noah? Mum! I was just checking the scores. Man United lost. It was brutal. And yeah, I saw Noah. We're going to try out the new arcade in Tamworth next weekend. Tamworth? That’s a bit of a trek, isn't it? They finally got a decent arcade? Apparently. It’s got, like, all the new VR games. Finn and Noah were saying it’s the best in the Midlands. Fancy a trip to Tamworth with the lads, then? Get some fresh air instead of staring at spreadsheets. Tempting, but I think I’ll stick to my kitchen explosions for now. Honestly, dear, I'm thinking about that holiday to Cornwall... I've been looking at some nice cottages near Padstow. Cornwall sounds lovely. We could finally go surfing. Although, you’ll probably spend the entire time complaining about the sand getting everywhere.

Honestly, this is breathtaking, isn’t it? I’ve seen pictures, of course, but nothing quite prepares you for the sheer scale of these trees. It’s humbling. Yeah, it's alright. Bit… green, innit? All this green. I’m used to slightly less verdant surroundings back home. Although, Enfield isn’t exactly the Amazon rainforest. You’re impossible. Less verdant? This is a natural wonder! Do you remember Aunt Carol’s obsession with Redwood seedlings when we were kids? She tried to grow one in her garden. Oh, God, yes! That tiny pot on her patio, barely bigger than my hand. She kept fretting that it wasn’t getting enough sunlight. And then when it inevitably died, she blamed the squirrels. Blamed the squirrels! She truly did. She swore they were deliberately sabotaging her horticultural efforts. Do you think she’d have liked this? Standing amongst these giants? She would have been hyperventilating, probably. Or trying to take photographs of every single leaf. And then complaining about the lack of tea facilities. You know how she is. Absolutely. Speaking of family, have you heard anything from your cousin, Liam? Last I heard, he was still trying to launch that drone photography business. Nope. Radio silence. Mum mentioned last week she hadn't spoken to him in a couple of weeks. Which, for Liam, is practically a lifetime. He usually calls at least once a week, just to complain about something. Probably just buried in editing or chasing invoices, you know how it is. Starting your own business… It’s brutal. Especially in this economy. He's got the talent, though, hasn't he? Those aerial shots he did of the Tower Bridge were incredible. Remember showing them to my old lecturers? They were really impressed. They were. He's got an eye. He just needs to… I don't know, be a bit less reliant on Mum for handouts, perhaps. Mum worries about him, you know. She’s constantly checking in. She always has. It's a classic Mum thing. So, how are things with you, temping-wise? Finding anything decent? It's… a bit of a rollercoaster. This week it's data entry for an accountancy firm. Last week, answering phones for a dog grooming business. The dog grooming was actually quite fun, surprisingly. Lots of fluffy little faces. Data entry… well, data entry is data entry. At least it's paying the bills.

Jaysus, this Kiev is grand, isn’t it? Proper creamy. Though I'm surprised you managed to get the garlic butter so even, Liam. Usually it's all swimming at the bottom. It’s easy, Dad. You just need to make sure you pipe it in layers, see? YouTube tutorial. Loads of 'em. Mum’s is always a disaster. Don’t you start, Liam. My Kievs are perfectly acceptable. And at least  I  actually cooked them, unlike someone glued to his phone watching videos. Ah, now, leave the lad alone, Sarah. He’s learning a valuable skill. Besides, you were moaning about your head earlier. Didn't want to be in the kitchen, did you? I was. But that's not the point. He’s always looking up how to do everything online. It's just backchat, isn't it? All this asserting about Kievs. You're fifteen, Liam, not a Michelin star chef. I'm asserting facts, Mum! And it’s not backchat. It’s... improving the family cuisine. Improving, is it? Well, it’s certainly tasty. Anyway, did you catch any of the match this afternoon, Liam? Mon the Ireland! Bit of a scrappy performance, to be fair. Gave that Wallies a bit too much space in the first half. Yeah, it was okay. They were a bit slow to start, definitely. But Farrell’s got them playing well, generally. Saw a load of clips on YouTube afterwards. Some dodgy tackling, though. YouTube again! Honestly, Liam. You’d think you'd talk to me about something proper, like... I don't know, Granny's been on at me to see if we're coming down next weekend. Granny would love to see you both. She's been asking about you, Liam, especially. Said she’s got a new batch of her raspberry jam. Raspberry jam? Sold! Maybe I can take some photos for Flickr. It's got a nice aesthetic. Flickr? Jaysus, what are you on about now? Why not just send her a picture on WhatsApp like a normal person? Because Flickr’s better for archival purposes, Dad! You can organize them into albums. And tags. And... it’s more professional. I was thinking of putting together a portfolio. A portfolio of raspberry jam photos? Dear Lord. He’s lost the plot, hasn’t he? He's a bright lad, Sarah. Let him have his hobbies. Though, you should probably back up those photos somewhere else, Liam.

Honestly, David, you won’t  believe  what I managed to snag on eBay this afternoon. Just came up, practically blinking at me - a full set of Shelley Dainty Blue cups and saucers. Mint condition, apparently. The seller was based in Somerset, can you imagine? Shelley Dainty Blue? Bit posh for our Tuesday night supper, isn't it? Though, I suppose buckwheat bread deserves a bit of elegance. Smells lovely, by the way. Did you get enough buckwheat flour? It is a bit extravagant, I admit. But they were going for a song! A mere £45 for the whole set! I had to be quick, of course. There were three other people bidding. And yes, plenty of buckwheat flour. I even found a recipe for a fig and walnut version. Think you’ll like it? It's a bit more...substantial than your usual sourdough. Figs and walnuts? Sounds promising. My stomach’s already rumbling. Somerset too, eh? You're becoming quite the eBay connoisseur, aren't you? Where did your sudden interest in vintage china come from anyway? It just... happened. I was looking for a replacement teacup after yours chipped, remember? And then I saw this gorgeous Paragon one, and it just spiralled from there. It’s strangely relaxing, searching for these things. Like a little treasure hunt. Plus, they’re beautiful. Real craftsmanship, you know? Mass-produced everything now... it's all so... bland. I get it. It's a proper antidote to the soul-crushing bureaucracy of my day. Though, finding something decent online takes a level of patience I sometimes struggle with. Did you check the delivery costs on this Shelley set? They can sting you, those unseen charges. Don’t worry, I accounted for that. It was all in there. £8.99. A steal, really. I’m just hoping they arrive safely. I’ve requested extra-care packaging. One can only hope. Anyway… how was your day? Still sorting out the arrangements for Brenda's leaving do? It feels like it’s been looming for ages. Looming is an understatement. It's been a logistical nightmare. Half the department wants a karaoke night, the other half wants a quiet pub dinner. I've managed to cobble together something that's hopefully going to satisfy everyone – a function room at The Old Crown, canapés, a DJ, but no compulsory karaoke. Though I’m strongly considering sneaking in a microphone just in case.

Right then, so you're sayin’ this… this 'structurin’,' as you call it, is like, normal practice sometimes? Like, banks just look the other way? Honestly, it sounds proper dodgy, doesn't it? I mean, you're tellin' me you've done it, Dad? Now, love, ‘dodgy’ is a strong word. It’s about efficiency, about making things work. The financial world isn't black and white, you know? Think of it like this: big businesses need to move money quickly, across borders. Sometimes the official channels are… cumbersome. Structuring allows that to happen smoothly. The banks, they have procedures to comply with regulations, of course, but they understand the bigger picture. It's about legitimate business, just… facilitated in a slightly different way. 'Slightly different' is a massive understatement, isn’t it, Dad? I mean, I've read some stuff. Some nasty stuff about where that money can  originate  from. You're playing a dangerous game, really. And what about the kids? What are you teaching them about ethics if you’re… well, skirting the law like this? Don’t go bringing the children into this, Eliza. It's not about ethics, it’s about survival. It’s about a thriving business. And believe me, I’ve shielded them from all the unpleasant realities. They know I work hard, they know I provide for them. That's all that matters. Anyway, the fines are manageable. It’s a calculated risk. The rewards outweigh the potential penalties. I’ve got a good solicitor - he knows how to navigate these things. Uh… Dad, remember that time when you got pulled over for speeding when I was a kid? You said it was a “calculated risk” too, tryin’ to get to Mum’s birthday dinner on time. Didn't go so well, did it? Massive fine. Don't you start, Finn. This is a tad more complicated than a speeding ticket. This is about safeguarding my livelihood, and yours, for that matter. Your mum – she wouldn't understand. Right. Okay. So, what about the new accounts you mentioned? The ones in the Caymans? Are those part of this… structuring thing? Because if they are, and the authorities ever looked into it… Details, details. It's just prudent financial planning. Diversification, you see. Minimising risk. Those accounts are separate, entirely legitimate. They hold investments. Perfectly above board. And they’re… confidential, naturally. Dad, you know I'm in business now, right?

Honestly, this weather is just bonkers, isn't it? One minute it's sunshine, the next it's threatening to rain sideways. Remember last summer? Could barely get a BBQ done. Aye, you’re right about that. Sutton Coldfield was practically swimming in puddles for weeks. Though, I suppose we need the rain, don't we? Fundraising dinners don't go well when the landscape looks parched. People get grumpy. It’s lovely though, isn't it? A bit gloomy, yes, but atmospheric. Just makes you want to curl up with a good book. The kids are loving the puddle jumping after school. It's chaos, but happy chaos. Happy chaos is a good way to put it! My store was packed today. Everyone seems determined to buy wellies, waterproof coats, and umbrellas. My stockroom is groaning. It's better than a slow day, though, I suppose. Speaking of busy… How are things going with the sign language class, love? You seemed really keen when you signed up. It's brilliant! Really challenging, but brilliant. We’re learning the alphabet, and then basic phrases - “hello”, “thank you”, “please”. The teacher is fantastic, really patient. I thought it would be useful for the kids at school, some of them could benefit from visual cues, you know? But it's actually amazing for my brain, keeping me switched on. That's wonderful, love. Always good to learn something new. Remember when I tried to learn Spanish for that conference in Madrid? Lasted about a week. Managed 'Hola' and 'Gracias'. That was it. You did try, Dad! You tried really,  really  hard to order a beer in Spanish. It was a vital part of my networking strategy! Besides, it's easier than sign language. That requires actual focus. So, are we all set for Auntie Maureen's birthday next weekend then? I've booked a table at The Oak Inn. Yep, I’ve sorted the present. I got her that bird bath she's been eyeing up at the garden centre. She’ll love it, she’s obsessed with the robins. I'm bringing the cake. Chocolate orange, her favourite. Although, I'm a bit nervous about travelling that far on a Saturday afternoon - the M6 can be a nightmare. We'll leave early, then. No need to stress. I'll drive. And I'll keep a very sharp eye out for lorries hogging the inside lane.

Honestly, I’m still wrapped up in this corpus of teenage slang. It's… a vortex. One minute they're saying "peng," the next it's "rizz." It's like the language is actively trying to exclude me. I feel like a dinosaur trying to understand TikTok. Tell me about it. I’m dealing with historical fiction manuscripts, which are equally resistant to understanding modern sensibilities. Had one author describe a young woman’s ambition as “forward.” Forward! As in, she’s daring to… want things? It’s just the speed of change, isn’t it? My mum’s still trying to figure out emojis. She sent me a crying-laughing emoji when I told her I got a promotion. Bless her. I had to explain. Multiple times. It's interesting though, isn’t it, how generational gaps manifest in language? My grandma, she still corrects my grammar. Even when I'm speaking perfectly standard English. She thinks “alright” is inherently rude. Oh, absolutely.
