Much better than Bury, to be fair. We get a lot of rain up north. Are you feeling alright, though? You seemed a bit puffed out earlier when we were unloading the camper. Oh, the usual. My stamina, you know. I really should be doing more. I bought that walking stick expecting to be clocking up the miles, but…life got in the way. And frankly, the hills around here look rather challenging. How’s your fitness routine going? You mentioned you were doing Pilates? Yeah, I am. It's doing wonders, actually. Back's feeling much better, and I’ve got a bit more tone going on. Still not where I want to be, though. You know me, always striving for something! I should probably drag you along sometime. We could even do some walks while we’re here. Poland's got some stunning national parks. Strenuous walking, you say? I'm not sure my knees would thank you. And the thought of showing off my…ahem…recent wardrobe choices in a national park… well, let’s just say I’m likely to stick to admiring the scenery from the comfort of this van. Though, goodness knows, I could use a bit of discipline. I’ve been relying rather heavily on biscuits lately. Well, that’s one way to fuel a holiday! Speaking of which, are you reading anything good at the moment? You always had a pile of books on the go. I am! Just started "Normal People" by Sally Rooney. It’s a bit bleak, truthfully, but strangely compelling. What about you? Still plugging through that Russian literature? Slowly but surely. Dostoevsky is… intense. I might need something a bit lighter after this. I was thinking of getting back into some Agatha Christie. Proper comfort reading. It's funny, isn’t it? How we crave that familiarity sometimes, especially when we're away from home. It makes you appreciate your little routines. Absolutely. Though routines have been somewhat…elusive for me of late. The TEFL work is sporadic, as you know. I miss having a proper career, something with a bit of structure and purpose. Have you ever considered volunteering after you finish your current contract?

Right then, ANON, you were saying about your nan’s memory… It’s a funny thing, isn't it? Ageing. I was reading up on telomeres the other day – you know, the protective caps on the end of our chromosomes? Apparently, shortening them is a big factor in how we age. Mad, isn't it, thinking your genes are basically ticking down a clock? It is mad! Nan’s got that sort of… selective memory. She'll remember details from sixty years ago, like the price of bread in 1964, but can't recall what I had for breakfast yesterday. It's frustrating, but also, a bit charming, y'know? I’ve been looking into geriatric care a bit, trying to understand what's happening. It’s a lot more complex than just ‘she’s old’. Aye, it is. They’re starting to think that just extending lifespan isn’t enough - we need to extend  healthspan  too. Keeping people active and engaged for longer. There's talk of gene therapy aiming to influence telomere length, but we're a long way off from achieving immortality, aren’t we? Though, who knows? People were saying the same about flying a century ago. Immortality… that’s a scary thought, actually. Being around forever. I’d rather a good, long life, filled with memories – even the blurry ones. Speaking of which, remember when little Leo, your nephew, barely spoke until he was three? Ah, Leo! A right quiet one he was. The speech therapist was convinced there was a developmental thing going on, something along the lines of autism, but he just grew out of it eventually. A late bloomer, that's all. It’s remarkable, isn't it, how differently kids develop? Different wiring, I suppose. It is. It made me think about icons and how we all interpret the world differently. Leo just processed things differently, took his time. Though, it's given me a newfound respect for patience, trying to understand a toddler… it’s a full-time job! Everything is important, every tiny little thing. I can imagine. You're doing a grand job, though. Listen, about getting away for the weekend... I was thinking we could head up to Connemara? Rent a little cottage by the sea. We could do some kayaking – remember how much you enjoyed that last summer? Connemara sounds lovely! Kayaking… yes please! I'm so desperate for a change of scenery.

Right, so, like, this voucher thing. Dad’s being a right pain about it. He says we can't just spend it anywhere, but Auntie Sheila specifically said it was good at any restaurant. Your dad's just being cautious, love. He always is. Remember when he made us check the expiry date on that box of biscuits three times? It’s a good thing, really, keeps us grounded. But yes, Sheila did say any restaurant. Let’s look at it properly. Was it from that gardening center, or the one that does the tourist brochures? Tourist brochures, lass. Definitely tourist brochures. Means it’s worth a decent bit, easy enough. Don't let your mum argue you out of it. We're treatin' ourselves to that Italian down the road, aren't we? Been ages. But he was saying something about hidden terms and conditions! Like, there’s probably a tiny print bit that says you can’t use it on a Sunday or something ridiculous. He’s probably right to be suspicious, honestly. Let’s check the small print, just to be safe. Although, if we're going to the Italian, it's unlikely. They’re pretty straightforward. Speaking of straightforward, have you figured out how to use that new coffee maker yet? It’s got more buttons than a spaceship! Honestly! It’s terrifying. I think I managed to make a pot yesterday, but it tasted a bit… off. Like burnt caramel. It kept beeping at me. Burnt caramel, eh? That’s the advanced setting. You’ve got it programmed for ‘Espresso Deluxia’. Turn it down a few notches, love. It's designed for wizards, that thing. I’ll show you later. I was thinking we could pop into town and get some new sunglasses later. The ones you've got, darling, are a bit… faded, aren't they? And I need something a bit more practical for gardening. Everything's getting dusty. Speaking of which, did you see how the roses are doing? They're struggling a bit with this heat. Yeah, they look a bit peaky. They’re needing a good soak, definitely. We should look to get that fruit tree we were talking about. Maybe an apple? Or a plum? A plum’s a good shout. Keeps the birds away better than apples, you know? Less temptation. Remember the referendum? Do you kids even think about that anymore?

Right then, love. Another pile of washing done. Honestly, it multiplies while you're not looking, doesn’t it? How was work today? Did you manage to finish that campaign copy you were struggling with? Actually, yeah! It clicked this afternoon. The client loved it, which is a relief. It was about sustainable coffee – bit dull on the face of it, but I ended up weaving in this whole thing about ethical sourcing and supporting small farmers. Feeling rather clever about it now, to be honest. Clever indeed! That's brilliant, darling. Always good when they're happy, innit? Less hassle all round. Speaking of happy, have you started thinking about the Christmas tree yet? Mrs. Henderson next door put hers up last weekend, can you believe it? Absolute whirlwind, that one. Put it up before Remembrance, she said! Makes your head spin. Mrs. Henderson’s always ahead of the curve. No, not yet. I’m thinking maybe this year we go for a real one? The smell is just… Christmas, isn’t it? But then all that needle-dropping! That’s the thing, isn't it? Real ones are lovely, but a right pain to clear up. Remember when we had that massive one when you were little? Covered the entire living room floor in needles for weeks! Still, that little Buster, remember how he’d try to eat them? Oh my god, yes! He looked so indignant when you’d take them off him. I miss him, sometimes. Do you think Finn will ever settle down with a cat? He keeps saying he’s not a ‘cat person,’ but… Don’t you go trying to push a cat on him, love! Let him come to it in his own time. Although, a little ginger tom would suit him, wouldn't it? Give him something to fuss over besides spreadsheets. Right, focus. Nail situation. You're still going with the grey polish, aren't you? Yeah, I like it. It's surprisingly versatile. It goes with everything. Plus, it hides chips better. You know I’m a menace with my typing. How are yours? Still the classic red? Always, darling. A girl’s gotta have a signature look, hasn’t she? Though I did nearly go for a lilac the other day. Nearly! But red’s reliable. It says ‘I’m in charge.’ Which is probably a good thing after a twelve-hour shift.

Right, well, we're  in . Officially. Feels a bit…empty, doesn't it? Like a showroom flat, almost. It does. But a showroom flat that's ours, which is a massive upgrade from your mum's spare room. Honestly, I was starting to feel like a permanent guest there. So much floral wallpaper. Don't remind me. Mum still refuses to admit patterned wallpaper is a crime against humanity. Okay, so, priorities. Internet? Absolutely crucial. Otherwise, I’m going to lose all my students. I’ve already got the router box, the one from your mum’s. We just need to call Virgin Media, don’t we? I was looking at their website – there's a deal on at the moment, but it requires a twelve-month contract. Twelve months is fine. Anything longer and I'll be twitching with commitment anxiety. Can you do that tomorrow? I need to wrestle with unpacking these boxes. The sheer volume of David Attenborough documentaries I’ve accumulated is frankly embarrassing. Yeah, I can. And we should probably get a SIM card for my phone too. Signal’s a bit patchy here, apparently. I checked online forums before we moved. Apparently Gillingham training was the best place to be, there's nothing out here. Typical. Right, food. I’m starving. Did you manage to grab anything from the Tesco Metro in Burgess Hill? Just a few basics. Bread, milk, some cheese. I thought we should properly stock up tomorrow. Farmer’s market in Haywards Heath is supposed to be really good. Loads of seasonal stuff. Asparagus is in, isn’t it? It is! Absolutely  must  get some asparagus. Grilled with a little lemon... Heaven. We could also get some strawberries, while they’re good. Thinking about it, we need proper cooking utensils and things. My travel kettle's doing the heavy lifting at the moment and that’s just not sustainable. Definitely. I’ve got a list somewhere... Ah, here it is. Spatula, frying pan – a decent one, not like the flimsy one you inherited from your nan – baking tray, chopping board... Oh, and a proper colander. You were attempting to strain pasta with a mug the other day. A dark day. A very dark day. Look, I’m going to go tackle this box of kitchen stuff. Just a warning - there's a packet of cigarettes in there somewhere. I’m trying to cut down, honest.

Rach! Honestly, it’s so good to see you! You look great! Liv! You too! It's been ages, hasn't it? Peterborough isn't exactly my usual stomping ground, but it was easier to meet you here than trek all the way down south. Tell me about it! I was just thinking about how much has changed since uni. Remember those awful instant noodles we used to live on? Oh god, don’t remind me! I still have nightmares about that questionable chicken flavour. I'm definitely not going back to that life anytime soon. So, what are you having? I’m starving. I'm thinking the halloumi burger. Looks delicious. I've been craving something a bit…substantial. Work's been mad busy lately, you know? Project deadlines looming and the usual office politics. Ugh, sounds stressful. What are you working on at the moment then? Still with the same company? Yeah, still there. I’m co-ordinating a new rollout of their online training platform. Sound boring, I know! But it’s actually quite interesting once you get into the details. Far removed from the days of writing essays on post-structuralism, that's for sure. What about you? Placement still going well? It’s... complicated. I'm with a marketing firm in Birmingham. The people are lovely, but the work is less exciting than I hoped. Mostly creating social media content for plumbing supplies. Plumbing supplies, Liv! Who knew there were so many different types of pipes to photograph? Seriously? That  is  a bit bleak. I’m sorry to hear that. But hey, experience is experience, right? Any chance you’re thinking of moving on after the placement? Honestly, I’m considering it. I’m just not sure what I  want  to do yet. Remember how we used to plan on becoming investigative journalists and exposing government conspiracies? Vaguely! We were ambitious teenagers! My investigative journalism skills are currently being used to find out why the office coffee machine is consistently broken. Though, that  is  a conspiracy in itself. True! Speaking of conspiracies, have you heard anything from your mum lately? She was talking about booking a trip to India, remember? She was! She’s still planning it, I think. She’s been obsessively researching different tour operators. Apparently, Dad is less enthusiastic. He wants to stay put with his prize-winning marrows. Typical Dad. My mum's been relentless about me coming home for Diwali.

Honestly, Liam, you wouldn’t  believe  the conversation I had with Brenda from Finance today. She was asking me if I’d ever seen snow that actually lasted. Like, more than half an hour. Right, Brenda from Finance. I’ve heard tales. The woman who thinks rain is “unpleasant weather.” Did you enlighten her on the wonders of a proper Sunderland blizzard? I tried, pet. I really did. I was painting this picture, like, “Imagine, Liam, the whole world white. The grey skies, the biting wind, piling up drifts against the terraced houses… you can barely see out!” She just looked at me like I was describing some sort of apocalyptic event. "Sounds dreadful, love," she said. "I much prefer a gentle drizzle." Gentle drizzle! You know, it’s funny how people define "weather." Being from Birmingham, our relationship with rain is…complicated. It’s just…there. Always. Not aggressively bad, just… persistent. No dramatic snow piling up either. More of a damp chill that seeps into your bones. Aye, damp chill’s a right proper feeling, isn't it? But different. There’s something… bracing about a good snowfall. A feeling of the whole world holding its breath, you know? Anyway, I was trying to explain that it’s not all bleak up North. There's beauty in it. Proper beauty. It's connected to the people, too. Everything's tighter when you're battling the elements together, that feeling of community. I can imagine. It must be quite a change from Cambridge, then? All these…pedestrians, strolling about, judging your outfit. Don't even get me started on the fashion here. It's a minefield, it is. Everyone's so…conscious. Like they're constantly posing for a lifestyle blog. Back home, you chuck on whatever's clean-ish and head out. Comfort's king. Comfort  is  key. I saw you in that amazing knitted jumper the other day, though. That was quite stylish, actually. I think it was Fair Isle, wasn't it? Aye, my Nana knitted it for me. Proper, cozy thing. Keeps the drafts out, anyway. These Cambridge students are all about minimalist chic, but I'll take a bit of Nana's warmth over a tailored linen shirt any day. So, you surviving the PhD grind? Still drowning in ancient Mesopotamian clay tablets? Drowning is a good word for it. It's fascinating, don’t get me wrong, but the sheer volume of…stuff…to sift through is overwhelming sometimes.

Alright, Gran? Fancy seeing you still stuck in this chair. Thought you’d be out in the garden wrestling the pigeons again. Wrestling pigeons? At my age, lad? My bones wouldn’t thank me. Besides, the pigeons are getting bolder, you know. Practically strut around like they own the place. A bit like those politicians, really. All puffed up with themselves. Aye, tell me about it. Saw something on the news about… well, it was a right mess, wasn't it? All shouting and no listening. Shouting is all they do these days. Used to be, you could listen to a debate, actually hear a proper argument. Now it's just… performative. All for the cameras. Do you know, your Grandpa used to say… Gran, please. Not another story about Grandpa and the miners’ strike, yeah? I've heard that one, like, a million times. Cheeky lad! It's a vital piece of history, Daniel. And it taught a lot about standing up for what you believe in. Something these lot seem to have forgotten. Remember when everyone was going on about ‘levelling up’? Sounded good on paper, didn’t it? It did, yeah. Promised a lot for places like Newcastle. More jobs, better schools… hasn’t really happened, has it? Still feels the same, really. Just a bit more expensive. That's exactly it. Empty promises. All talk and no trousers, as your Grandpa used to say. It's the same story, isn’t it? Every few years, they come along with their fancy promises, get elected, and then… nothing. The ordinary folk, we’re always the ones left picking up the pieces. It’s just… frustrating, isn’t it? Like, what's the point of voting if nothing ever changes? My mates are starting to reckon it’s a waste of time. Don't you ever think like that, Daniel. Never. Giving up on voting is giving up on your voice. Your Grandpa wouldn't have stood for it. He fought for everything he believed in. Coal, unions, fairness… his whole life. It wasn't always pretty, mind. There were hard times. But he kept fighting. So, you reckon we should just keep voting, even if it doesn't make a difference? It makes a difference, Daniel. It might not be a big change overnight, but it's a start. And every little bit helps. You have to hold them accountable.

Right, so, Finnian nearly launched a pea across the table at poor Granny just now. Honestly, the boy! Manners, Finnian, manners! It’s not that hard. It wasn't  at  Granny, Dad. It just… slipped. He's just excited, Liam. He's got that blood moon on his mind. Every kid is talking about it at school. Apparently, they’re having a special astronomy club thing tomorrow night to watch it. A blood moon, ye say? Back in my day, a blood moon meant a bad storm was brewin’. Used to tell the children that at school. Kept them snug in their corners. Though, I suppose that was a bit dramatic of me. Likely! Though, I can see why Finnian's got a bit of an obsession. He’s been reading up on lunar eclipses. He even tried to explain it to me using… well, I'm not sure what he was using, but it involved a lot of marshmallows and a lamp. That sounds about right. He tried to explain the solar system to the cat yesterday. The cat wasn’t impressed. Jasper just slept through it. He finds science boring. He’s got a point, to be fair. Still, it's good he’s taking an interest. Better than glued to that Fortnite thing all day, eh? Speaking of taking an interest, I told him he needs to keep his elbows off the table. Simple. Aye, elbows off the table! That was drilled into us, it was. My mother would have a fit if she saw the state of some of yer dinners! We had to sit up straight, backs against the chairs, and say “please” and “thank you” for every single bite. A bit much, wasn’t it, Mum? I mean, it’s a family meal. It should be relaxing. Relaxing? In my day, meals were a sacred occasion! Everything had to be just so. Proper tablecloth, china plates, silver cutlery… Nowadays, it's plastic plates and everyone's on their phones. Where's the connection? Well, Granny, we're trying to strike a balance. We want him to have good manners, obviously. But we don't want him dreading dinner time. It  is  nice to just gather together, even if it's a bit chaotic. You know, like when you come down to visit. It's lovely. Exactly. And it's brilliant you're able to help out with the wee ones next weekend.

Dreadful weather, isn’t it, Arthur? Makes you want to curl up with a good book and forget the world. Though, frankly, forgetting the world is becoming increasingly difficult these days. This whole Scottish thing… it's got everyone on edge, hasn't it? Aye, it has, Bernard. You’re telling me. Been following it pretty closely. Business-wise, it's a worry, of course. Uncertainty never bodes well for trade. Though, personally… I’m still on the fence, to be honest. Difficult to know what's best, isn't it? Independence...it's a big leap. A monumental one. And the arguments... well, they're spiraling. Did you hear what Alistair Darling said yesterday? Utterly dismissive of their arguments for fiscal autonomy. It's bound to provoke, isn't it? Heard snippets. Don't get me wrong, Darling’s a sharp chap, but he can be a bit… lacking in tact. Remember that debacle with the pubs back in ’98? Bit like that, playing right into their hands. Ah, yes. The Great Pub Tax Uproar. I’d almost forgotten that. Anyway, enough about Scotland and politicians. Did you hear about Penelope's son, David? The one who’s been looking for work for… what feels like an eternity? David? No, not really. What's happened? He had an interview! At that recruitment agency, Sterling & Finch. Apparently, it went rather well, from what Penelope tells me. He was interviewing for a junior marketing position. Jolly good! That’s brilliant news. Long overdue, poor lad. Marketing, eh? Good field to be in these days. He nervous? Apparently, utterly terrified. He kept pacing around the house, reciting facts about market segmentation until he was blue in the face. Penelope nearly had to confiscate his notes. Though, she said he held his own against the interviewer – a rather formidable woman, apparently. Women in recruitment  are  formidable. Remember when I was trying to find someone to overhaul my delivery system? Went through three agencies! Ended up hiring a chap who'd been a butcher. Turned out, logistics were surprisingly similar. You always did have a knack for finding talent in unexpected places, Arthur. Speaking of unexpected places… old Mr. Finchley, from the History department, announced his retirement yesterday. After forty years! Forty years! Goodness me. Forty years! That's a lifetime. Who’s taking his place? They haven’t said yet. Word is, they’re interviewing candidates from all over the country.

Right, so, Luton airport, then? Another three hours of this, yeah? Could murder a pasty right now. Proper Cornish, mind, not that stuff they flog at Greggs. Luton? I thought we were going to Mum's first, Aaron. You said you’d pop over and help her unpack a few boxes. Yeah, yeah, Mum’s. Forgot. Just…long day, innit? All that packing and sorting. You wouldn’t believe the amount of old Christmas decorations we found. Enough to decorate Buckingham Palace, practically. You'll be alright, Aaron. At least the weather’s reasonable. Could have been chucking it down, eh? Remember that trip to Cornwall last summer? Proper biblical it was. Biblical's putting it mildly, lad. I was there. Got stuck in a lane that flooded faster than you could say ‘insurance claim.’ Lost a decent pair of wellies that day. See? Always something. Right, speaking of losing things, have you seen my charger? For my laptop? Pretty sure I packed it. Need it to do the last bits of work for that client. You always lose things, love. Honestly, you’re just like your father. Always misplacing his keys. Did you see what prices are like at Tesco these days? Absolutely extortionate. I ended up getting most of the bits for dinner at Aldi. Much better value, eh, David? Aldi's alright. Bit hit and miss though, isn’t it? Sometimes you get decent cuts of meat, other times… well, let’s just say my sausages last week tasted suspiciously of sawdust. You and your sausages, David! You're always complaining about food. I’d be happy with a simple sandwich right now. Wonder if they sell pasties at the service station up ahead. That’s what I’m talking about! A proper service station pasty! So, tuition fees… still a head-scratcher, aren't they? Mum keeps going on about it. Says I should be looking at a postgraduate loan. Well, you’ve got to think about it, haven’t you? It’s an investment, in a way. But with the way things are going… it’s scary, really. These young people are starting their lives with so much debt. I remember when I was your age, you could get a job straight out of Sixth Form and well, things were different then. It’s not just tuition fees, is it? Rent’s through the roof, energy bills… everything’s going up.

Aye, this road’s a right fiddle, isn't it? Keepin’ a proper eye out for tractors and sheep and all sorts. Nearly took out a scarecrow last week, I did. Proper life-sized thing, stood right in the middle o' the lane. Gave me a proper fright, it did. Scarecrows, eh? Reminds me of when your grandmother and I used to visit Farmer Giles down the road. He had the biggest pumpkins you ever did see. Absolutely enormous. Could’ve sat on 'em, we could. Used to say he put a bit o’ magic in the soil, Giles did. Probably just good manure, mind you. Magic soil? That's a fascinating concept. There's actually research into the microbiome of soil and how it influences plant growth. It's not exactly 'magic,' though. More…complex symbiotic relationships. Specific fungal networks acting as nutrient pathways, that kind of thing. Oh, here we go. Engineer-speak. Just let the man believe in a bit o’ magic, lad. It’s more fun. Grandad’s always got a story about something. Remember when he told us about the sheep that followed him home, practically walked themselves? That's right! Bold as brass, they were. A whole flock, just trottin' along behind me. Folks said I had a way with animals. Probably just smelled my sandwiches. Always had a good lunch, I did. Ham and pickle, my favourite. And a nice cup o' tea. Not that instant stuff, mind. Proper brew. Right, so genetically, sheep are hardwired to follow a lead, especially if there's a potential food source involved. It's a herd instinct, basically. Familiar scents trigger it. So, less about your mysterious charm, more about readily available lunch. See? Always got to take the romance out of everything, don’t you? It's not just about the sandwiches, though. He’s got a good heart, Grandad does. He loves them animals. Gets properly distressed if one's poorly. Distressed? Aye, I do. Remember Old Bess, the ewe with the wonky horn? Lost her lamb. I spent hours sittin’ with her, just talkin’ to her. Tried to cheer her up. Don't know if it helped much, but she seemed to appreciate the company. Animal companionship is proven to reduce stress hormones in humans, which could have a beneficial effect on  them , too. So, in a weird way, you were engaging in a reciprocal therapeutic relationship.

Honestly, Lizzie, this lamb stew is grand. It's exactly how my mother used to make it. Though, she’d have added a bit more Guinness, I reckon. You’re awfully quiet tonight, love. Everything alright? Yeah, everything's fine, Mum. Just...work's been a bit hectic. They've got this new project, archiving old transcripts from a historical society. It's fascinating, but the deadlines are brutal. Mountains of Victorian slang! I’m starting to dream in archaic grammar. Victorian slang, eh? Sounds like a right palaver. Remember when I used to get you lads lecturing me on proper grammar? Seems like yesterday. Though, your mum always did have a knack for spotting a misplaced comma, didn't she, Margaret? Even in my carefully worded planning reports. You were always a bit lax, John! Still, there’s no harm in a bit of casual conversation. Speaking of lacking…has anyone heard from Daniel about Christmas? He said he’d let us know about flights, but... radio silence. I messaged him this morning. He said he’s wrestling with work commitments and said he'll get back to me by the end of the week. He's stressed, poor thing, taking on extra shifts. He always was a slave to deadlines. Just like… well, just like I was, in my own way. Remember all those exam papers I marked? Weekends, holidays…vanished. I rather miss it sometimes, you know. The structure of it all. You miss the marking, Margaret? You always complained about the kids’ atrocious handwriting! And the endless re-marking! Ah, that's just part of it. It wasn't just the marking, John. It was…a purpose. And seeing their faces when they finally understood a difficult concept? That was something. Though, I'm not sure I’d want to go back to dealing with teenagers again! Especially after Mrs. Hawthorne’s class last year. Honestly, the disruptions… Oh, don't remind me. Grandma told me about some of the things that went on. Apparently, there was a whole incident involving glitter and the science lab. Glitter! In the science lab! That's brilliant. Though, knowing Mrs. Hawthorne, she probably blamed young Liam O’Connell. He was always getting into scrapes. He was a lovely boy, Liam. A bit mischievous, granted, but a good heart. I always tried to encourage his creativity, even if it did involve glitter.

Right then. Parent’s evening. It's… a mixed bag, isn't it? Mostly positive, thankfully. Mr. Davies seemed pleased with both of you. Said you were both “engaged” and “demonstrating a good understanding.” Big words for little ears, eh? Engaged? Does that mean I was wiggling my toes a lot? I  was  wiggling my toes under the table in history. It was boring. I was drawing a dragon! Mr. Davies said it was ‘very detailed’! Yes, darling, a very detailed dragon. That’s lovely, sweetheart. But it did distract you a little, didn't it? Mr. Davies did mention… well, he suggested we try to channel that creativity into the tasks a bit more, rather than onto scrap paper. But dragons  are  important! They breathe fire! And they have pointy bits! And wings! Absolutely, dragons are incredibly important. Just maybe… while you’re doing your sums? Which brings me to… the Maths. He seemed a little concerned about your progress with fractions, both of you. Fractions are hard! They’re bits. Like when I eat half a biscuit. That’s a fraction. That’s a very good example, actually! And a very relatable one. But when you’re adding and subtracting fractions, things get trickier. We need to work on it. I was thinking of trying some games this weekend. Maybe that times tables app again? That app is boring. Can we go to the circus instead? I saw an advert! With acrobats and clowns! The circus  does  sound lovely, doesn’t it? We could look into that. But Maths first, fun second. Deal? Now, moving on… World Book Day is next week! Are you both excited? I’m going as Hermione! I have my wand and my books! I’m going to boss everyone around! I'm Captain Underpants! I’ve made my own pants out of a pillowcase! Mummy, look! Oh, that’s brilliant, darling! Very resourceful. Now, let's talk about the characters you’re reading about. Hermione is such a strong character – brave, intelligent… What do you think makes her so compelling, ? She knows  lots  of spells! And she’s really good at potions. And she’s always helpful. Even when Ron is being really annoying. Exactly! And , who’s your favourite character in your Captain Underpants books? George and Harold! Because they’re silly! And they trick Mr. Krupp! They certainly do! So, alright, before I completely lose track of everything...

Right then, so, about Oisin's birthday. Forty kids, you said, Fiona? Forty wee blighters all crammed into the back garden? Jaysus, Mary and Joseph. Yes, he wants forty. He seems to think everyone in Ballincollig is his best friend. And he’s already drawing up elaborate plans for a bouncy castle and face painting. It’s… a lot. Booo-ncy! Booo-ncy! Forty is a grand number, dear. A lovely milestone. Though, I remember when my wee Jamie turned five, we just had a few neighbours and a plate of fairy cakes. Simpler times. Aye, simpler times. Though, I suppose that’s modern parenting for ye. Everything’s gotta be an event these days. Fiona, are you thinking about getting those fairy lights up again? They looked brilliant last year, even if half of them were flickering like mad. I was, yes. And I was thinking of ordering those little pizza things from Mario's? They’re always a hit. Easier than making forty individual pizzas, you know. Though, his Auntie Bridie keeps saying I should bake a cake. A three-tier cake, apparently. Bridie and her cakes! The woman could feed a small army. Don't let her guilt you into it, love. Trust me, forty kids and a three-tier cake is a recipe for disaster. I’d be terrified of it toppling and flattening the lot of them. He’s right, dear. Less is often more. Though, a wee touch of homemade is always lovely. Maybe some cupcakes alongside the pizza? Maybe. Now, I was also thinking about decorations… balloons, streamers… Oisin keeps saying he wants a pirate theme. He’s obsessed. He even talks like a pirate sometimes. Does he now? Like what? "Arrr, me hearty, pass the gravy, please?" Something like that! He'll say things like, "Shiver me timbers, that’s a big sandwich!" It’s just the cutest thing, you know? Keeps me entertained. He’s a wee cracker, that boy. A proper little character. Now, about that rugby match next Saturday… I managed to get us a couple of tickets to the Munster game. Think you'd be up for it, Fiona? Oh, I’d love to! But… the toddler. You know. It's just finding someone reliable to watch him. I spoke to Mary earlier. She said she’d be available. She’s keen to see Oisin, anyways. Rest assured, he’ll be in safe hands.

Right then, you two. Show us what you've got. This "Lexical Labyrinth" thing you were rabbiting on about earlier. Sounds right complicated. Is it like, Scrabble but… worse? Worse? No, no, not worse, El. Just… different. It's designed to be more about the subtle nuances of language. Think of it as Scrabble for linguists, or at least those who appreciate the  idea  of linguists. Essentially, it’s about forming chains of words based on semantic relationships. Not just rhyming, or sharing letters, but a deeper connection. Like, 'autumn' might lead to 'harvest,' which could lead to 'rust,' and so on. The connections can be quite winding, and there’s a points system based on the difficulty of the links, and how far you can stretch a chain. Rust? Autumn to harvest I get, loosely. But rust? That's a stretch, innit? Sounds like you’re just picking words at random. Back home, we'd call that “blind man’s bluff.” It’s not random, El! It's associative. Think of it thematically. Autumn evokes decay, leaves falling... rust is a form of oxidation, a kind of decay. It’s all connected, just in a more poetic, less obvious way. We've got a dictionary programmed in, so it only accepts valid connections. It's quite the clever bit of software I built, truth be told. It's trickier than it sounds. The AI detects connections based on multiple factors – synonymy, antonymy, hyponymy, meronymy… the whole lot. It’s a brilliant exercise for expanding your vocabulary and thinking about the intricate ways words relate to each other. Hyponymy? Sounds like a posh word for “something smaller than something else,” doesn’t it? Like a kitten is a hyponym of a cat. Is that right? I'm guessing I’m gonna need a glossary to play this game. Honestly, you two and yer fancy words. Reminds me of me grandad trying to explain trigonometry. Eyes glazed over within five seconds. It’s a bit more nuanced than that, but you've got the essence of it. It's all about hierarchies of meaning. And yes, there's a glossary. I can print one out. It’s a comprehensive thing, really. Designed for optimal lexical understanding. Don't let El fool you. She’s sharper than she lets on. She picks up on things quicker than she gives herself credit for.

Look at this! Remember this? Freshers’ Week, dressed as giant bananas? Absolute state we were in. Oh, reet, I'd forgotten about that. You’ve got banana mush all over your face! And my hair… honestly, it looked like a bird had built a nest in it. Why did we think that was a good idea? It seemed brilliant at the time! Everyone was doing themed nights. Besides, you were championing it. You were the one insisting we needed to be 'memorable'. Aye, well, we definitely were memorable. Just not in the way I intended, I suppose. Still makes me cringe a bit, though. I’m glad those photos didn't end up on Facebook. Mum would’ve killed us. She probably still would, even now, seeing them! Right, seriously though, I reckon I've just invented the perfect afternoon. Oh, go on then, enlighten me. Sounds dangerous. Right, so... get home, put on a proper comfy jumper – you know, the softest one – and have a solid three-hour nap. No alarms. Just drift off. Three hours? You practically live on campus, you're gonna miss lectures. Aye, but think about it. Three hours of pure, uninterrupted bliss. And then, you wake up, and you listen to The Smiths. All of their albums, in order. Proper wallow in it, know what I mean? You’re a right misery guts sometimes. But yeah, that  does  sound... appealing. I could do with a kip, to be honest. Been burning the candle at both ends with that dissertation. Exactly! And what's everyone else up to? Have you heard from Liam and Chloe? They were supposed to be hitting up that new indie place in town last night. Nah, haven't spoken to them. Chloe posted a story on Instagram, they were having a right laugh though. Loads of people there. I’ll give Liam a message later. You reckon he'll be up for going climbing this weekend? He'd love it! He's been moaning about needing to get out and do something. Just don't let him drag you up that ridiculous slab on the edge of the reservoir again. My palms were sweating for a full hour after that. It was a challenge! You were brilliant though, you got to the top. Easy for you to say, clinging on like a limpet! Anyway… back to my perfect afternoon. Followed by a massive Sunday roast.

Right, so, let’s actually  do  this. I keep getting distracted by the sheer volume of feedback on the Willow Creek application. It’s… overwhelming. Overwhelming is putting it mildly. I swear, half the responses are just people complaining about the colour of the fences. Seriously, Willow Creek needs affordable housing, not a debate about beige versus cream. Exactly! And the council planning committee meeting is next week. I’m terrified. You know they love to drag things out, don’t they? I need to be tight, concise. No room for meandering prose about the benefits of sustainable development. They'll just glaze over. You're brilliant at the sustainable development prose, love. That's your strength. But you’re right, for this, brevity is key. So, structure – you thinking a classic problem/solution approach? Highlight the housing shortage, demonstrate Willow Creek addresses it, then preempt their objections? That’s what I  think . But outlining the objections is the tricky bit. Old Mrs. Higgins is already sharpening her pitchfork over the increased traffic, and Mr. Davies is convinced it will lower his property value. The usual suspects. They’re a predictable bunch. We neutralize them. Traffic – mention the proposed pedestrianisation scheme. Property values – highlight the potential for revitalising the area, bringing in new businesses, footfall...economic stimulus, that sort of thing. It's a bit cynical, but it works. Cynical, but clever. You always do have a knack for spinning things. Okay, so traffic and property... what about the ‘character of the area’ argument? That’s always a big one. People get very attached to their leafy lanes. Right. Character... Okay, we frame it as  enhancing  the character. Willow Creek isn't some monstrous block of flats. It's designed to blend in, use local materials, incorporate green spaces. We emphasize the community aspect – the shared gardens, the potential for local events… Yes, bringing people  into  the area, rather than pushing them out. Good. That’s much better than passively defending against the ‘it’ll ruin everything’ argument. Right, so have you managed to sort out the inventory list for the antique shop? That’s been hanging over me all day. Almost. It's proving to be more tedious than I anticipated. Honestly, cataloguing a lifetime of accumulated knick-knacks is a truly Herculean task. I've got the furniture mostly down, just trying to wrangle a valuation for all the… well,  stuff .

Honestly, this Earl Grey tastes like dishwater today. Did you change brands, Liv? Nope, same one. Maybe you're just having one of  those  days, Rach. What's got your knickers in a twist? Everything! Work was a nightmare. The Peterson project is spiralling, and Gareth keeps asking me to reschedule meetings when he  knows  I've got a million other things on. It’s like he thinks time just vanishes for everyone else. Gareth's always been like that, hasn't he? Remember in sixth form when he’d conveniently forget homework deadlines, then blame the printer? Oh god, don't remind me! He was such a little… prince. Still is, really. And then Sarah from accounts sent me a passive-aggressive email about the coffee machine. As if  I  hoard the good beans! People are just bizarre, aren’t they? Speaking of bizarre, have you seen Mrs. Henderson's garden lately? It’s gone completely wild. Like a jungle. I swear she’s giving up. No! Really? I thought she was so meticulous about it. Remember when she had a full-blown argument with Mr. Davies over his rose bush encroaching on her boundary? I know! It was epic. The shouting, the pointing... the trowel! Honestly, I thought someone was going to call the police. Anyway, are you hungry? I'm making pancakes. Pancakes sound amazing. Actually, I was thinking… remember Sarah and Liam from school? Liam, the footballer? Vaguely. Didn’t he leave before A-levels? Moved to Bournemouth, didn't he? He did. Apparently, he’s back in town for a few weeks. I saw him at The Crown last Friday. He's… well, he’s got a bit of a dad bod now, but still, decent looking. Oh really? And? Did you exchange pleasantries? Just a quick "hello." He looked… preoccupied. Mentioned he was seeing some old mates. But still... it was nice to see a familiar face. It just made me think about how everyone's lives have changed, you know? Like, Sarah's married with two kids, Liam's back in town... and we're here, battling Gareth and rogue rose bushes. True. Life’s a funny old thing. Though, I'm not complaining  too  much. At least we’ve got pancakes. Did you see that new film, “Across the Stars”? Everyone’s raving about it. No, I haven’t! Is it good? I’m in the mood for something... escapist.

Dead set on this telly, innit? Proper binge-watching material. This advert though… honestly, it's ridiculous. Selling teeth whitening strips like they’re the answer to world peace. It's clever, though, isn't it? It’s tapping into everyone's insecurities. Makes you feel like you  need  to buy it. The psychology behind advertising is fascinating, really. It’s almost like a tiny, manipulative form of NLP. NLP? Blimey, using your fancy brain already, are ya? I just see it as a load of rubbish trying to get me to part with me money. Speaking of which, I need to sort out a car boot sale, don’t I? Got loads of stuff piled up in the spare room. You reckon anyone'd want me old Liverpool shirt? Definitely. Especially if it's from a decent season. But seriously, NLP - Neuro-Linguistic Programming. It’s about understanding how people think and communicate, and how to influence that. Advertising uses it all the time. Want to chat about it properly later? I’ve been reading a paper on how they use it with emotional appeals. Emotional appeals, eh? So, exploiting our feelings to sell us stuff. Makes sense, doesn’t it? Like, those chocolate adverts at Christmas. Pure emotional blackmail. Right, car boot sale. I'll have a proper clear-out. Thinking of getting rid of me old mobile phone too. It's older than you, it is! It probably is. Though I bet that old brick can still access Facebook. Remember Sarah saying she saw some dodgy stuff being shared on there related to the local crime rates? Her cousin works for the police, apparently. It’s getting pretty worrying, isn't it? All those break-ins around here. Aye, grim, innit? Need to get a security camera sorted. Should’ve done it ages ago. It’s just… everything feels like a chore these days. Like, I promised I'd dust the living room today, didn’t I? And sort the laundry... Everything's piling up. Speaking of chores, you making that chicken and veg stir-fry tonight? Been trying to cut down on takeaways. Dieting’s a right nightmare. Yes, definitely. It’s healthier and cheaper. And I have some lovely lemon and ginger dressing. It's actually surprisingly good for curbing cravings. I’ve been reading about the gut-brain connection and how that can affect our eating habits.

Honestly, this weather is doing my head in. One minute it’s glorious sunshine, the next it's spitting rain. Can’t plan anything, can you? Tell me about it! Been trying to get a round of golf in all week. Kept getting rained off. Typical Birmingham weather, innit? Though, to be fair, it IS nice to be indoors with you lot. Speaking of being indoors… have you guys tried that new Duolingo feature? It’s got these little stories now, and it’s actually quite engaging. Much better than just repeating phrases. Duolingo? Really, Liam? That's what you're excited about? You work for the BBC! You're surrounded by actual writers and stories. Hey! It's a good way to chill out after a long day of wrangling producers and chasing deadlines. Plus, I’m trying to brush up on my Spanish for that trip I’m planning. Wrangling producers! Sounds about right. I had a right nightmare yesterday with a field recording. The sheep kept baaing over the interview! Honestly, you wouldn’t believe it. Oh, Emily, you're a trooper. I remember when you were trying to get those interviews with the Yorkshire pudding champion. That was a saga! Yorkshire pudding champion? Seriously? There's a championship for  that ? Absolutely. It’s fierce competition, let me tell you. The gravy needs to be  perfect . Anyway, I was thinking, has anyone been to that new Indian place, ‘Spice Merchant’ over on Broad Street? Heard it’s incredible. I went last weekend! It was fantastic. The butter chicken was unreal, and their naan bread… forget about it. A little pricey, though. Pricey is always the problem, isn't it? I'm trying to save for a deposit on a house, and it feels utterly impossible. Every time I think I’m making progress, the interest rates go up or the estate agent jacks up the price. Same here, actually. The housing market is mental. We’ve been looking in Moseley, but it’s become ridiculous. Thought we'd maybe try further out, towards Sutton Coldfield. Sutton Coldfield’s got its charms. Good schools, decent parks… though the commute into the city can be a killer. I commute from Solihull, and even that’s stressful sometimes. Speaking of stressful, have you all seen the new film, ‘Across the Sea’? Heard it’s brilliant. Apparently, the cinematography is stunning. I’m trying to get tickets for Friday.

It’s lovely to have you all here. It's been far too long since we've all been together properly. Honestly, these monthly gatherings at ANON’s place are the highlight of my week. Remember how daunting it was moving here in '68? So many new faces, everything different. Daunting, yes, but invigorating too! Ramsgate was… well, Ramsgate. A bit too quiet for a young man with ambitions. The interview for the teaching post here was a disaster, actually. I was so nervous, I tripped over the headmaster’s foot! Nearly took him down with me. He did have a marvelous sense of humour though, thankfully. A disaster, eh? Sounds familiar. When I first arrived, looking for digs, I ended up in a house with a woman who kept a collection of taxidermied squirrels wearing tiny hats. Tiny hats! I lasted exactly one night. Taxidermied squirrels. My dear fellow, you have a flair for the dramatic, don't you? My own house hunt back then was less eccentric, though considerably more stressful. I remember coming for the interview – this was 1966, wasn’t it? - and the sheer scale of the waiting room at the practice was overwhelming. Row upon row of perfectly polite, equally terrified applicants. Yes, 66! I recall it vividly. Houses were…challenging to find, weren’t they? I ended up in a converted stable for nearly two years. Damp as a fish, but the rent was manageable. I remember perpetually having to wipe down the windows. Absolutely. We were incredibly lucky to find that little cottage on Elm Street. Needed a complete overhaul, of course. The kitchen was basically a cupboard, but it had a garden! And it was within walking distance of the school. Divine. Do you remember the interest rates back then? Astronomical. We practically mortgaged our futures just to buy it. Elm Street! I think I remember walking past. The squirrels' owner lived just a few houses down. It’s remarkable how much the area has changed. Remember when this whole area felt on the periphery of everything? Everything seemed to be centred around the town square. Indeed. Though I'd argue the dentist's surgery was the true centre. People prioritize their teeth, you know. Honestly, those were simpler times, weren't they? Though dentistry then… well, let's just say it didn't involve nearly as much technology as it does now.

Oh, do have another biscuit, dear. They’re shortbread, made fresh this morning. Lovely and crumbly, aren’t they? Bit like a good Somerset landscape, really – layered and ever-changing. Thank you, Marion. They are delicious, truly. And I quite agree about the landscapes. Reminds me a bit of the Blue Mountains back home, although the light’s a bit different, of course. Everything feels…so much more  contained  here. Not in a bad way, mind you. Just… settled. Settled's a good word for it. Taunton’s always been settled. Not a great deal happens here, you know. Can be a blessing and a curse, I reckon. You said you were a speech and language therapist? That’s fascinating. Did you enjoy it? I can’t imagine a more rewarding profession, really. I did, immensely. It was… demanding, certainly, particularly at the start of my career, but seeing a child finally say their first words, or an adult finding their voice again after a stroke... it was profoundly satisfying. Bit heartbreaking at times too, you know? But more rewarding than heartbreaking. What about you, Marion? An artist and antique dealer? A most unusual combination! Well, the art came first, naturally. Always had a knack for it, I did. My mother, bless her heart, thought I’d be a proper artist, a grand one! Sent me off to art school in Bristol, even. But then, you know how it is, life has a way of nudging you down different paths. The antiques rather crept in, really. Started with a few bits and bobs in the gallery, you see, to supplement the art sales. Then it just… grew. Now, the gallery proper is more antiques than art, truth be told. Sometimes things just find their own momentum, don’t they? It's lovely that you've been able to combine your passions, even if the balance shifted. Did you paint landscapes mostly? Somerset landscapes, almost exclusively. The light… it just called to me, didn't it? The rolling hills, the ancient stone walls, the hazy sunsets… I tried other things, of course, portraits mostly during my art school years. Dreadful they were, if I’m honest. Captured none of the spirit. Give me a field of buttercups any day. Reminds me of my childhood, running through the fields near my Nan’s farm. She lived just outside of Wells, on the edge of the levels.

Right, so, parsnips are done. Carrots next. Honestly, this roast dinner is gonna be epic. You reckon Liam will eat all that gravy? He’s a gravy fiend, that one. Liam will inhale the entire vat, yeah. He practically lives for gravy. And don’t even get me started on the Yorkshire puddings. Did you remember to get the extra-large muffin tin? Last Christmas, they were flatter than pancakes. A national tragedy, honestly. Yeah, got the tin. Massive one. Should produce about a dozen proper, puffy puddings. I’m thinking cranberry sauce this year, too. Not that weird jelly stuff, proper homemade. Bit of orange zest, some port… what do you reckon? Ooh, that sounds lovely! Definitely homemade. The shop-bought stuff is just… sad. You know, I've been thinking about getting a little tattoo. A tattoo? Seriously? You? You're the most… sensible one of us. What would you even get? I don’t know yet! Something small, maybe. A little sprig of rosemary? Floral thing. Something to remind me of… well, of baking, I suppose. It feels a bit cliché, I know, but... Cliché can be good. It’s you, innit? A little sprig of rosemary? Sounds dead nice, actually. Where were you thinking of going? Not some dodgy bloke in a back alley, eh? No, no! A proper studio. I’ve been looking at 'Ink & Bloom' down in Shoreditch. They do really delicate line work. It’s just… a thought. What about you? Any wild tattoo plans brewing? You and your philosophy degree; I reckon you’re plotting something deep and meaningful. Nah, nothing that intense. Thinking about a tiny little lion, maybe, on my wrist. Bit of a throwback to primary school. Used to draw lions all the time. Stupid, I know. Not stupid at all! It's a nice little memory. Right, dough’s proving nicely. Think Chloe'll be here soon? I messaged her about the Christmas decorations. Yeah, she said she’d be round around six. Honestly, I'm dreading the decorations. Last year, she insisted on putting up those ridiculous inflatable reindeer. They looked like they were about to attack the house. That'll be her! Right, put the kettle on, yeah? We can offer her a cuppa while we finish prepping. Sorry I'm late! Traffic was a nightmare. Honestly, London at this time of year...ugh. Right, I brought the baubles!

Blimey, Mum, this is nice, innit? Just… driving. No deadlines looming, no readings piling up. Feels almost… luxurious. It is, darling. You deserve a bit of luxurious. All that thesis work must have taken its toll. You look tired, actually. Are you sleeping alright? Yeah, mostly. Just the usual student sleep patterns, you know? Feast or famine. Right now, it’s famine. I’m really hoping to have a solid draft done by Christmas, though. Professor Davies seems… cautiously optimistic. Cautiously optimistic is good, isn’t it? Better than pessimistic, at least. What’s he saying specifically? About the methodology, was it? You were worried about that, weren’t you? Yeah, that's it. He thinks my approach to analyzing the Keats letters is… unconventional. But, he conceded that if I can pull it off, it’ll be a fresh perspective. The pressure's on, though. It's a bit terrifying, to be honest. Sweetheart, you've always been one for a bit of a challenge. Remember that time you decided to learn the ukulele in a week? You didn’t become a virtuoso, but the effort was admirable. This is similar, really. You're tackling something complex, putting your own stamp on it. That's what university’s for. True. It’s just... everyone else seems so on top of things. All my mates are talking about internships and graduate schemes and, like, actual plans. I’m still just trying to figure out if I can even finish my bloody thesis. Don't compare yourself to others, Liam. Seriously. Their paths aren't your path. Besides, internships and schemes? Pah! You’d be bored stiff in a corporate job. You need something that sparks your intellect, something with… soul. Like your writing. That's what I keep telling myself. But then I think about, you know, practicalities. Like, where am I going to live after this? Rent in London is absolutely mental. We talked about this. You could stay here a bit longer, you know. Just until you get your feet under you. It’s not ideal, I know, with me rattling around in this place on my own, but… Mum, don't. I wouldn’t want to be a burden. It's a big house for one person. Maybe I should look at those new developments just outside the city? There’s a couple of shared ownership schemes that seem… manageable.

Honestly, I’m still a bit dizzy. All those talks today! Professor Davies’ on historical linguistics was brilliant, but my brain feels like overspilled custard. Did you manage to catch any interesting ones? I did! The presentation on legal precedents in Roman law was… dense. Very dense. But fascinating. I was trying to follow along, but I kept drifting off and thinking about the dig in Somerset I read about – apparently they unearthed a whole Roman villa! It made me wonder about the everyday lives of people back then, you know? Not just the emperors and senators. Absolutely! That’s what draws me to language research, actually. It's not just about grammar and syntax. It's a window into culture, into how people  thought  and  felt  centuries ago. You can trace migrations, trade routes, societal shifts, just from how language evolves. Have you ever travelled much, connected to, say, archaeology? A little. I went to Italy a few years back - Rome, Florence, Pompeii. Pompeii was incredible, wasn’t it? The sheer scale of preservation… you could practically feel the panic. But nothing really active – just observing the remnants. What about you? I tried to get involved in a dig in rural China a while back, studying local dialects, practically prehistoric ones. It fell through, unfortunately. Logistics were a nightmare. Being there, though, even briefly, really sparked something - those isolated villages clinging to languages largely unchanged for centuries… it’s breathtaking. Did you know some of their dialects are mutually unintelligible with Mandarin even? Remarkable, truly. The preservation of older linguistic forms in geographically isolated areas is something I’ve devoted a considerable portion of my career to. Shropshire, where I hail from, holds a surprising number of archaic words still in common usage. Hardly the stuff of high academia, mind you, but fascinating nonetheless. Oh, really? I'd love to hear about that. I’m Eleanor, by the way. Research Co-ordinator for the department. I’m Chloe, Administrator for the same department. And you are…? Arthur Finch. Retired lecturer from the History department. Oswestry, originally. Pleased to meet you both. It's wonderful to see so many bright, engaged faces at Alumni Day. These events are invaluable, aren't they? Reminds you why you dedicated your life to the pursuit of knowledge. Absolutely. It's lovely to connect with people with such a wide range of interests. You mentioned Shropshire, Professor Finch?

Right, so, another week done. Honestly, uni's been a right slog this past few days. Professor Davies is having a field day with postmodernism. Makes my head spin, proper does. Postmodernism, eh? Sounds intense. At least my sourdough starter is behaving itself. That’s excitement enough for me this week. Had a proper queue down the street yesterday. Someone put a picture of my lemon drizzle cake on TikTok, can you believe? TikTok? Seriously? That's how you get business now? My Instagram’s practically a ghost town. Maybe I should outsource my social media. Though I can barely work the coffee machine some days, never mind TikTok trends. Lemon drizzle cake going viral? That’s brilliant, Chloe! It’s mad how quickly things take off. I’ve been chasing a viral moment for years with my production stuff, hasn’t happened yet. Keeps you on your toes, though, doesn't it? Seeing something completely random blow up. It’s mental, innit? Shows you don’t need a degree or fancy qualifications to make a living these days. Honestly, sometimes I wonder if all this studying is even worth it. My cousin, Liam, he dropped out after a year, started fixing bikes. He's earning more than me and having a better time, I reckon. Don't say that, Finn! You're brilliant. And your degree  will  be useful. But I see your point. There’s definitely a shift happening. People are finding different routes. It’s not all about getting a ‘good’ degree anymore. I mean, I’ve got a degree in History, but I’m kneading dough most days. Happy dough kneading, though! Exactly! Like me. Sixth form, got a bit fed up of being told what to do, opened the café. It’s hard work, don’t get me wrong. Long hours, stress… but it’s  mine . And I’m making a decent cup of coffee, that’s something. Though finding good staff… that’s a whole other nightmare. It is, isn’t it? The talent pool seems pretty shallow sometimes. I’m struggling to find an assistant editor who isn’t terrified of Premiere Pro. It worries me, the skills gap. And young people these days... I swear, they’re all obsessed with screen time. It's tricky finding someone with a genuine passion for  making  things, not just consuming them. You know, my younger brother, Charlie, he’s really struggling in school.

Honestly, David, this whole NHS thing is just… exhausting. I spent nearly an hour on hold this morning trying to get Mum an appointment with the rheumatologist. An  hour , David! And then they told me she needs to be referred by her GP again, even though she was already seeing one! Tell me about it. It’s a nightmare. I was chatting to Sarah from the History department the other day, and she was saying her daughter's been waiting six months for orthodontic treatment. Six months! It’s absolutely scandalous. It is. And it's not just appointments. It's the general mood, isn't it? The nurses at Mum's care home are constantly stressed, understaffed, and demoralised. They’re doing an incredible job, but you can see the strain. I offered to buy the night nurse a cup of tea and a biscuit yesterday, just to… I don’t know, show a bit of appreciation. She looked like she was about to cry. It's the legacy of years of austerity, isn't it? Politicians making promises they can’t keep, and then slashing budgets when they’re in power. And don’t even get me started on this new Health Secretary. He seems to think just  talking  about efficiency improvements will solve the problem. It's performative nonsense. Exactly! It's all rhetoric. And the waiting lists are just exploding. I'm worried about Mum, obviously, but even for minor things, it’s ridiculous. I bumped my knee last week, just a little niggle, but I’m thinking twice about even bothering to get it checked. What’s the point if I’ll just be put on a waiting list for another two months? It's a vicious cycle, isn’t it? People avoid seeking care because of the delays, then conditions worsen, require more intensive treatment, and the whole system ends up even more overloaded. It’s utterly absurd. Though, on a slightly less depressing note, did you manage to sort out that inheritance tax issue with the solicitor? Don't even. It’s a complete mess. Apparently, there's some obscure clause in Great Aunt Mildred's will about antique porcelain, and it's causing all sorts of complications. The solicitor is billing us by the hour, naturally. I swear, I'm starting to regret inheriting anything. Well, Mildred was always a peculiar woman. Remember her collection of miniature spoons?

Honestly, this quiche is absolutely lovely, Anne. You’ve really outdone yourself this time. Much better than that shop-bought one we had last month, remember? Tasted like cardboard. Oh, Mum, you always say that! It wasn't  that  bad. Though, I am pleased you like this one. It's a new recipe I found online, actually. Apparently, a tiny bit of nutmeg makes all the difference. Nutmeg, eh? Fancy that. Never thought of nutmeg in quiche. My Elsie used to put a bit of cheddar in hers, always said it gave it a bit of a kick. She was a woman who liked a bit of a kick. Elsie was a force of nature, Arthur. Remember when she tried to teach us all how to Morris dance? That was a disaster. I nearly knocked over Mrs. Higgins’ prize-winning begonias. I’ve only heard about the Morris dancing! You and Aunt Elsie… that must have been something to witness. Dad told me you both ended up tangled in the maypole ribbons. Tangled is putting it mildly! We looked like a flock of startled pigeons. But Elsie, she just laughed it off. Said it was good exercise. She was always up for a laugh, our Elsie. By the way, did you see that Leicester game yesterday, Anne? Absolute shambles, it was. Oh, I didn't. I was trying to get through a rather dense paper on quantum entanglement for work. Not exactly the most thrilling Saturday afternoon. My boss is convinced I need to develop some science communication videos, aimed at the general public. Can you imagine? Me, explaining quantum physics! Good heavens! Quantum whatsit? It all sounds terribly complicated, dear. Though, I suppose it’s important to make science accessible, isn’t it? Back in my day, we struggled with the periodic table. Remember Mr. Peterson's chemistry class? The smell of sulphur still haunts me. Peterson… that was a character. Tried to teach us Bunsen burners one minute and reciting poetry the next. Never knew what to expect! Still, he got us through our exams. You know, speaking of the past, I came across some old photos the other day. Remember that holiday we took to Skegness in '78? The wind nearly blew us all into the sea! Oh my goodness, Skegness! Dad has a picture of me covered in sand, crying because I lost my ice cream. It’s hilarious now.

Right then, so Liam, you were tellin’ us about this…Cyber Knights, was it? Sounds a bit ferocious for a lad your age. Yeah, Cyber Knights. It’s a strategy game, Dad. It’s not  ferocious , it’s… tactical. You gotta build up your base and train your units and…well, you attack other players’ bases. It's brilliant. Sounds rather intense. Is it very…complicated? I always got lost in those sorts of games. Remember Solitaire, David? That was about the limit of my gaming skills. Solitaire? Ah, your golden days, Sarah. This is a wee bit more involved than draggin’ cards around. Liam’s been practically livin’ on that screen these past few weeks. It's not that bad! I just… I'm trying to climb the leaderboard. There’s this one player, ‘IronCladDestroyer,’ he's always beating me. It's frustrating! Oh, dear. A nemesis? Sounds dramatic. Well, you mustn’t let him get to you. It’s just a game, love. She's right, Liam. Don't be gettin' yourself all worked up over pixels. Besides, look at little Finnigan over there. He hasn't a care in the world about leaderboards or "IronCladDestroyers." Careful, Finn! You're a menace to the furniture! Honestly, watching him play with those toys is more entertaining than any computer game. He created a whole city out of them! It’s all roads and houses and… a suspiciously shaped dinosaur playing the role of the mayor. A dinosaur mayor? That’s not very strategic. Everything's strategic to a toddler, Sarah. They're plottin' world domination one soft block at a time. Remember when he tried to use your handbag as a hat? Don’t remind me. It took me an hour to get the sequins off. He truly believes he’s a regal being, that one. So, Dad, how about you try playing Cyber Knights with me? You might actually be a good strategist, you know? You’re always good at figurin’ things out. Me, playin’ your fancy computer game? I’d be lost within five minutes, I reckon. I’m better at coaxin’ Finnigan into nappin’ time than I am at buildin’ virtual bases. Speaking of which, the spuds are nearly ready. Anyone fancy a bit of mash with their dinner? Oh, mash sounds lovely. Although, Finnigan might try to build a tower out of it, knowing him.

Cor, this is reet nice, innit? Proper warm. An’ ANON's got a good fire goin’. Much better than that frosty drive over. Nearly froze me fingers off, I did. You always say that, Arthur. Every Christmas, every visit, "nearly froze me fingers off." It’s become your catchphrase! The drive wasn't  that  bad. Just a little chilly. And Harrow was a lot colder this year, you know. Less wind, but a deeper chill. You two are a wonder. A chilly drive, apparently, is a life-threatening ordeal in Arthur's world. I thought the M6 was the real challenge today, though. Absolute chaos. Took me nearly an hour longer than anticipated. Did anyone see that lorry nearly clip the central reservation? Oh my god, no! Were you alright, Mr. Davies? That sounds terrifying! All part of the fun, pet. Just had to swerve a bit. Reminded me of that time I was stuck behind a horse box for ages on the A38. Absolute nightmare. Ended up missing the first act of Romeo and Juliet. The kids were furious. Horses, eh? Remember old Farmer Giles, down Costessey way? Had a prize-winning shire, he did. Big ol’ beast, it was. Used to give the little 'uns rides. Proper sturdy. My sister, bless 'er, nearly fell off once. Gave 'er a fright, she did. My nan used to tell me stories about Farmer Giles! She said he could talk to the horses. Do you think that’s true, Grandpa Arthur? Wouldn’t put it past 'im, to be honest. He was a funny one, that Giles. Always had a smile on 'is face. You know, speaking of funny, I heard a good one the other day… Oh here we go. Another one of Arthur’s jokes. Please tell us, Arthur. It'll be something about a chicken and a farmer, I'm sure. Now, now, Margaret, don’t be like that. This one’s different, I promise. What's brown and sticky? Eww, I don’t want to know! Come on, Arthur, don’t leave us hanging. A stick! Get it? A stick! Oh, Arthur! Classic. Absolutely classic. Never change. That was…okay. It  was  a bit silly! Alright, alright, settle down! I've been thinking about Christmas dinner. Are we doing turkey again this year, ANON? Or are we branching out? Last year's goose was a bit…dry.

Right then, who fancies a bit of apple crumble later? Got a load of Cox's apples from Mr. Henderson down the lane – proper beauties they were. Best I've had all year, honestly. Sounds lovely, love. You’re always making the best crumble. Beats anything you can get in the shops, that’s for sure. Just finished reading about that debacle at the council meeting. Honestly, you wouldn't believe the arguments they were having about the new playground equipment. Apple crumble sounds amazing! I'm starving. Is there any chance of a sneaky slice now? Or at least some of those shortbread biscuits you got? You’re always hungry, aren't you, poppet? Not until it's properly baked, I'm afraid. Shortbread, though? Yes, there's a tin. Help yourself. It's a bit of a lifesaver when I'm on a particularly hectic shift at the hospital, you know. Just something quick and comforting. Speaking of shifts, how are things at St. Jude's, Sarah? Still running like a well-oiled machine, I presume? They said it was busy down there. Busy is an understatement, John. We're stretched thin. That new flu strain is really hitting people, and half the nurses are off sick themselves. It's absolutely relentless. I had a young lad in last night, barely twenty, struggling to breathe. It’s heartbreaking, seeing young people so poorly. Oh, that sounds awful. You're amazing, Auntie Sarah. Truly. It must be so exhausting. Are you sleeping alright? I get by. Earl Grey tea and a good book usually do the trick, though I'm probably brewing myself into a twitching mess. What about you, Liv? Still wrestling with those tricky campaign slogans? Surprisingly, yes! It’s harder than it looks, crafting something that's both catchy and, you know, actually  good . This client wants something... 'aspirational' and 'disruptive'. Which, let's be honest, just sounds like marketing jargon. Honestly, sometimes I feel like I'm writing poetry for robots. Aspirational and disruptive. Sounds like my descriptions of the council on a bad day. Speaking of disruptive, did you hear about Brenda from accounts? Apparently, she's booked a week-long pottery course in Tuscany! Fancy that. Brenda? Pottery in Tuscany! Good for her. She needs a proper holiday. She looks perpetually stressed. I keep telling her, you need to look after yourself, love. We all do.

Cor blimey, this draught’s a right nipper, innit? Feels like November already, even tho’ it’s barely September. Could do with a bit more of that paraffin heater goin’, could. Though Doreen’ll have a blue on, she will, about the fumes. Winston, darling, stop trying to steal Uncle Arthur’s biscuit. Honestly, you’d eat the furniture if I let you. Arthur, you're spoiling him. And you’re right about the draught. I’ve put another blanket on the radiator. It’s not much, I know, but it helps a bit. Doreen’s worried about the cost of the electricity, you see. You know, from a business perspective, investing in proper double glazing would pay for itself in energy savings within a few years. A good finance package, a reputable firm… it's not just about comfort, it’s about fiscal responsibility. Reminds me of when I was trying to persuade my board to modernise the warehouse… they resisted at first, of course. Always do. Oh, here we go. Business Arthur applying his mind to domestic heating. Trying to convince Doreen of a five-figure investment, are we? Good luck with that. She’s got a mind of her own, that one. Speaking of minds, did you see Big Brother last night? Honestly, the drama! You wouldn't believe the screaming... reminds me of some staff meetings I've been in, frankly. Big Brother? Never did get the hang of that. All that shoutin’ and carryin’ on. Give me a bit of cricket any day. Better for the ears, less stress. Doreen’s mad for it, though. Says it's a proper insight into human nature. I reckon it’s just a load of people trying to wind each other up. I enjoy it, Arthur. A bit of mindless entertainment. Though some of the behaviour  is  quite shocking. It's bringing out the worst in people, isn't it? It does make you think about how you treat people around you. It's an artificially stressful environment designed to elicit reactions. Interesting sociological study, really. Though I can’t say I’d spend my evenings watching it. Building a successful business is stressful enough, thank you very much. Though, speaking of stress… how is the Reverend's wife dealing with that… situation? You know, the one with the flower arranging club treasurer? Don’t. Just don’t go there, Arthur.

Right, nearly there then. Smells better than it looks, doesn't it? It's a bit…rustic, I'll admit. Gran's recipe for Lancashire hotpot, mind. Always makes the house smell like Sunday afternoons at her place. It smells amazing, honestly! Don’t worry about the aesthetics. My cooking skills peak at boiling pasta, so you’re already winning. Did you manage to find those specific potatoes Gran used to rave about? The really floury ones? Aye, got 'em. Took three different shops, though! The little old greengrocer in the market had a proper moan about folks wanting heritage varieties. Said nobody buys 'em anymore, just the perfectly uniform Maris Pipers. Honestly, some people! Tell me about it. Everything’s about convenience these days. Speaking of convenience, did you see the trailer for that new Wes Anderson film?  Asteroid City ? Looks absolutely gorgeous. Nah, not yet. Is it any good? I'm a bit wary of Wes Anderson, to be honest. All that symmetry and pastels can be a bit much for a lass like me. Give me a good, gritty drama any day. Like  The Banshees of Inisherin . Now  that  was something, wasn't it? Proper bleak. It was brilliant, completely gut-wrenching. But  Asteroid City  looks lighter, supposedly. Sort of nostalgic, whimsical…lots of bright colours and quirky characters. I reckon you’d secretly love it. It's got Jason Schwartzman and Scarlett Johansson, which is always a good sign. Hmmm, Jason Schwartzman…I did fancy him in  Rushmore . Right, you’ve convinced me. Put it on after we've scoffed this lot, yeah? Unless you’ve suddenly got something else planned? Nope, just lounging about. My mum keeps sending me snippets about the family Christmas plans. Apparently, Uncle Barry is insisting on doing the Christmas pudding  again . Oh, God. Barry and his Christmas puddings are a national crisis. Remember last year? He set the kitchen on fire with brandy! How could I forget? We all had to stand outside in our onesies, watching the fire brigade hose down the house. Mum's still furious he used her favourite Le Creuset casserole dish to flambé it. He’s a legend, that one. A certifiable, pudding-related legend. Is Auntie Carol still trying to convince everyone to have a ‘sustainable Christmas’? Remember the hemp wrapping paper and the ethically sourced reindeer moss? Oh, absolutely. She’s already sent a lengthy email detailing the importance of avoiding glitter.

Honestly, Thomas, I’m fair stressed about this Scottish referendum. It’s a right carry-on, isn’t it? All that shouting on the telly. Makes a body want to hide under the duvet. It’s just politics, Auntie Maggie. People arguing. Happens all the time. It's all over TikTok too, loads of opinions. Politics ain’t just arguing, love. This is about the whole country changing, potentially. Think about it! A separate Scotland. We’re talking about centuries of history, Thomas. Centuries! And now seemingly a vote every generation. But people in Scotland seem to want it, don’t they? The polls, anyway. Polls! Don't you put much stock in polls. They shift like the wind. Remember Brexit? Everyone was saying one thing, then… well, you know what happened. This feels a bit like that, too. A lot of noise, a lot of emotion. Yeah, but Brexit was complicated. This seems simpler. They either stay or they go. Simpler on the surface, perhaps. But the ripple effects… where do you think the money’s all going to come from? What about the oil revenues? And the borders, Thomas! Who's controlling them? What about trade? All those logistical nightmares. They keep talkin’ about a ‘special relationship’ with the rest of the UK, but everything’s a negotiation, isn’t it? A right squabble. They say they can make more money by trading with Europe. Aye, but have you seen the bureaucracy involved in European trade? It’s enough to give you a headache just thinking about it. My cousin Brenda, she owned a little bakery over in Hull, for years, and trying to export her Yorkshire puddings to France… forget about it! Forms, tariffs, regulations… it nearly bankrupted her. And those were just puddings. Imagine the complexity of everything else. Did she ever… you know… manage to? No, love. She gave it up. Said it wasn’t worth the bother. And she was a grafter, your cousin Brenda. Never backed down from anything. It just shows you, even with the best intentions, things can go wrong. And independence… that's a bigger gamble than trying to get Yorkshire puddings across the Channel. My history teacher says it’s about more than just money, though. It's about identity. Being Scottish, wanting to control their own destiny. I understand that, Thomas, I truly do. Feeling of belongin', wanting to shape your own future.

Honestly, look at 'em. Proper meltin' pots, aren’t they? Soundin' like they've swallowed a dictionary, all of 'em. You're saying that about Jeremy Kyle guests, love? Give them a break, they're usually having a right rough time. Though, I will admit, some of the accents are something else. Did you hear that lass with the voice like she’s permanently got a cold? It’s the Midlands, innit? They do that sort of flattened vowels. Makes everything sound a bit… subdued. Like they’re holdin' somethin' back, the poor loves. Subdued? You're kiddin'! It's just lazy speakin'! Especially with the elision. "Gonna" instead of "going to." "Wanna" instead of "want to." Drives me mad, it does. Like they can’t be bothered to say the whole word. Me mum’d have had a right go if I talked like that. Aye, exactly! Proper sloppy. Remember Mrs. Grimshaw in Year 7? She used to go on about it. Said it was “detractin’ from the beauty of the Queen’s English.” Honestly, though, nobody listened to her. See that bloke, that one arguin’ about DNA? He’s practically swallowin’ his words. Trying to sound all serious, but it just comes across as mumbly. And he’s clearly from somewhere up North, like me. But it’s not a proper Yorkshire accent, is it?
